speechtext: MACLEAN (East York) moved for leave to Introduce Bill (No. 173) to change the name of Hudson's Bay.

maintopic: TO CHANGE THE NAME OF HUDSON'S BAY.
speechtext:
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentlemen will hear me. I think there is good political reason and good national reason for the introduction of this Bill. It is an assertion of our supremacy

over the waters of Hudson's Bay and the adjoining territory. We have not been very successful in maintaining our supremacy and control over the northern half of this continent in the past. We lost the great valley of the Mississippi through inattention ; we lost Louisiana ; we lost Texas ; we lost Oregon and the Pacific coast-

maintopic: TO CHANGE THE NAME OF HUDSON'S BAY.
speechtext: And the state of Maine.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

maintopic: TO CHANGE THE NAME OF HUDSON'S BAY.
speechtext: We lost Alaska

maintopic: TO CHANGE THE NAME OF HUDSON'S BAY.
speechtext: And you lost North Ontario.

maintopic: TO CHANGE THE NAME OF HUDSON'S BAY.
speechtext: And hon. gentlemen opposite may lose something else later on- they may lose their present seats. Our right and title to a portion of the Yukon is now disputed. And, as has been said, we lost the state of Maine. And nearly all these losses occurred because Canadians themselves failed to assert their rights and to assert their supremacy over their own country. The Hudson's Bay country is coming to be a valuable country. I believe there is a great future for us in that respect, and I say we ought to begin now to assert our supremacy in regard to that territory, we ought to give it a distinctively Canadian name, and I do not know any better name to apply to those waters than to call them the Canadian sea. There are but two seas larger than Hudson's Bay, the Mediterranean and the Carribean sea.

maintopic: TO CHANGE THE NAME OF HUDSON'S BAY.
speechtext: What about the Caspian sea ?

maintopic: TO CHANGE THE NAME OF HUDSON'S BAY.
speechtext: The Caspian sea is much smaller than Hudson's Bay, and we ought to be patriotic enough and Canadian enough

maintopic: TO CHANGE THE NAME OF HUDSON'S BAY.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman intend to include all these three seas in his Bill ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: TO CHANGE THE NAME OF HUDSON'S BAY.
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman think I do ? I am comparing these seas to Hudson's Bay, though it is not a bay, it is a great sea with an area of over half a million square miles. The area of Hudson's Bay is larger than that of all our lakes combined. The great lakes of Canada only include 100,000 square miles, but Hudson Bay includes half a million square miles, and has a name that is not properly applied to it. It may be said that I propose to remove an old historical landmark and to change the name. But, Sir, the discoverer of Hudson's Bay, or rather the man by whose name it is known, has a monument in the Hudson river in New York state, and he would still have a monument, if this Bill goes through, in Hudson Straits, and he is embalmed in Rip Van Winkle in a way that will last for ever. The motion I make has been suggested to me by men who have been studying the facts in connection with Mr. MACLEAN.
Hudson's Bay, by men who have been studying the geography of that country, by men who have been reading the history of the country, and the way in which we have lost territory. I think a very good opportunity is now presented to us for asserting our supremacy in that country. I hope it is true that the government in some way are already asserting supremacy in that country, that they are at the present time collecting customs duties there and planting the flag. If we do not plant the flag in Hudson's Bay, there are enterprising men and rivals of ours who will soon do it, and who have been setting up pretensions there, as they have set up pretensions in the Yukon. These things ought to cause us to reflect, and while hon. gentlemen opposite who have not been very anxious about protecting Canadian territory, and who have been anxious to see the old flag removed from the northern half of it-some of them may jeer and laugh at it-

maintopic: TO CHANGE THE NAME OF HUDSON'S BAY.

speechtext: Now the sore point comes. Now I touch on the raw. Now is the time to turn the other way. In the light of all our past experience, of this loss of territory, of this abandonment of territory, I say it is in the public interest that such a Bill as this should be introduced. It is the duty of the government to show that they take an interest iu a question like this, that they are interested in the maintenance of Canadian supremacy on this half of the continent, and that they are doing something now to hold that country for Canada. I hope they intend to give some encouragement to our friend Capt. Bernier in his efforts to plant ihe flag on the North Pole. I am quite willing so far as I am concerned, to support that scheme. I say this Bill is of the greatest national importance, it is important to the empire, and although it may be modified in the way it is drafted, I hope it will meet with the unanimous support of this House.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

["What struck me in connection with this interesting and important debate is that the government are perhaps most to blame for having gone into a transaction of this sort without their evidently having any knowledge of the requirements of the country. I asked the right hon. the Prime Minister whether he had any report as to the probable cost of tlie work which is supposed to be covered by tlie Treadgold concession, and I gathered from his reply that the government had no report, and had not caused any reports to be made as to what the cost of this necessary work would be. Surely, in the case

of a private individual owning such a territory and owning valuable property rights which were to be developed to bring in revenue; surely before such a concession as this was granted a private individual would have had his own engineers and his own scientific officers to report as to the probable cost of the work proposed to be done by people asking for such a valuable franchise. I gather that the government took no steps to ascertain what the proposed work would cost. The first Order in- Council was given in June, 1901, and very shortly after that strong opposition was made to the terms of the grant. Later on another order was passed altering in some points the case in which there has been practically a case in which there has been practically a continuous opposition and not one demand from the people of that country for the confirmation of this concession; from that day to this the government apparently have taken no steps whatever to ascertain what the cost of these works would be. Now, as a rule, 1 am against the government undertaking works of this kind, but I hold that it was the first duty of the government before granting the concession, to ascertain what the cost of such work would be to the con-eesionaires. In the face of the government having no such knowledge, they gave to this company an option-because it is simply and solely an option-for six years of what may be enormously valuable privileges, and the concessionaires are not required to spend a dollar of money for six years. Naturally a body of men with a concession like that, having six years in which to make the most of it, will not be in a hurry to carry the work out or to put such a concession on the market. The market for a year past has not been a favourable one for floating a concern of this kind. The conditions may change at any time within six years, and these men may take advantage of any change in the money market. Naturally they would do so. It would be quite proper for them to do so. Having obtained the concession from this government, it would be quite proper for them, as a pure business proposition, to hold it until they could bring it out at the most favourable time to float it. Naturally they will hold it until they can unload it with the largest amount of profit to themselves. And for six years you are depriving these miners, who you say are so anxious to have water, of the possibility of getting water unless these concessionaires can see the chance in the meantime of selling what you give them at a very large profit. I think it was the first duty of the government, when they found that such a work was required, to ascertain what such a work would cost, and how far it was required to be gone on with at once, and, having done that, to have invited tenders, or let the public know that they were open and willing to receive offers for building these water flumes and de-92
veloping the water power in that country. On these two points I think the government are very seriously to blame, and have possibly committed that part of the country to a serious loss.

I beg to bring before the notice of this House the question of which I gave notice some time ago, concerning the Treadgold concessions, in the Yukon. At the last session of this House a debate arose upon these concessions, but it was in the dying hours of the session, and not as much attention was given to it as would otherwise have been given. I find on referring to the

' Hansard ' that tlie Minister of tlie Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton), in replying to some remarks made by the leader of the opposition, spoke as follows :
Perhaps it would have been more satisfactory to the House if, at an earlier period of the session, when we were not in a hurry with the proceedings necessarily pressing upon our minds at the close of parliament, a fuller dis-cusion of this whole matter could have taken place. I have only to say that I should welcome the subject if it is brought up by my hon. friend or by any other member of the House, at some future time, because the whole suhiect is one in regard to which I will welcome full and complete discussion.
Now, Sir, wo are only complying with the invitation given to us last session by the hon. gentleman, in bringing this matter to the notice of the House. As hon. gentlemen will see, it is an important matter, these are very important concessions, and we think it is advisable that the House should know the conditions under which these concessions were made, their importance, and the extent of the grants which are given to Mr. Treadgold and his associates. There were two sets of Orders in Council. The first set is composed of three orders which were passed on the 12th of June, the 29th of June and the 7th of December, 1901. Then on the 21st of April, 1902, as I will show later on, after some representations had been made to the government, the Orders in Council passed in 1901 wtere cancelled, and the Order in Council dated the 21st of April, 1902, was passed, making almost the same grants to Mr. Treadgold and his associates. It is necessary for me first of all to point out to the House the importance of the water supply in the Yukon, and of some system by which miners in the Yukon district may be supplied with water. I can find no better authority upon this subject than the remarks which were made on the occasion I have alluded to by the Minister of the Interior. Speaking on the 13th of May last, he said :
The whole subject has given the government a great deal of consideration, and anxious consideration, in order to bring about the best results. A question which has not yet been realized in regard to the development of the mining ground of the Yukon Territory as completely as it will be realized, is the question of the water supply. So long as the rich pockets upon the creeks now well known continue to be worked, the effects of the lack of a proper water supply are not likely to be seriously felt. But as soon as these beds begin to be exhausted and we are getting pretty near to that now the difficulty about the water supply will press for attention. There is an enormous quantity of gravel of a much lower grade than the miners have been heretofore operating upon, which it will be necessary to work if that portion of the country which is producing the largest quantity of gold is to be kept up to its present position. It was the desire of the government to secure the inauguration of some scheme whereby water would be brought in on a large
scale, and, to do that we fei; that it would be justifiable and proper in the interest of the country that pretty liberal privileges and concessions should be given.
In order to further show the importance of the water supply in the Yukon. I beg leave to quote from a letter which was addressed on the 11th of November, 1901, by an engineer of repute in the Yukon, to the then Minister of Justice, he said :
The cutting of the timber and opening up of the country has changed the conditions so that as soon as our spring opens up the snow melts much faster than in past years when we had more timber. The majority of miners who are situated on small streams, gulches and hillsides find that their water supply dries up so early In the summer that ihey had not even time to wash out their winter dumps, so that the water supply Is a very serious one, and the lack of it has retarded the mining interests in the past year very much	It would require, at least 10,000 inches of water distributed through the district-the district referred to is at least sixty-three miles-to supply the different miners within this district, water to wash their gold from their different claims that are now known to be good properties, to say nothing of other ground that may prove good on being developed.
Water must take the place of wood ; most of the creeks have had all the wood cut from them. The miners have had to go some distance, so that the cost now runs up to $25 per cord in some places, and will cost more as it becomes more scarce. In using water, all c.f the higher banks can be washed from top to bottom, instead of working only a few feet, of the drifted ground three feet more or less where it is found the richest. AH of the creek beds that have been partially worked by the ordinary method can be worked over again and be made to pay by the use of water.
This is a very important statement in view of what has taken place in granting the concessions of which I have spoken.
So you see it Is important that some means must be taken whereby a supply of water can be placed at the disposal of the Yukon miner or the gold will not be removed for hundreds of years.
In 1900 a petition was signed by the inhabitants of the Yukon territory to the Governor General. I see that a committee bad been entrusted by their fellow citizens in the Yukon with the duty of making representations to the government in regard to what was going on in the Yukon at that time. These gentlemen, in the first paragraph of this petition say :
That on the 13th day of February, 1900, the undersigned were duly appointed a committee of the citizens of the Yukon Territory, to petition for and secure representation of the said citizens on the Yukon council and in the House of Commons of Canada.
Then, they go on to say, amongst other things, speaking of the concessions which have been made in the Yukon :
On the 25th day of November, 1897, the then gold commissioner, contrary to the mining regulations then in force and in direct breach of faith with the miners who were then exploring

and prospecting Dominion creels, closed the said creek against locations, and in 1S98, the gold commissioner, together with the then commissioner of the Yukon territory, closed the hillsides and benches along said Dominion creek, against locations by the free miners of the Yukon Territory, and this closure was enforced by the recognized authorities until the 11th day of July, A.D. 1898.
On the 13th day of March, 1899, contrary t.o the regulations made by Order in Council, all benches and hillsides on Bonanza and Eldorado creeks

I understand that these two creeks are amongst the most valuable in the Yukon district.
-were closed against locations by free miners and said action, was, on the 5th day of September, 1899, confirmed by the Privy Council of Canada, and said districts have never been reopened to the locations of placer mining claims.
During the time when these closures were being made and enforced on the various creeks, hillside and bench claims, in the gold mining region of the Yukon Territory, large parts ol' the said closed portions and other parts of tho Yukon Teritory were granted by the government of Ottawa to certain persons many of whom never at any time were in the Yukon Territory, as hydraulic concessions, and certain fractions have been granted in compensation for alleged grievances, which alleged grievances ought never to have been in existence.
Thus while the creeks were closed to the ordinary and necessary prospector as above set forth, in the autumn of 1899, the relocation of abandoned claims were entirely done away with In the Yukon Territory. Population was driven from the Yukon Territory by what was a practical prohibition of development, large tracts of richest placer mining ground of the Yukon Territory have been handed over in concessions and the said concessions include and take in valuable fractions which have been denied (o the prospector and have been handed over to the concessionaires for the small sum of one hundred and fifty- dollars per mile, so that at the present time prospection and new discoveries have practically ceased.
They then pray to the Governor General in Council as follows :	\
Wherefore your petitioners pray that :
Third, the necessity of opening "for location to free miners all parts of the Yukon Territory owned by the government which are fit for placer mining.
Fifth, the necessity for altering the hydraulic mining regulations so as to secure for the free miner the right to locate, record and work any ground which is fit for placer mining whether covered by a concession or not.
Sixth, the adoption and enforcement of such mining regulations as will encourage to the utmost the prospector, first, the miner, second, and the investor, third, and throw open the country for the fullest and free development.
Now, Sir, while these locations were closed, as was represented by this petition to the Governor General this was going on in Ottawa here : In March, 1898, the Minister of the Interior directed that Bonanza, Eldorado and their tributaries and benches should be closed against location. This was followed on October 7. 1899, by a regula-Mr. CASGRAIN.
tiou closing all lapsed claims in the territory against re-location. In the year and a half which followed, without the knowledge of the Yukon people the greater part of our richest placer ground was included in so-called hydraulic concessions. On Hunker creek were granted-the Williams (21 square miles) ; the Milne (2 square miles) ; the Anderson (24 square miles). On the Klondike, including Bear and Lindow creeks, was granted,-the Boyle (50 square miles). On Bonanza-the Philip (5 square miles) ; the Bronson & Bay (15 square miles), and the Matson-Doyle (3 square miles) were granted. On Quartz creek another concession (about 4 square miles) was granted to the same Boyle, while the other creeks heretofore mentioned were almost similarly blanketed by concessions which were obtained by fraud in most cases.
Then came the Order in Council of June 12, 1.901, to which I now wish to direct the attention of the House. The Order in Council consists of the preamble and the tender made by Treadgold and his associates was included in the Order in Council, as appears to me, without any amendment whatever; that is to say that these gentlemen made a proposal to the government, they wrote the government a letter in which they said : We want a concession in the Yukon on such and such terms, and the government simply took the letter and Incorporated it In the Order in Council without, as it appears, as far as I can see, changing any part of it. The preamble of the Order in Council says :
Whereas the mining now carried on in the Klondike district is. because of the inadequate supply of water necessarily confined to the washing of the richest gravel only comparatively small in area, thus leaving large tracts of gold-bearing gravels unworked ; and from the information obtained from the gold commissioner of the Yukon Territory and others it is believed that the riches of the Klondike district can only be properly utilized by such a water supply as that which the before mentioned applicants are prepared to establish.
Then the Order in Council goes on to say that :
Therefore, the Governor General in Council Is pleased to order and doth hereby order, that the said application by the said Malcom H. Orr-Ewing, A. N. C. Treadgold and Walter Bar-wick, bearing date the 31st May, 1901, a copy of which is hereto annexed, and which is hereby made a part of this Order in Council, shall he and the same is hereby accepted.
This Order in Council is the most extraordinary document, perhaps, to which the attention of this House has ever been called. A proper value can only be put upon the concessions made by this Order in Council when the Order in Council is properly dissected and properly reflected upon. First of all the Order in Council gives the concessionaires, or the grantees :
The sole right to divert and take water from the Klondike river at any point or points he-

tween its entry into the Yukon river and Flat creek for the purpose of generating power with which to pump water to work the auriferous deposits in the district hereinafter termed ' The District ') comprising the beds, banks, valleys, slopes and hills of the Klondike river, of Bonanza, Bear and Hunter creeks and their tributaries.	.
1 will show afterwards by quoting from some authorities who live in the Yukon Territory the extent of the district and I think X will be able to shorn that the district comprises probably the richest part of the Klondike. These people have a prior right to divert the water and establish their pumping stations so as to create this power over an extent of forty miles of country from the Yukon to Flat creek. Then, having given them the sole right to thus divert the water of the Klondike river, the Order in Council goes on to give them :
The prior right ... to divert and take water from the Klondike river for distribution and use in the district especially upon the hills and benches.
The right on any creek or tributary within the district to divert, take, impound and store for mining purposes any water not used by any free miner for the working of his claim on such creek or tributary under the regulations now in force for placer mining, or respecting the diversion of water for mining purposes in the Yukon Territory.
Afterwards, by an Order in Council of the 7th December, 1901, this right on Rock creek which is the principle creek in that district, was limited to 2,500 miners' inches. I presume that many gentlemen in this House are as ignorant of what is a ' miner's inch,' as I was before I began the study of this question, and it will probably be well to define the term here. When you say a ' miner's inch ' one would think that this was a small quantity of water, but I find in the official ' Gazette ' of 1902 page S2 that a miner's inch has been defined by the Department of the Interior as follows :
A miner's inch shall mean the passage of one and a half cubic feet of water per minute.
And if we consult the dictionaries, we find that a miner's inch is defined to be :
The amount of water that will pass in twenty-four hours through an opening one inch square under a pressure of 6 inches.
X have also heard from a competent authority, that a miner's inch is equal to a volume of water twelve feet square.
The Order in Council goes on to give the right:
The right at any point or points in the bed, banks, valley, slopes and hills of the Klondike river between its mouth and Flat creek to construct and maintain dams, cribs, intakes, flumes and any other works necessary for the generation of power and the right of entry upon and way through any lands and any mining ground for the purpose of such construction and maintenance.
The right to purchase any Crown lands required by the grantees for the purposes of their works at a price not exceeding ten dollars per
acre, saving and reserving all the timber, mines and minerals upon or under such lands.
The right at any point or points in the district to build, maintain and operate pumping stations, electrical works and reservoirs.
The right of entry upon and way through any lands and any mining ground for the purpose of constructing, laying and maintaining flumes, ditches and pipe lines for conveying the grantees' water supply to any point within the district.	*
The right of entry upon and way through any lands and any mining ground within the district and within the Indian river district for the purpose of constructing and maintaining overhead or underground wires and any other structures for the transmission of electricity for any purpose whatsoever throughout the said districts, and the right to levy and collect such tolls as may be approved by the Governor General in Council for the use of electricity in the said districts.
Then it gives the right
To use, distribute and dispose of the water delivered by the grantees within the district.
Therefore these grantees got first of all, the sole right to divert and take water from the IHondike river in this large district; they got the prior right under this Order in Council to take all the water which is necessary and which they wanted to take, and then they got the right to use, dispose of, and to distribute this water within the district. They got this right subject to no payment except the royalty :
The right, subject to no payment except the royalty prescribed upon output, to enter upon, make entry for any work all mining locations now or hereafter abandoned on Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks and their tributaries.
It would seem at first glance that this power is not very important, because as the House wil notice it only gives the right of entry over the abandoned claims, but anybody who knows anything about this question ; anybody who has studied it at all, will see that this right is of paramount importance. Abandoned claims are not at all claims which have been abandoned because they are not good claims. For instance, when a miner has staked out a claim and he has not sufficient means to work it, or has not sufficient appliances, he will work it for a short time, and then abandon it, but here are a great many claims, there are thousands of claims in the Klondike as in all other gold-bearing regions, which have been abandoned and which have been worked over again at enormous profit. The House will, therefore, see the importance of the statement which was made in the petition to the Governor General in Council that I have just read. The House will also note the Importance of the closing up of this rich district to the prospector and to the free miner ; the prohibition which was imposed upon them against retaking or reclaiming the abandoned claims. The House will remember that at a certain period in 1898 and 1899 these districts were closed

against the free miner by regulations emanating from the department at Ottawa. These very same claims, the abandonment of which had been ordered by regulation of the Department of the Interior, were handed over by this regulation to the grantees, the only obligation imposed upon them being the payment of royalty. There was no stipulation for any other payment whatever. Therefore, at once, these grantees came into competition with the free miner, and with such competition the free miner was not in a position to compete, and so these gentlemen got the abandoned claims that were to be found in this very rich district. I call the attention of the House particularly to this, because it is one of the parts of the Order In Council which was not repealed or changed in any manner, shape or form, by the subsequent Order in Council which was passed on the 21st of April, 1902.
Then they have the prior right:
The prior right, if mineral-bearing lodes or deposits of any kind whatever be discovered through the operations of the grantees upon Crown lands, or upon lands or locations owned or leased by the grantees within the district, to enter upon and purchase locations embracing the discoveries in the manner prescribed by the regulations governing mining in the Yukon Territory.
Then they have the right to take timber from Crown lands subject to the payment of dues, and they have also :
The exclusive right, subject to the regulations hereinafter contained, to construct, lay, maintain, supply with water and operate bedrock flumes, and any other flumes for supplying water in the district ; provided that every free miner shall have the right of constructing flumes for the purpose of conveying to his claim the lawful amount of water to which he is entitled under the regulations now in force for placer mining in the Yukon Territory, and any water that he shall purchase from the grantees ; and he shall also have the right of constructing flumes for the purpose of draining his claim.
Therefore, under this Order in Council, they have the right to dispose of and sell the water which they had the prior right to take out of the Klondike, and they were the only people who could lay pipes or flumes so as to distribute this water throughout this district. Now, Mr. Speaker, it will be in order to discover what is the area of the territory which was handed over to these concessionaries. I quote from ' Hansard ' a question which was put to the ministry during last session of parliament. It is as follows :
What area of the Klondike is by this concession given over to such syndicate, and closed to the general public ?
The answer to that question was given in the following words by the Minister of the Interior :
Claims on' Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks and their tributaries, which have been staked out by miners and thereafter abandoned and allowed to lapse.

Now, Sir, this will not probably give the House a true conception of the extent and the value of this immense concession. I beg leave to quote from a newspaper which no doubt my hon. friends on the Treasury benches know very well. It is the Dawson ' Morning Sun.' This paper, I may tell the House, is the government organ in the Yukon ; or it is the most friendly paper in the Yukon to the ministers, and the fact of the matter is that the Saturday edition of the Dawson ' Morning Sun ' is the official ' Gazette ' for the 'district. I find this among the papers in a return which was brought down by the government in reply to a motion made in the House. The * Morning Sun ' of February 14th, 1902, came out with some startling headlines. I must say that it seemed to take a long time for the people of the Yukon to correctly seize the importance of the concessions which had been handed over to Mr. Treadgold and his associates, but they apparently woke up one fine morning, and the Dawson ' Morning Sun ' came out with an article which I shall quote, and which was preceded by very large headlines. Some one asked me a moment ago what this district comprised, and in answer to that I shall quote this newspaper, which I suppose is well informed, and which would certainly not give information to the public wantonly, nor would it be likely to give any information which would be false, especially if that information were to injure the government which this newspaper then supported. It says :

Three hundred and fifty square miles of territory.
Two hundred and twenty-five thousand square acres.
Twenty thousand dollars a day earned now.
Five hundred and twenty thousand dollars a month earned now.
Three million one hundred and twenty thousand dollars earned in six months.
Ten million dollars earned in three years.
Three thousand eight hundred relocations last year.
Three thousand seven hundred renewals last year.
Loss of revenue to the government.
Loss of business to merchants.
Shrinkage in securities.
Values reduced.
Miners deserting territory.
Confidence gone.
The ' Sun ' then goes on to say :
Public opinion was quickly aroused when the ' News ' appeared on the streets last night with the first exposure of the gigantic mining grab attempted by Treadgold & Co. A mass meeting was auickly arranged for and the A. B. Hall promptly engaged for Monday evening at 8 o'clock. Every man who has anything at stake in the country should be present and support the resolution which will be presented for the endorsement of the people present.
The map published In the Dally ' News ' yesterday, showing the dimensions of the enormous wet blanket upon future development which is cast upon the Dawson mining division by the

Treadgold concession, was an object lesson that probably did more to arouse a deep public interest in the subject than any arguments against the creation of this iniquitous monopoly that have been or can be made.
The map shows a territory covered by this concession of about 350 square miles, or over 225.000 acres. It shows also that this is the richest portion of Yukon territory in its number of gold-bearing streams and its mining development. It shows about eighty streams that have been located and in addition many others that have not as yet been named. With this area there are thousands of claims-creek, bench and hillside-that would in a short time be staked and developed were it not for the fact that the individual miner has been robbed of this mining territory so near to his base of supplies, in order that a wealthy syndicate might be made a present of it; to have and to hold until 1905, whether they do any development on it before that year or not.
That some of the claims embraced have been abandoned is no argument. In every placer mining camp claims are abandoned as worthless and afterwards relocated and worked at a profit. Many of the Klondike pioneers, for instance, abandoned their claims on Eldorado, and even during last year only 3,800 miners relocated claims that other miners had abandoned. Here follows a list of the principal creeks and gulches that are closed to development by the concession.
The paper goes on to give an enumeration of the creeks and their tributaries which were conceded to these people, or over which they had a monopoly; and it gives this result : the Upper Bonanza, with fourteen tributaries; Last Chance, with three tributaries; Hunker Creek, with sixteen tributaries; Eldorado, with eleven tributaries; Lower Bonanza, with twenty-six tributaries; Bear Creek, with one tributary; and Gold Bottom, with three tributaries. The paper adds :
In addition to the above are innumerable creeks and gulches which have no names that appear on any map, but upon each and all of them there are claims a number of which lapse each year.
The House will see the value of the concession which was given to these people, not by any comment I am making on the Order in Council, but by the explanation given by this organ of the government, and, I take it, a paper which must be well informed as to the state of affairs in the Yukon territory.
Now, what were the conditions imposed on these people by the Order in Council ?- Because the House will say, surely these great privileges and monopolies were not given to the grantees unless some conditions were imposed on them, or unless an equivalent was given, if not to the government, at least to the unhappy miners who had been, I may say. defrauded by the concessions which were given by the government. By the Order in Council which was passed on the 12th of June, 1901, it was provided :
The grantees shall before December 31, 1902, have expended upon the objects of their enterprise at least the sum of $250,000.
It was also stipulated that before the end of December, 1902, they were to deliver within the district during the summer season of 1905, not later than July 1, 1905, at least 1,000 miners' inches of water. I may say that by the Order in Council of the 7th of December, 1901, this was altered. They were still obliged to expend $250,000 in work so as to bring this concession into operation, and to supply the miners in the district with at least 2,000 inches of water. There were other important particulars in this first Order in Council which were not changed by the second, and this very important concession was given to them :
The grantees shall not be required to pay to the Crown or to the district or local authorities any rentals, occupation rents, assessments, or other dues in respect of any lands except timber lands, or in respect of any flumes, drains, properties or profits other than import customs duties, school taxes and a royalty on the gold mined in the mines owned by them, or any tax or assessment which may be substituted for such royalty.
The properties of the grantees shall be exempt from representation.
To the ordinary mind the word representation here does not mean much; but when I tell the House what it means, the House will see the enormous value of the concession given to these gentlemen. Under the regulations, which I have here, the ordinary free miner is obliged first of all to pay $15 to become a free miner; he is obliged to get a certificate, which costs $10 or $15, and he has to pay every year a renewal fee of $15. That is not all : he has either to work liis claim to the extent of $200 or pay $200 to the government every year. That is what is called representation. These gentlemen, for some reason, were exempt from representation. They were put on a footing much better than that of the ordinary free miner. They had not to pay anything for their certificate; they had not to do any work whatever on their claims; and if they did not, they were not obliged, like the ordinary free minei' to pay this sum of $200 to the government. The House will see at a glance what an enormous loss of revenue this is to the treasury of the country. Why was this concession given to the grantees ? I would like some explanation on that point. Then, under the regulation which was passed in accordance with this Order in Council, they have the greatest rights of expropriation.
The rights conferred upon the grantees shall extend for the period of thirty years, at the expiration of which period all exclusive and prior rights granted to them shall cease and be determined, but the works and structures built by the grantees together with the lands, rights and easements which they shall have purchased and acquired shall remain the gran-I tees' private property.

The grantees shall have the light to assign the rights conferred upon them to any company or companfes or to any persons associated together for the purpose of carrying into effect the objects of the grant or any part of them.
Now, I call the attention of the House to this part of the Order in Council :
The charge which the grantees shall be entitled to make for the use of such water on each claim shall not exceed one dollar per miner's inch per hour.
So that the miners were obliged to take water from these people. They could not build a flume for themselves or take any water from the Klondike to work the richest parts of the Klondike, but they were obliged to pay these people one dollar for every miner's inch of water per hour. By the Order in Council of 7th December, 1901, this charge for water was reduced from one dollar to twenty-five cents per miner's inch per hour. The implication is that there must have been something wrong in this concession at the outset-that the enormous price put upon this water was put upon it either in absolute ignorance of the position of affairs in the Yukon or from some other motive, which I will not characterize at this moment. As I have said, it took some time before the citizens of the Yukon realized the extent and the importance of the monopoly which had been given to Mr. Treadgold and his associates. I find in the return brought down, a communication from the late Senator Wood, to the Department of the Interior, Inclosing a letter from the firm of Holme Miller & Company, of Dawson. This letter is addressed to the firm of the late Senator Wood, in Hamilton, and is dated February the 13th, 1902, some time after the passing of the Order in Council, which was passed on the 7th of December, 1901. From that moment therefore the government were made aware of the appalling state of affairs created by this concession. They were then put upon their guard and notified to have this condition of things put an end to immediately. The letter is as follows We are sending you a marked copy of a Dawson paper, which marked article we wish to call your attention to.
If this is allowed to stand, it means that two-thirds of our gold-bearing area is closed to the prospector and miner, and absolutely tied up for a period of three years and possibly longer. It will mean a falling off in trade in all lines from 25 per cent to 50 per cent. Surely you cannot be so disinterested in the development and the advancement of this section as to sit quietly by and to allow such an outrage to common decency in matters of government to be committed.
Every manufacturer, every wholesaler in Canada is indirectly interested in this matter, and should not rest until this order of affairs is reversed.
Just such administration of affairs in the Yukon has driven over 8,000 honest, law-abiding English, Canadian, Australian, and American prospectors from this section, and if this condition of affairs continues to exist, there

will be nothing left but a skeleton of a once prosperous and wealthy community.
If you could come with us to a visit to the creeks we would show you miles of ground held under concession lying idle, while adjoining ground resembles a human beehive, alive with men delving for the golden treasure.
We do not over-estimate this matter. We have been silent heretofore, but the time is now arrived when every man, every woman and every child in the Yukon Territory should enter a protest against a measure aimed against their prosperity and their homes.
Believing you will consider this matter carefully and act accordingly.
We remain, yours truly, HOLME, MILLER & CO.
In a subsequent letter of February the 17th, the same gentleman writes :
We are sending you to-day marked copies of the Dawson ' Daily News ' and the 1 Morning Sun.' The latter paper is the government's organ here. We wish to call your attention to the articles referring to the * Treadgold grants.'
We wish to enlist your services in an endeavour to have this grant repealed. This means the success or failure of many a business enterprise in Dawson. To us it means a loss in trade of 25 to 50 per cent. Neither the ' Daily News,' which is an independent paper, or the * Sun,' the government's organ, over-estimate the damage this grant will do to the commercial interests here.
If there is anything you can do in this matter, any influences you can bring to bear, we trust you can see your way clear to do so.
This firm must have been a reputable concern or the late Senator Wood, who was a very estimable gentleman and a very good friend of the government, would not have thought it worth while to transmit this communication to the department with the extracts from the newspapers referred to.
I am not making any comments on the concession, because no comments of mine could convey such an idea of the iniquity of the grant as those passed by the people themselves in the Yukon district. The * Daily Sun ' of the 15th February said-and I am taking this again from the return laid on the Table :
People are just commencing to realize the enormity of the steal attempted by the Treadgold concession holders. No other term will correctly indicate the nature of the transaction. Rights which belong to the public are being taken without compensation or shadow of authority. What can this be called other than a theft ?
There was also a meeting held at Dawson city, a full report of which is given in the ' Morning Sun ' of the 16th February. This was not a meeting of citizens, prepared in any event to condemn the government unheard, it was not a meeting of opponents of the government, but a meeting of the Liberal club of Dawson city.
The 'Sun' said describing this'meeting :
An earnest and enthusiastic meeting of the Liberal club was held last evening at Pioneer Hall for the purpose of discussing the recent Order in Council concerning the Treadgold concession.

That meeting was presided over by the Crown Prosecutor, who was then held In great esteem in government circles, and who is now the governor or commissioner of Yukon. The ' Sun ' report goes on to say :
One hundred and fifty members were present, and vice-president F. T. Congdon, called the meeting to order. He stated that, while the meeting had been called at the instance of the Liberal club, the subject under discussion was of such vital interests to the country that anyone who felt interested would be privileged to speak.
Mr. Congdon spoke of the aroused feeling of the people-aroused justly on account of the injustice of such a grant, and that it was the duty of the Liberal club to point out the wrong that had been made. He declared it to be a violation of all the principles of government, and that it had evidently been gained by the grossest misrepresentations. They should not go to extremes in the matter as was being done at present but calmly discuss its great mistake. The government should not give such grants, for it was but the trustees of the people and it was the purpose of the people to see that they were considered in such affairs. He read some extracts of law on contracts and closed his remarks by saying that with a united effort of the Liberal club they should get good results from the commissioner's visit to Ottawa.
I believe that Mr. Ross, the present member for the Yukon district, was then the commissioner and was on his way to Ottawa. The ' Sun ' report continues :
The next speaker called on was orator Charles Macdonald, who said :
I have not the slightest reluctance in improving this oportunity to state my feelings concerning the Treadgold concessions. I only wish that men more conversant than myself- and there are many here-had been called upon. But we would be false friends to the Liberal government if we did not point out the mistakes of the party. (Hear, hear.)
As we all know a mighty concession ha3 been given, yet the government has no right to make such a gift, for it is merely the trustee of the people. This matter of the Tre.idgold concession must and cannot be carried into effect. It is our duty to act promptly (hear, hear) and point out the wrong. There can be no two opinions. It should not become law. (Hear, hear.)
It is rather strange that these gentlemen up there, friends of the government, should have felt called upon to read this lesson to the government. It is rather strange that they should have felt under the necessity of impressing on the government what is an undoubted principle of constitutional law, namely, that such a concession as this should not be given by Order in Council. Again I quote from the * Sun

George, another newspaper man in the Yukon, likened the Klondike to a great reservoir upon which the country drew for a supply. He made a pretty illustration of how a claim being abandoned to-day in one district would be made up by the discovery of another. He had worked out rwo claims himself, and yet there was ground still untouched and awaiting the hands of the miner.
' Now,' he said, ' if this opportunity is taken away from three or four thousand men, the work in this district, as individuals, we will only have in its place in a few years five hundred men and our boss, Mr. Treadgold.'
Mr. George thought there should be a rattling of dry bones and made that remark apply to his belief, that not only this, but other concessions should be looked into.

Stackpole said :
I have been a Liberal all my life, but I would not stay with any party that has acted like the present government. My interests are in the Yukon and that's the part I am wanting protected.

McFarlane did not hesitate to say that if the government was in ignorance of this country, it was about time to quit sending delegations to Ottawa, and have them send delegations here. He suggested that Mr. Sifton be asked to take a trip in over the ice.
Now, it is strange that the government bad not more information about this country. This was in 1902, and work lias been going on in the Yukon since 1896 or 1897. The government had their officials there, and I believe some of the ministers had visited that country. At all events it was their bounden duty to know the state of that country, to know the condition of affairs there; and if they passed Orders in Council, giving concessions and grants deserving of this denunciation by their friends, what should be the opinion of members of this House before whom are being placed all the facts of the case ?
The resolutions were moved by Mr. J. H. Davison and seconded by J. C. Noel.
I know Mr. Noel, and I know that a better Liberal or a more devoted admirer of my right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) does not exist in the country. The resolutions passed were as follows :
That a committee be appointed to collect statistics and other information regarding the concessions and the probable consequences of its operation, with a view of providing the commissioner with the same.
It is further resolved that telegrams be sent to the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier and to the other members of his cabinet protesting against the Treadgold Order in Council and praying that its operation be suspended pending the arrival at Ottawa of the commissioner of the Yukon Territory.
Whereas, the Liberal association of Dawson has summoned this meeting of the association to discuss the Treadgold concession and to make such representations in respect thereto to the government as might be deemed necessary, and has invited all Liberals, whether members of the association or not, to attend this meeting ; and
Whereas, this meeting has the greatest confidence in the judgment and ability of the commissioner of the Yukon Territory and in his desire and determination to guard the interests of the people of this territory ; and
Whereas, in the opinion of this meeting their confidence in the commissioner is shared by the people of the territory at large; therefore be it
Resolved, that the meeting requests the commissioner to undertake the presentation to the

government of the representations which it is desired to make in regard to such concession, and that the meeting urges the commissioner to use all his great influence to secure a cancellation of the obnoxious features of the recent Order in Council, and the other Order in Council relating to such concession, and to relieve this territory from the disastrous consequences certain to ensue if such Order in Council is allowed to stand in full ; and be it further
Resolved, that the commissioner's attention be called to the fact that he be requested to represent to the government that, in the opinion of this meeting, the insertion of such features in the Order in Council could only have been procured by the grossest misrepresentations and fraudulent concealment ; that it never could have been represented to the minister who proposed said orders, or to the Governor in Council that the orders were an interference with the abrogation of vested rights ; that it was retroactive in operation and most far-reaching and uncertain in effect ; that it was certain to produce distrust and lack of confidence among the mining communities of this territory, and prove fatal to the progress of the territory ; nor could it have been presented and made apparent that the only consideration promised for the enormous interest granted was a monopoly to supply water at an exorbitant and prohibitive price.
Then the ' Sun ' goes on with its comments as follows :
The whole populace of Dawson and the creeks is in a furore of excitement bordering on consternation over the far-reaching effects of the amended Treadgold concession . . . Hunker, Bear and Bonanza and all of their tributaries and ground contiguous thereto are within the reach and grasp of the great concessionaire syndicate. That means every paying creek in the country flowing into the Klondike river. Those which empty into the Indian river and the Yukon are the only ones omitted and every miner in the country knows how few those are	 Only a few days remain to the people here who hope to retain what they consider their most sacred rights before it is possible that the giant octopus will have fastened its tenacles upon the country that the poor prospectors have conquered and placed in the list of proud territories of the Dominion of Canada and which with the process of strangulation once in effect, will divest the country of Its population and cheat the government of its income from this source. ... It was the talk all round and there is no use trying to deny or conceal it-that the Treadgold Concession will sap the life of the country. . . . Not for the mining industry alone do the people object but on account of the life of the city of Dawson Itself. They are firmly of the belief that the place will be little more than a memory with the Treadgold people In power, and that where now palatial public buildings and costly banks and big stores and warehouses all sland, will be no more than a reminder of once when there was a prosperous country somewhere in the far north.
What Is that from ?

This is from the Dawson ' Sun,' the government organ in the Yukon. It says also :
It is apparent that there must have been a vast combination of misrepresentations regard-

ing the Yukon formed to assail the authorities at Ottawa to induce them to come to the conclusion that this territory cannot get along without Treadgold, and that it is a very insignificant matter to hand over to him all the abandoned claims on certain creeks. It is certain that nobody outside knows much about the Yukon, and the editor confesses that he has been here for so short a time, that for a while, and until he was enlightened, he could not see any great value in abandoned claims. He said, and, no doubt the authorities at Ottawa said : What good would the claims be if the present owners valued them so little as to lose them rather than pay the small renewal fee ? Why not give them to some one like Treadgold, who will appreciate them and work them ?
One only needs, however, to examine the matter for a little on the spot to understand fully how erroneous such an idea is, and to appreciate how great must ha_ve been the imposition practiced to obtain such an order. Treadgold and his associates are horribly anxious to develop this country. They are grieved to think our people are suffering for water. It will be observed, however, that their efforts to develop are confined to districts where other men have found and opened the richest mines on earth. They do not care to strike out into new regions for themselves. They cannot be induced to leave the Klondike. Their excuse for confining themselves to this region is that Bonanza, Hunker, Eldorado, &c., are in distress for water, and they desire to relieve this distress at the small ocst of twenty-five cents per miner's inch.
I have read these copious extracts to show what the real nature of these grants Is. I think it is most interesting to know that these comments should have been made upon the first Orders in Council, because it seems to me, as I shall endeavour to show (with good result, I think), that there is no material difference between the Order in Council now in existence and the Orders in Council against which these denunciations were launched not only by adversaries of the government, not only by people indifferent in politics, but by the Liberal club and by some of the strongest partisans of the government in the Yukon district. I have already said that the new Order in Council was passed on the 21st of April, 1902. Now, Sir, I will not read all the new Order in Council, 'but I will simply indicate to the House some of the salient points of that order. Some of its clauses were exactly the same as those of the former Order in Council. Let me say at the outset that the sole right to divert and take water from the Klondike river at any point or points between its entry into the Yukon river and Flat creek was preserved to the grantees by the new Order in Council. So they have the sole right to take the water from the Klondike river for a distance of forty miles between Yukon river and Flat creek, to erect pumping stations so as to pump water to work the auriferous beds, banks, valleys, slopes and hills of the Klondike river, or Bononza, Bear and Hunker creeks, exactly as granted to these gentlemen by the first Order In, Council to which I have

referred. In the second clause there Is a difference-a limitation.	It will be remembered by the House that, at first, a right was given to the grantees to take water from the Klondike river for distribution from the Klondike without any limitation. By the second Order in Council they have not the right to take all the water they chose from the Klondike river for the purpose of operating their own works, but they have a prior right to take water from the Klondike up to 5,000 miners' inches.
Now, I submit to the House that, having this prior right to take from the river the water for distribution and use in the district up to 5,000 miners' inches, nobody else could come into that district and take water. It stands to reason that these gentlemen have still, under the second Order in Council, the right to build dams across the river, the sole right is given to them to expropriate property for the object of their concession. They have the right to erect pumping stations, they alone have this right, they have the sole right to divert water from the Klondike river according to this first clause. So I say this is a monopoly ; and nobody else, even if he had authority, even if he got a subsequent grant from the government, would be so foolhardy as to go up there and establish competing pumping works, or works of any kind so long as this concession is given to the present owners. Then they have the same rights to .purchase any Crown lands, and build and operate pumping stations, and enter upon any lands or mining grounds, to construct and maintain overhead and underground wires for the purpose of supplying this district with electricity and electrical power. They have the right,-
Subject to the regulations hereinafter contained, to establish, distribute and dispose of by sale or otherwise, the water delivered by the grantees within the district.
Now, a notable omission of this Order in Council is that these people have the sole and exclusive right to divert the waters of the Klondike, the prior right to take the
5,000	miners' inches. They have the sole right to use, and the sole right to distribute this water, and no price is imposed upon them by this Order in Council. The first Order in Council said that the price to be paid by the miners was $1, this was subsequently changed to 25 cents per miners' inch per hour. This Order in Council does not say what price these people are to pay. Therefore, to anybody reading this last Order in Council it will be evident that these people have there a monopoly to distribute and to sell water, that nobody else can distribute and sell it, and that they can sell it at any price they deem fit. They can sell it at one dollar, or two dollars, or fifty cents for a miners' inch per hour, there is nothing to restrict them. Therefore, I say this Order in Council is at least as bad as the former Orders in Council which were
repealed by the Order in Council of the 21st of April, 1902.
The grantees have the prior right if mineralbearing lodes or deposits of any kind whatever be discovered through the operations of the grantees upon Crown lands, or upon lands or locations owned or leased by the grantees within the district, to enter upon and purchase locations embracing the discoveries in the manner prescribed by the regulations governing mining in the Yukon Territory; the right, subject to no payment except the royalty prescribed upon output, to obtain entry for and work all mining locations now or hereafter abandoned on Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks and their tributaries.
The House will remember that one of the features which was most denounced by friends of the government in the first Order in Council was the right these gentlemen had of making entry for and working abandoned mining claims in this rich district. The very same right is given to them by the subsequent Order in Council. Then again :
The grantees shall not be required to pay to the Crown or to the district or local authorities any rentals, occupation rents, assessments or other dues in respect of any lands except timber lands or in respect of any flumes, drains, properties or profits other than import customs duties, school taxes and a royalty on the gold mined In the mines owned by them, or any tax or assessment which may be substituted for such royalty.
Here again one of the objectionable features which was to be found in the first Order in Council is reproduced in the second Order in Council. The only material difference between this Order in Council and the others, so far as I have gone, is that by the first Order in Council a prior right was given to these gentlemen to divert the waters of the Klondike without any limitation whatever ; whilst in this Order in Council they still have the prior right to divert that water to the extent of 5,000 miners' inches per hour. But, I say that when these people have this prior right, after having been given the sole right to divert the waters on this extent of territory, nobody would dare to go up there and establish any hydraulic or other system for supplying water to the miners in face of the monopoly created by this second Order in Council. The rights conferred upon the parties by this Order in Council extend also for the period of thirty years, and they also have the right, as they had under the first Order in Council, to assign their rights to any person or corporate bodies.
The House will remember that one of the conditions imposed upon these people was that they were to do work within the short space of a few months to the extent of $250,000. They were to give evidence of their bona fides, and of their ability to carry out this concession, by spending in that district for the benefit of the miners the sum of $250,000. They were also obliged to bring in at least 2,000 miners into this dis-

trict before ; they could make entry for and work upon these claims in the rich creeks I have already mentioned. Singularly enough, by the Order in Council, no such conditions are imposed upon these gentlemen. They are not obliged to expend this $250,000, and they are not obliged, either to construct or' to make those works within the time specified by the first Order in Council. The question presents itself. Where has this $250,000 gone ? That question would strike anybody. These people came up with the evident intention of establishing these works and of putting up a large sum of money to show their ability to construct these works, to show their bona fides, and all at once, by this Order in Council, they are relieved of this obligation of spending $250,000, and even for the space of six years to do any work whatever in this district. So under the Order in Council which gives them the right to assign these powers given to them, .they may, during six years, hold up this country as it were, while they are floating their company in England, while they are trying to get somebody in England to put money into this scheme, while they are trying to float a company which will take hold of this valuable concession. If this Order in Council is maintained by this government, I have no doubt a company will be formed to reap the rich benefits which have been sown by Mr. Treadgold and his associates.
Now, Sir, a short time after this second Order in Council had been passed, as we know, an election was held in the Yukon district, and the electors sent here my hon. friend (Mr. Ross) who now represents this district, but who. I am sorry to say, is not in the House. It would have been well if he had been here, and I have no doubt that the reasons of his absence are valid and good reasons, and that he would not be absent unless it was absolutely impossible for him to be here. I regret it, because I have no doubt that he could have given to this House his experience and a great many explanations which this House needs in order to grapple with this most intricate question. As I said before, an election was held. Now what was the first plank laid down by the convention which selected this gentleman who now represents that district, the conventibn which gave him written instructions as to what he was to do when he came into this House. I hold in my hand now the Liberal platform which was adopted by the Liberal convention at the election in question. Among other things, here is what was laid down as one of the planks of that platform :
Whereas, the supply of water and power to the mines on the creeks is one of the most serious questions of the day in the Yukon territory, and whereas, in the opinion of the convention the matter of such supply on fair and reasonable terms could best be dealt with by the government itself and should not be left to private individuals ;

Therefore, be it resolved, that the government be requested immediately to make careful examination and obtain reports upon the subject with the view of cancelling forthwith the Tread-gold concessions, and undertaking such supply as may be needed.
Now, Sir, this Is not the concession which was given to these people in the first Order in Council, this is not the concession condemned by the Liberal convention, which was given by the first set of Orders in Council to Mr. Treadgold and his associates; but this is the Order in Council which was passed during the last session while we were sitting here in the House on the 21st of April, 1902. One of the very first planks which was laid down in the Liberal convention called before the election in the Yukon district is that representations should be made by the member who is to be elected for the district so that the government shall forthwith cancel this Treadgold concession.
Is that the one that is in force to-day ?

That is the one that is in force to-day-the Order in Council which was passed on the 21st April, 1902, and which is still in force. The platform goes on to say :
Resolved, that in the opinion of this convention many of the concessions now held were obtained by fraud or imposition.
The House will remember that I read over a list of the concessions-the Boyle concession and others which were given by this government, and against which the citizens of the Yukon district protested in a petition addressed by them to the Governor General in 1900. It is alleged that these concessions were obtained by fraud, that they were obtained by misrepresentation, that they were obtained by concealment. The convention went on to eomplaiu that the government had given these concessions to some of its own favourites. It says that:
It is in the interests of this territory that such concessions should be annulled and to that end that an inquiry should be set on foot to ascertain the circumstances of such fraud and imposition, and action taken by the Attorney General of Canada in the premises.
I would ask my hon. and learned friend if he has instituted the inquiries in regard to these concessions which are called here by the friends of the government fraudulent concessions ? Then it goes on to say :
Resolved, that a policy should be adopted which would prevent the obtaining of concessions for hydraulicking except in places where the dirt is of such low grade that it could not profitably be worked by other methods; and that before any hydraulic lease should issue, notice should be given by the applicant by publication in the newspapers of his intention of applying for such lease, so as to enable protests to be entered against the granting of the

same; and that the owners of hydraulic concessions already granted should he compelled to carry out the strict terms of their leases, and that in default of their so doing, their leases should he cancelled.
While these leases continue in existence nobody can work the mines for which hydraulic leases are given. This vast mining territory is there idle and, as is stated in the papers from which I have read, the men are leaving the Yukon because they cannot work these claims. That is the platform adopted at the Liberal convention which chose the hon. member who now represents the Yukon territory (Mr. Ross), and his answer is contained in a letter which I also hold in my hand :
I have received-
Mr. Ross says-
-a copy of the platform adopted by the convention which honoured me by its nomination as a candidate for the House of Commons for Canada. I freely subscribe to every measure suggested therein.
That hon. gentleman comes to this House pledged to have this concession repealed and to have it cancelled forthwith. Why is it not cancelled to-day, because it was obtained by fraud and misrepresentation ? The Order in Council still exists to-day, and such a monopoly exists as will drive people away from the Yukon and prevent them from coming in to work the mines. He gives them solemnly a pledge to see that this Order in Council granting this and other concessions, which it is alleged were obtained by fraud, should be immediately cancelled, and that this country should be relieved from what the ' Daily Sun ' describes as a giant octopus. He goes on to say :
I recognize that the whole business life of the Yukon depends upon the success of the prospector and miner, and they above all others must be encouraged. With this in view I shall advocate the reduction of fees, which, I think, may now be safely done without impairing the revenue; the thorough investigation of the charges of fraud made in respect to the manner in which certain concessions are alleged to have been obtained, and if such fraud is established, the immediate commencement of such proceedings as may be required to vacate the grants, and the enforcement of strict compliance with the conditions embodied in all Crown grants in the Yukon.
I am sorry that it is impossible for the hon. gentleman to be here, because I have uo doubt lie would give some good reasons for liis silence so long- in this House after having received this command from his constituents to see that these concessions were forthwith repealed. At the same time some questions were put to him by a gentleman in the Yukon representing a certain section of the electors of that district, and here are some of the questions ;

Will you pledge yourself to advocate for and insist upon the punishment and exposure of officials both in Dawson and Ottawa by whose fraud or culpable negligence or inefficiency those concessions were granted in the first instance, or are now continued in force after the same by their terms should be cancelled ?

The hon. gentleman was not himself able to give an answer to these questions, but it was answered by his right bower, the gentleman who is now Governor of the Yukon territory, Mr. F. T. Congdon, who wrote as follows

Sir,-I beg to say that your questions were received and forwarded to Mr. Ross at too late a date for it to be possible for him to have answered them by this time. So that this hon. gentleman was elected on the distinct pledge that he would come to Ottawa and have these concessions cancelled forthwith. This Order in Council should be cancelled now If everything I have read from these documents is true. It should never have been passed in the first place. After all the condemnation which has been brought down upon the heads of the government by the passing of the first Order in Council, this second Order in Council, which does not materially differ from the first Order in Council, should never have been passed, and I say that the government should be condemned by this House for passing the second Order in Council after having been warned by its own friends of the detrimental effects which this concession would have upon the Yukon district. I have evidence of this in a question which was put to the administration not long ago. The Dawson hoard of trade telegraphed to certain gentlemen in this House, and amongst others to the right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier), in the following terms :
Oppose any attempt to pass Order in Council' or Act in parliament that will in any way confirm Treadgold concession. Are having monster petition signed and reliable data prepared to



forward to Ottawa, asking government to aid in furnishing -water for mining purposes. People are a unit in making demands and will insist on government protection from monopoly of Treadgold octopus.
To which the right hon. leader of the government replied :
You are altogether mininformed as to what you call the Treadgold concession.
No such action contemplated either by legislation or government order.
The people of the Yukon should have had a satisfactory answer from the right hon. leader of the government, but this was a rather ambiguous answer. I do not quite understand the reply which the right hon. leader of the government made to the very distinct telegram which was sent to him by the president of the Dawson board of trade. The right hon. leader of the government says :
No such action contemplated either by legislation or government order.
What does the right hon. gentleman mean? Does he mean that this Order in Council required no confirmation at the hands of this parliament ? Does he mean that the Order in Council is a valid concession of the franchise which the government purpose to give these people ? Is that the meaning of the telegram; or does my right hon. friend by this telegram mean, that he will not do anything at all; that he will let this concession stand or fall on its owu merits, but he will not ask his government or ask this House to confirm it in any manner whatever. I really do not know what the right hon. gentleman meant by this. However, this fact remains; that the Order in Council has not been repealed; that it is still in existence, and that although it is as obnoxious and as illegal and as unconstitutional as the first Order in Council, no steps have been taken yet by the government to repeal it and to give satisfaction to these people in the Yukon who have been crying out against this shameful state of things. The Dawson Board of Trade, after having seen this telegram also sent a petition which is on file here, and which is signed by a large number of the people of the Yukon. The Dawson Board of Trade addressed a letter to the newspapers in which the Treadgold concession which is now in force is commented upon in the following terms :
The Treadgold concession and water grant as granted by an Order in Council and which when ratified by the parliament at its next session will become law is, in the opinion of this board, one of the most iniquitous measures that was ever inflicted upon a people, and (in the consideration of the Dawson Board of Trade) will work a great hardship upon the people of this territory since it will mean the virtual bankruptcy of all the property owners of Dawson and surrounding territory, and instead of the Klondike becoming the prosperous country we expect, it will virtually become the property Mr. CASGRAIN.
of Mr. Treadgold and those who are associated with him in his scheme.
In this community tbe Treadgold concession is called 'the infamous Treadgold grant,' and is alluded to as an ' iniquitous concession,' and in the petition which was sent to the House of Commons this language is used. After reciting part of the Order in Council, it says :
2.	That the benefits conferred upon the grantees are of incalculable value and involve an enormous exploitation of the public resources of this territory for the benefit of a few favoured concessionaires.
3.	That In the opinion of your petitioners the accumulation of extraordinary powers in the hands of a single corporation such as is affected by the above Order in Council, will lead to the paralysis of the independent, commercial and industrial life of the community and will prove In the highest degree oppressive and injurious to the public welfare, since the grantees are thereby enabled to crush out competition and to reduce to a position of practical servitude the individual miners in the extensive district affected, which includes the richest portion of the Klondike.
4.	That the need of this territory is not the creation of monopolies, but their prevention, and the encouragement of the individual miners by securing equal privileges and opportunities to ail as far as the law and the administration can provide them.

Your petitioners therefore pray :
1. That the Order in Council of April 21, 1902, may be cancelled completely, and that no special privileges shall hereafter be granted within this territory with respect to wood, mining, water or any other class of rights affecting the general public; hut that all persons shall be restricted in such matters to the rights conferred upon every member of the community by the mining regulations.
Now, Sir, the House will see that the very same condemnation which was brought down upon the government for passing the first Order in Council is brought down upon their heads to-day for passing the second Order in Council. I take it that the Dawson Board of Trade, in the very nature of things, is not composed entirely of opponents of the government, and in the estimation of that board of trade this huge monopoly conferred by the second Order in Council should be cancelled immediately. They state that if it is not cancelled it will do a great injustice to the miners of the Yukon district, and that it is calculated to injuriously affect the interests not only of the Klondike but to injure the commercial interests of Canada as a whole.
Hear, hear.

The Dawson city council passed exactly the same resolution and sent a petition to the House of Commons, and these resolutions being couched precisely in
