the same terms as those passed by the Board of Trade which I have just read, it will be unnecessary for me to repeat them. And here I am again face to face with my friends of the Liberal club of Dawson. You will remember, that although they are friends of the present administration, they thought it was their bounden. duty to condemn that first concession which was given to Mr. Treadgold and his associates. Apparently they do not find a very great difference between the first concession and the concession which is in existence to-day. They do not find the great changes which the Minister of the Interior tried to persuade this House last session had been made in the second Order in Council. On the contrary, they go on with their agitation against the second Order in Council and they have petitioned the government and this parliament to withdraw or to cancel the second concession as being just as bad as the first one, against which, they protested in the month of February, 1902. The petition of the Liberal Association of Dawson and of the Yukon Territory, goes on to say :
That the development of the resources of the Yukon has been seriously impeded by the appropriation of extensive areas of rich placer ground by hydraulic concessions believed in some instances to have been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation.
This alludes not only to the Treadgold concession, but it relates also to the other concessions which are mentioned in the petition to the Governor General in Council in 1900, and which were referred to in the platform of the Liberal convention when the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Boss) was elected, and also in the questions which were put to the hon. member (Mr. Ross) and which he answered by his friend Mr. Congdon, before he was elected. These concessions not only include the Treadgold concession, but also the concessions which I enumerated to the House. We find the Liberal club stating that these concessions were obtained by fraud and misrepresentation. Now, Sir, if the government has been the victim of fraud or misrepresentation, it is its bounden duty to immediately cancel not only the Treadgold concession, but the other hydraulic mining concessions which were given to the other parties I have named. This demand is made on the government by their awn friends in the district and by people who seem to know what they are talking about. The petition of the Liberal club says :
Your petitioners therefore pray :
That the Order in Council of April 21, 1902, granting certain rights and privileges to Mal-com Orr Ewing, A. N. C. Treadgold and Walter Barwick, may be rescinded absolutely.
That the government institute forthwith a careful investigation by competent engineers and obtain reports upon the subject with a view to undertaking the construction of a public water supply as a national enterprise.

That the water of Rock creek be retained by the government for public purposes and that no special privileges either in such creek or with respect to wood, water or mining rights within this territory, be granted to any individual or private corporation, but that all persons be restricted in such matters to the rights accorded the general public under the mining regulations.
That all hydraulic concessions whose owners have not observed the conditions of their leases and the provisions of the mining regulations may be rescinded.
That an inquiry may be set on foot to ascertain the circumstances under which the leading hydraulic concessions were obtained in order that action may be taken by the Attorney General of Canada in the premises.
That the Attorney General of Canada do issue a fiat authorizing prceedings to be taken in his name in every case where action is begun against an hydraulic concession in which fraud or misrepresentation is charged, including all such actions as are now pending.
Therefore, I repeat, that in view of these petitions signed by the great majority of the people in the Klondike district, and the great majority of the Liberals at that, it is the bounden duty of the government to see that these concessions are cancelled. It seems to me that if the inquiries which have been asked for in these petitions are not granted, it is either because the government wants to favour those to whom these concessions have been made by fraud and misrepresentation, or, that the government itself is guilty of fraud in giving these concessions to these individuals.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

I do not see how the government can escape from that dilemma. Now, Sir, a delegation has been appointed, not only from Dawson City, but from the different points at which gold is mined in the Yukon district. That delegation is composed of Mr. Clarke and Mr. Pringle. Mr. Pringle, I am told, is an excellent Liberal, and he is coming to Ottawa or has arrived here, to insist on the cancellation of this Treadgold concession. At a meeting which was held at Bonanza, Mr. Pringle spoke as follows :
The assay office is the most pressing demand. I say it now and I said it then. The Treadgold concession is in fact the paramount question. after all. Because, if Treadgold owns the country, there will be no gold to assay and no need for banks. But the miners want the assay office first, and they want the Treadgold concession cancelled next.
I am a Liberal and have always been a Liberal. But it seems to me the Liberal government in its administration in the Yuko.n has driven a coach and four through everything I ever knew that was Liberal.
We can live in this country if you stop graft. I stand against graft.
The appointed members of the Yukon council refused to sign our telegram to Ottawa against the Treadgold concessions because they said it would be a slap in the face of the government. They will vote against us for the same reason when the council meets.

The telegram which was proposed to be sent by the council of the Yukon to the government is in the following terms-it was signed by Messrs. Clarke, Pringle, Thompson and Landreville, the elective members of the council:
We, the elected members of the Yukon council ask the government to recind the Tread-gold concession in toto.
We represent a people who are absolutely united in their demand for the cancellation of the present Order in Council. Its continued existence means the ruin of business and of the placer mining industry in the Yukon Territory.
That telegram was sent to the government.
Now, Sir, not only were these grants made improvidently, not only were they most detrimental to the best interests of the Yukon and of the country at large, but it seems to me that they are absolutely illegal-that the Governor in Council had no right to make them. There is no doubt-and on this proposition I think I shall be borne out by my learned friend the Minister of Justice-that public lands or the public domain belonging to the Crown cannot be granted by Order in Council, except in those particular instances in which the Governor in Council is by statute given power or authority to make such grants. I think that is a sound proposition in constitutional law ; for, after all, the government are only a committee of this House, and they have no other powers than those which this House specifically delegates to them. They have power to administer, but they have not power to grant or even sell any part of the domain of the Crown. Take, for instance, the Dominion Lands Act. By section 29 of that Act, specific power is given to the Minister of the Interior and his agents under certain conditions to grant public lands to settlers ; but this provision goes to show that in other circumstances the Crown domain is sacred, and can only be conceded or sold by the authority of parliament, and not by the authority of the ministers, who are only a committee of this House. The Crown domain consists not only of the public lands of this country, but also of the rivers and streams which flow through it. Of course, the navigable streams all belong to the public domain and cannot be given away, granted or sold by Order in Council. But in a territory like the Yukon, where the government is the proprietor, the owner, on both sides of streams which are not navigable, I take it that the Crown is equally the proprietor and owner of the streams. These concessions which were granted by the Order in Council were concessions to private individuals of certain parts of the Crown domain. The very franchise itself by which these gentlemen were permitted to build dams across rivers and streams, to build pumping stations anywhere they saw fit, to maintain electric works for the purpose of transmitting electric power all Mr. CASGRAIN.	[DOT]
through that district, to expropriate private lands and lands belonging to the government, is a franchise that belongs to the Crown. Every day before the Private Bills Committee and the Railway Committee, persons appear for the purpose of obtaining franchises belonging to the Crown for the purpose of expropriating the lands of private individuals or lands belonging to the Crown ; and if it were only a franchise in the water that was given to these people, it would be a grant of a certain portion of the property vested in the Crown, of which the Governor in Council had no right to divest the Crown. The authority under which the second Order in Council was passed is stated in the preamble of the Order in Council itself. The following statutes are quoted :	Clause 47 of the
Dominion Lands Act as amended by section 5, of chapter 15, of 55-56 Victoria ; section 8, of the Yukon Territories Act, as amended by chapter 11 of 62-63 Victoria. The minister has taken the precaution of giving us the quotation from the statutes under which he proposes to Act, and he says in the preamble of this Order in Council that it is in virtue of these two statutes. No doubt, if he could find any other statutes which would give the Governor General in Council power and authority to make these concessions, he would have quoted them also. Now, let us take the first statute which he quotes, the 47th section of the Dominion Lands Act, as amended by section 5, of chapter 15, of 55-56 Victoria, which reads thus :
Lands containing coal or other minerals, including lands in the Rocky Mountains park, shall not be subject to the provisions of this Act respecting sale or homestead entry, but the Governor General in Council may, from time to time, make regulations for the working and development of mines on such lands, and for the sale, leasing, licensing or other disposal thereof.
The effect of this statute is this :	First,
it takes away from the minister and the Governor General iu Council the right to do with these lands what the minister does with the ordinary Dominion lands which lie concedes or grants to settlers. The legislature says by this section, that he shall not treat mineral lands in that way, but that he can make regulations for the working and development of mines on such lands, and for the sale, leasing, licensing or other disposal thereof. So that what should have been done would have been to pass regulations for so dealing with this part of the public domain. The regulation takes the place of the law. For instance, under the Dominion Lands Act the settler' applies for a part of the public domain as a homestead. Therefure, if regulations were passed for the sale or lease of mineral lands, anybody could come in and say to the government:	I have complied
with the regulations and am entitled to a grant of mineral lands.
Are these all mineral lands ?

Yes. This is the very section which is quoted, and I do not see how the minister can take any relief from it. He is doing exactly what the law forbids. The law says that he can only lease or grant lands under the general regulations which govern all the subjects of Her Majesty, so that any man who complies with these regulations and conditions is entitled to the benefit of them. But until he does comply with them, the Governor General in Council is powerless to grant, concede or sell any part of these mineral lands. Let me however refer to the second statute quoted in the preamble of the Order in Council and see whether the hon. gentleman can take any relief from it. This statute is section eight of the Yukon Territory Act, as amended by 62-63 Victoria. I call attention to this section because I cannot see how the Minister of the Interior could have gone before his colleagues and quoted to them this law as authorizing him to make this concession. I cannot come to any other conclusion than that this grant was put through council hastily and carelessly, and that none of the hon. gentleman's colleagues could have looked at the statutes or realized the enormity of the concessions which they were asked to give. Section eight of the Yukon Territory Act, as amended, says :-	*
Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Governor in Council can make ordinances for the peace, order and good government of the territory, and of Her Majesty's subjects and others therein ; but no ordinances made by the Governor in Council or the commissioner in council, shall-
(c) Appropriate any public land or other property of Canada without authority of parliament, or impose any duty of customs or any excise.
So that the very statute which the hon. gentleman quotes in the Order in Council says that the Governor in Council shall have no right to appropriate any public land or other property of Canada without the authority of parliament. The very authority which the hon. gentleman quotes is against him. It is an authority which says that he cannot do what he proposes to carry out. I await the explanation of the government on this point with a great deal of interest. Of course I know that we can sometimes drive a coach and four through any law, but it will certainly require great skill to overcome these two statutes cited in the Order in Council. It seems to me that these concessions should be immediately repealed. They are certainly against the interests of the miners and other citizens of the Yukon. They will certainly prove prejudicial to the interests of Canada as a whole, and I beg therefore to move :-
That all the words after ' that ' in the proposed motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor :-
This House regrets that by an Order in Council of date the 21st day of April, 1902, the government for the ostensible purpose of establishing hydraulic works to supply water for the efficient working of auriferous deposits have granted to one A. N. C. Treadgold, of London, England, and his associates, vast powers, franchises, and concessions in and upon the beds, banks, valleys, slopes and hills of the Klondike river, Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks, and in and upon the waters of Rock creek, in the Yukon Territory, with the right to establish for the benefit and advantage of the concessionaires in and through the region and district through which these rivers and creeks run, hydraulic, electrical and other systems, and to enter and to take up and operate mining and other lands :
This House is of opinion that the said powers, franchises and concessions constitute in favour of the said Treadgold and his associates a gigantic monopoly, which, while depriving the treasury of enormous revenues, is most detrimental to the mining industry of the Yukon : And that in so making the said grants and concessions by Order in Council, the government have exceeded their authority and have committed a gross breach of the duty entrusted to them under the constitution.

The subject, Mr. Speaker, which the hon. gentleman has brought to the attention of the House is one of considerable importance, largely involving legal questions, but at the same time not free from questions of public policy. The hon. gentleman quoted some interesting extracts from newspaper reports and other anonymous communications and utterances of various kinds.

Would the hon. gentleman give the names of the gentlemen who wrote the various documents, editorials and so on, which he quoted ?
I said that it was the editor of the Dawson ' Sun ' who wrote the articles, and that these were sent to the government by the late Senator Wood.

My hon. friend has taken the proceeding-unusual in courts of justice though not always in popular tribunals-of quoting newspaper reports and articles, and other uncorroborated utterances and building thereon an elaborate argument, which may appeal with some force to people who are not familiar with the facts. It appears to me that the address and the argument of the hon. gentleman on this occasion would have been much more fittingly made in the Yukon district itself, at the time, shortly before this session opened, when the people there were given the opportunity of pronouncing a verdict on the administration of this government. This is not the first time that hon.

gentlemen opposite have taken advantage of their position as members of this House, to rise in their seats and attempt to vilify the administration of the Yukon, and spread broadcast throughout the country the most unfounded aspersions on the policy and the conduct of the government. While I am not taking any exception to the ventilating of this matter again in this House, I think that I have the right to point out that there was a most appropriate occasion, not long ago, when the hon. gentleman could have addressed to a tribunal composed of the people directly interested, the arguments he has just made here. I refer to the electors of the Yukon. Why the present session should have been selected rather than that occasion, it is for the hon. gentleman to explain. During many sessions another hon. gentleman in this House took the interests of the Yukon district under his special care. He was the self-constituted guardian in this House of everything dear to those people. I refer to the hon. and senior member for Pictou (Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper). But neither did that hon. gentleman venture beyond these precincts. Neither did he go to the Yukon and there make his charges before the people who are most familiar with the facts and best able to pass judgment on them. But he preferred making them at this convenient distance. Now, there was abundant opportunity given at the late election for hon. gentlemen opposite to have denounced before the electors of the Yukon the administration of that district in their most vigorous fashion. They were given ample notice. They had six months notice. We passed an Act a year ago giving representation to the people of the Yukon; and we challenged these hon. gentlemen on the floor of this House to meet us during the recess before the people of the Yukon and tight out these charges, so properly determinable by the people, before the electors themselves. Sir, they did not appear on that occasion; they abandoned the issue. They had not the courage to make the charges before the electors of the Yukon. We put a candidate in the field and the electors of the Yukon returned him as a supporter of this government by an overwhelming majority. Unfortunately that hon. gentleman (Mr. Boss, Yukon) for reasons which we all regret, is absent from the House to-day. He is absent from Ottawa. Otherwise, perhaps, he would be heard upon this matter. It is also to be regretted-and by none more than by myself-that the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) who is so familiar with the details of these transactions, is also absent from the House, attending to public business of a high character in London, England. I can only speak from such information as comes readily to my hand through reviewing the papers in the department. To that extent, therefore, I will address myself to the particular subject in question.

The hon. gentleman took many exceptions to the/ Order in Council. Let me first, so far as I know it, describe the situation and the outlook for the government. When the Yukon was discovered and it was learned to be rich, in placer mines, everything was prosperous. But the time came when the placer mining began to give out. Still, every one felt that there must be a future for that district, and it was the duty of the government to endeavour in all possible ways to aid in furthering mining operations. There are many kinds of gold mining. There is placer mining, hydraulic mining, quartz mining, as well as the recovery of gold from water. These are various methods for utilizing the 'rich gifts of Providence to the Yukon. When the lower claims near the water level became exhausted, it was necessary to consider by what means the government could succeed in delivering water on the elevations, that it might be available there for washing out the gravel upon the benches and hills. Manifestly, that is a task not to be carried on by each individual for himself. Business suggests at once that a large scheme for the development of power and the pumping of water is the proper way of supplying the individual with the necessary water. It is just as it is in cities to-day. Municipalities deem it wiser to establish water-works and operate public service, rather than leave it to each individual as in primitive times, to supply his own conveniences. And so, for the purpose of working these claims above the creek and a little distance away from the water, it, manifestly, is the mo lie businesslike and economical and profitable method to carry on that business by having a company or some wholesale system, whereby each person can purchase just such water as he requires without each having to duplicate the capital expenditure necessary for the establishment of works to supply himself with water. And so, the Department of the Interior endeavoured to obtain offers in order to provide water for the upper mining district. Manyi schemes had been suggested. But the Department of the Interior was extremely desirous of placing this franchise, if possible, in the hands of men of reputation, men of financial strength. My hon. friend has read from the newspapers charging fraud all round, he has charged concealment, misrepresentation and fraud. I do not know! whether he alludes to the gentlemen to whom these grants were made. But, if he does, I think they have good ground to complain. One of these gentlemen is well known to every hon. gentleman in this House. He is well known iu this country; and highly as I respect the reputation of my colleagues on both sides in this House, I think I am not going beyond the facts when I say, that there is no man who enjoys more the respect of the people of Canada as an upright man than one of the grantees whom my hon. friend charges with having been guilty of fraud of

many kinds towards this country. I refer to Mr. Walter Barwick. I would also say to my hon. friend who tells us that he is so desirous of investigation that I am sure he must well know that ft has been long the fixed intention of thy government to hold such an investigation. The hon. gentleman must remember that, when the election was held, promises were given to the people of the Yukon that there would be a commission to inquire into the whole administration of that territory. There has been no opportunity since that date until the present to send in commissioners. I doubt if navigation is more than open, even if it is yet open. When the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Boss) returns to Ottawa, -lie is at present in British Columbia, I understand-and we can have the benefit of his advice, it is our intention to fully carry out the representations made to the citizens of the Yukon to have a full investigation into all charges or suspicions that lion, gentlemen may be good enough to mention or entertain in regard to any matters connected with the Yukon administration. X give that public notice to my hon. friend, so that, in addition to the advantage he has had of ventilating his views on the floor of this House, he will have an opportunity to make good, if he can, any of his charges or suspicions /before a; tribunajl where newspaper extracts and letters will not be the only evidence, but where gentlemen will have the privilege of pledging their oaths to the truth of all they say. I would point, out that, in his zeal to magnify, he has entirely misapprehended the scope of the Order in Council. He reads from newspapers to show that we abandoned 850 square miles of territory comprising all these rich creeks and gulches and rivers. The hon. gentleman is a lawyer, and he proposed to make a legal speech and to give the legal effect of documents; yet there is not even a layman in this House but, I am sure, will see that he has entirely misrepresented-I speak without meaning anything offensive-he lias given to the House an entirely erroneous impression of the scope of the concessions spoken of. Though there is a grant of power to erect a dam upon the river, to take water and generate power, and because that gives these concessionaires the right to sell that power throughout that district, by what process of reasoning does he say that the whole district with all its wealth is handed over as a grant to these concessionaires ? Why, Sir, when you grant a privilege to erect dams and generate electricity on a river and give the grantees the right to sell that power to the public, unless you restrict the deed, the grantees have the right to sell power throughout the whole of Canada. And if it should happen that such a grant were given, my hon. friend, according to his present reasoning, would argue that such a grant carried the exclusive possession and ownership of Canada. That is the necessary result of his reasoning-because they are given the privilege of selling electricity over a certain area, that carries with it all other possible rights. Now, what does the Order in Council grant? The Order in Council of June, 1901, differs materially from the Order in Council of 1902. My hon. friend says there is no material difference. Let us see. lie is a lawyer, and has carefully studied these questions, he has had these papers in his hands since last session and knows all about them. I have the two copies here, my hon. friend has the two copies also. I,et us see if he will adhere to his statement that there is no material difference between the one and the other Order in Council. Under the first Order in Council a considerable term of years was granted. Under the first Order in Council it was necessary for certain works to be done within a certain time. There has been a modification, my hon. friend will say for the worse, by having substituted six years for a shorter period. I merely remark that in one sense the work required under the second Order has not to be completed as quickly as under the first. But I pass to the new section, and I commend it to the hon. gentleman's attention :
Provided, that if any power is developed and rendered available by the grantees under this section which they do not make use of, then the' same should be offered for sale to the public, and the rates to be charged therefor shall be subject to the control of the Governor General in Council.
Now, 1 would say that is an entirely new clause. When the first Order in Council was a subject of criticism in the Yukon, a meeting of the miners was held, and they appointed two delegates to come to Ottawa and ask for modifications, not for a repeal of this Order in Council. The majority of the miners of the Yukon, so far as we know, do not desire the repeal of all the Orders in Council, they do not ask for a repeal of the old Orders in Council, but they ask for modifications, and the modifications they asked for were of the following character :	They objected, for example,
to the exclusive right given by the first Order in Council to erect bedrock flumes. That was regarded as a very objectionable feature of the first order. That objectionable feature is removed, and does not appear in the second Order in Council. Not only does it not appear, but privileges are given to every person, reserved to every person to erect bedrock flumes. One of the great questions in the Yukon in regard to the first Order in Council was the exclusive right granted to construct, maintain and use bedrock flumes. People were excited upon that point, and they sent two delegates, Mr. Williams and Mr. Sugrue, to consult with the government and ask that all objectionable features might be removed from the first Order in Council. That was the first point that the people proposed, and that point was arranged. That former objection disappeared, and yet my hon. friend

says there is no material difference in the two Orders in Council.
The hon. gentleman says that the majority of the miners did not want that concession repealed. I would like to ask how the majority of the miners voiced their opinion ?

The two representatives of the miners who came to Ottawa, purporting to represent the opinions and wishes of the miners, did not ask for repeal, but for modifications, and those modifications were granted. I think it is reasonable to assume, when they came down on a mission of that kind and presented their arguments, that they were voicing the sentiments of those they were representing here. Again, my hon. friend says there is no difference between these two Orders in Council. The first Order in Council allowed the grantees to develop power and use it all for themselves. There was no duty cast upon them under the first order to sell power to anybody. How Is it under the new Order in Council ? Will my hon. friend tell me this is not a material change ?
Provided that if any power is developed and rendered available by the grantees under this section which they do not make use of, then this same shall he offered for sale to the public.
Is that not a material change ? My hon. friend does not see that under the new order the public are the beneficiaries to the extent that they have a right to purchase the power that may be generated under this concession.
At what price ?

I will proceed to read. Hon. gentlemen should restrain themselves, they will get all this information in due time. They would have been much wiser if they had known the Orders in Council before malting these inflammatory speeches.
We know them.

My hon. friend from Compton (Mr. Pope) asks at what price.
The rates to be charged therefor shall be subject to the control of the Governor General in Council.
That is the way the rates are fixed in this country in many other cases. The Governor in Council fixes the railway rates and many other kinds of rates ; and here the Governor in Council, responsible to parliament and to the public, are the parties who stand as an independent tribunal between the buyers and sellers of power, so that under the amended Order in Council the general public have vested rights entitling them to power and entitling them to protection against unfair prices.
Does the power mean water ?

No. There the hon. gentlemen show a limited knowledge of this scheme. Power means the electrical power that is going to be developed by the use of water. There is going to be a dam, or a backing up of water. Hon. gentlemen smile ; let me read the olanse :
The sole right to divert and take water from the Klondike river at any point or points between its entry into the Yukon river and the Flat creek for the purpose o.f generating power with which to pump water to work the auriferous deposits in the district.
This is an entirely different proposition from the right to take water from the bed of the river and to raise it up, whether it may or may not return to the river.
Have these concessionaires no right to sell power under the first Order in Council ? Had the public no right to compel them to sell power ?
We will see about that.
Where is there anything in the Order in Council about it ?

When they have the power generated then they have to sell it, if there is any one to buy it, and if there is any to spare. I turn to section 2. Under the first Order in Council it has been correctly stated that the grantees had the right to divert and take water from the Klondike for distribution in the district generally, for the use of benches and other claims. Under the new order, the amount that they may take exclusively is 5.000 miners' inches.
How much does that amount to ?
I wonder if the hon. gentleman has any idea how much water is available in that district.

We are asking for information. What volume of water does that
5,000	inches mean ?

I will explain that in a moment. Let me first explain that under the second Order in Council there is a prior right given to license holders :
Provided that licensed holders of mining locations situated on the Klondike river should be entitled as against the grantees to the use of a flow of water sufficient for working their claims but not exceed in all 3,500 miners' inches, equal to 5,250 cubic feet per minute.
A miners' inch, therefore, is equal to a cubic foot and a-lialf per minute. First of all, license holders take their 5,250 cubic feet per minute, then these grantees are entitled to take 5,000 miners' inches per minute. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) desires to know what proportion that bears to the capacity of the river. I have here a memorandum from Professor Haanel in these words :

On the authority of Professor Herdt, of Montreal, the velocity of the Klondike is seven miles an hour, the average width 275 feet and the average depth feet. This will correspond to a delivery of 395,266 miners' inches.
The miners' inch was defined by Order it Council of the 19th of May, 1902, to be a discharge of 11 cubic feet per minute.
Tims the hon. gentleman will see that these 395,266 miners' inches representing nearly 11 cubic feet per minute of a flow, would certainly leave what is called a margin for the general public even if some one was to get 5,200 cubic feet per minute.

X thought the miners were to have 3,500 miners' inches and that all the rest was to go to these concessionaires. The Order in Council says :
Provided the licensed holders of mining locations situated on the Klondike river shall be entitled as against the grantees to the use of a flow of water sufficient for working their claims hut not exceeding in all three thousand five hundred (3,500) miners' inches, equal to five thousand two hundred and fifty (5,250) cubic feet per minute.
After the miners get their 5,250 cubic feet all the rest will belong to these concessionaires.
That may be the hon. gentleman's opinion as a member of this House, but I do not think it is his opinion as a member of the bar.
I will tell the hon. gentleman what my opinion is as a member of the bar if he wants it.
I am sure he would not say that it would lead to any such conclusion.
What is your conclusion ?

My conclusion is that the license holders on the Klondike river have a prior right to 3,500 miners' inches. The grant made to the grantees is named. If the whole of the rest of the water was to be given to the grantees what would be the sense of saying that they should have the right to the use of the water up to 5,250 cubic feet. I am sure my hon. friend will not press that point any further.
My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is evidently right and you are evidently wrong.

It is not so very long ago that hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House were evidently right on a legal question-the construction of the British North America Act. One after another got up in this House and presented an elaborate and learned argument to show that the representation of the various provinces should go in a certain way. It was found a few days, afterwards by the Supreme Court that every one of
these lion, gentlemen was wrong in his opinion of the law. They are bold to give their opinion again on the law.
Are you paying a compliment to the Supreme Court now ?
I am not paying any compliment, but I am just paying what is justly due to the Supreme Court.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would just give his own construction as he says we are wrong as to sections 1 and 2.
Does my hon. friend refer to the first or second Order iu Council ?

To the second Order in Council-that of April 21, 1902.
I want to understand it.

That is fair. Under section one, the concessionaires are given power to erect dams on the Klondike and take water from the Klondike for the purpose of generating power with which to pump the water for use iu a certain district named. Power is not given to them to take water for hydraulic or mining purposes, but to take water to generate electric power which will in turn set their machinery to work which will pump the water. That is the power which is given to them.
Have they the sole power to do that ?
Yes, my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) has the clause before him.

As I read section one of the last Order in Council it says :
The sole right to divert and take water from the Klondike river at any point or points between its entry into the Yukon river and Plat creek.
Then it says :
Provided that if the right given by this section is not exercised within six years from the date hereof, it may be revoked by order of the Governor General in Council.
Is that right to be tied up for a period of six years to these concessionaires ? Could not these concessionaires by injunction restrain any other company or individual from taking water from the Klondike river between these points.

No, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman does not appear to know that this Order in Council as yet has no legal validity. It gives no legal right. There are other things that have to be done with Orders in Council before they can have the force of law, but this Order in Council is an evidence of faith towards the concessionaires in the hope that they may be enabled-to induce capital to come to Canada and erect these works.
Does the hon. Postmaster General admit that the Order in Council is not valid ?
I mean to say that an additional step has to be taken to confer legal rights under the Order in Council.
What additional step i

Orders in Council such as these dealing with mining rights do not give powers to the grantees to exercise these rights until these Orders in Council are gazetted. Then, they become law. They are not gazetted at the present time. They are reserved, but if the concessionaires should show that they are able to raise the funds to erect these valuable public works, then it will be for the government to consider whether or not they would confirm the concession, but at the present time they simply have these Orders in Council indicating what they think it would be proper to do provided they could see that they are able to proceed satisfactorily.
What about the telegram from the board of trade ?

I now come to section 10. The hon. member for Montmorency said that there was no material difference between the two Orders in Council. The meeting of miners asked that in addition to relief from the monopoly in respect to bed rock flumes there should also be a change in the regulations in regard to abandoned claims. They contended that in a former Order in Council the grantees secured rights to abandoned claims and were not therefore obliged to do any work in the way of providing hydraulic power. But, the abandoned claims would not have had any value without the addition of the water. When the representatives of the Yukon miners appeared before the government. this point was thoroughly discussed and a new clause was framed and this has taken the place of the old one in the new Order in Council. I would refer my hon. friend to section 10. Section 10 reads as follows :
The right subject to no payment except the royalty prescribed upon output to make entry for and work any abandoned mining claim or claims on Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks, such right to he exercisable only when the grantees by the construction of works in pursuance of this franchise are in a position to deliver water upon such claim or claims for the working thereof.
Under the former order, it was argued that they might appropriate the abandoned claims and never expend a dollar in the erection of these works, but under the present order that is entirely changed, and tliev have no right whatever to an abandoned claim until they have laid water to it, and Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
then they have only the chanee of the general public who may step in and stake a claim and prevent the concessionaries getting it. So far as staking abandoned claims is concerned, they are only given the same rights as are given to any other person who may go to the Yukon. My hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) takes exception to the clause in this agreement which exempts the grantees from representation or the payment of fees. It is correct that the grantees are so exempt, but there are reasons for that. It is the effort of the government to induce these grantees to proceed and if possible to successfully carry out this undertaking. This is not -a very attractive proposition to the grantees. Up to this moment they have not been able to find capitalists to see anything in it. They got the first concession in January, 1901. Over two years have elapsed since then, and if this were such a valuable franchise ; if there were such fortunes in it, don't you think that the shrewd business world of London, where those people are men of influence, would have long since contributed to the capital to provide for the carrying out of this alleged improvident transaction ? But as yet they have not been able to convince any person that there is any money in this enterprise. When the second Order in Council was passed, consideration had to be had to expenditures already made. My hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) says that tinder the new arrangement we abandon the clause requiring the expenditure of $250,000. That is correct. The first Order in Council called for the expenditure of money, and the grantees proceeded to expend money. They engaged some of the most able hydraulic engineers of England ; they sent out to the Klondike Sir Thomas Tancred, a very high authority, -and they expended a large sum of money in investigation and research.
How much ?
I am told by Mr. Bnrwick, that up to the time of the cancellation of the order the grantees had expended over $50,000.
Was there any work done on the ground ?

Not on the ground. They had to pay very large fees to the engineers, and other expenses, which Mr. Barwick informs me amounted to over $50,000. They had that amount of money at stake when the first Order in Council was cancelled, and therefore, they had the material interest of following their money in prosecuting the work. They have already, therefore, $50,000 in jeopardy, all of which will be lost unless they can turn the grant to practical use.-

Was there anybody else
Invited to go and examine the ground and
see what the proposition had in it ?
I think there were various parties making other proposals.
Will these proposals he laid on the Table ?

I only know that from general hearsay.
Mi-. CLARKE. Newspaper reports V

I am told that all the papers have been brought down. Then I come to another provision in this agreement, and I think lion, gentlemen will see that it is a clause which does a great service to the community. The scheme, whilst giving to the grantees the right to erect works, to generate power, and the right to make use of the water the same as others ; does not give them the exclusive right, but entitles the general public to water just the same as the general public are entitled to water from the city of Ottawa. The public of the Yukon have the same right to water and power as any private citizen in this city, and therefore, this is a public enterprise in which the whole community, on payment of a proper toll, will be entitled to share. Under the regulations it is left to the Gold Commissioner to fix all compensation arising under this grant. If the private user desires to have the price fixed, and if he cannot agree with the company, the Gold Commissioner fixes the price subject to an appeal to a higher tribunal.
How does the Gold Commissioner or the government know whether the price fixed is a reasonable one or not ?

The Gold Commissioner lives in the Yukon, and the people of the Yukon will know. There will be some way of ascertaining what is reasonable ; that is a question of opinion. At all events it is left to the Gold Commissioner and the Territorial Court of the district to settle a question of that kind. I do not know of a fairer tribunal ; perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) does. However, that may be, in trusting the rights of the people in an important matter of this kind to the Gold Commissioner, with the right of appeal to the Territorial Court, it does not, at least to my mind, indicate carelessness, improvidence, or fraud when we are trying to bring water within the reach of the people in order to develop that country.
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir William Mulock) is relying on the words : ' Any question of compensation.'

Yes, certainly, under the grant. The three differences which I have pointed out to the House are the three variations that the representations of the miners' have asked to be made. These three variations were made, and I would mention this circumstance : that when
the Minister of the Interior contemplated considering the change in this Order in Council, he found no hesitation whatever on the part of the grantees to the change being made. On the contrary, so little importance did they attach to their rights under the circumstances, they being so unprofitable up to that moment, that they readily consented to the cancellation of the Order in Council. There are a number of provisions in the Order in Council of 1901 which have been omitted from the new Order in Council. For example, section 3, of the old Order in Council has been omitted, and it reads as follows :
The right on the creels or tributary within the district to divert, take, impound and store for mining purposes any water not used by any free miner for the working of his claim on such creek or tributary under the regulations now in force for placer mining or respecting the diversion of water for mining purposes in the Yukon Territory.
That section has been left out of the new Order in Council. Again under the old Order in Council, it was provided that' the grantees should have an extension of time for the completion of their works in the event of delay caused by various things, such as floods, war, civil commotions, accidents to ( machinery or works, and other inevitable causes. That is omitted from the new Order in Council, and they are held more firmly to the time than before. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have pointed out a number of very material variations between the old order and the new ; and yet my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) said he saw no difference whatever between the old and the new. With reference to that part of my hon. friend's speech wherein he first of all stated that there had been large tracts of country withdrawn from entry, I think he was under the impression that they were withdrawn from entry before the granting of the first Order in Council. I take the liberty of correcting him. He read from the Dawson ' Sun ' a statement showing, as he supposed, a large area which that paper said was granted to these concessionaries. My hon. friend seems to suggest that entry had been closed in respect to a number of these creeks in order to enlarge the area to be granted to these concessionaries. He tells us it will have that effect. On that point he was not just.
That is imt my contention. Do not put words in my mouth which I did not use.

I do not intend to do so. I have given the hon. gentleman credit for a desire not to mislead, but I want to correct him. It is true, at one time, Dominion creek and Bonanza creek and their tributaries were closed against entry; but it is not correct to say that they were closed against entry at the time of the granting of the first Order in

Council, 'They had been re-opened prior to that time.
When ?
I cannot give the exact date.
I have it here.
Then the hon. gentleman can give it.
The lltli of April, 1902, by a telegram from the Minister of the Interior.
No, that is wrong.
Then the return to the motion is wrong, because that is where I got it.

I can give the hon. gentleman the text of it if he wishes :
Office of tlie Gold Commissioner of the Yukon Territory,
Dawson, Y.T., April 11, 1902.
The Secretary,
Department of the Interior,
Ottawa.
Sir,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of the following telegram from the Hon. Clifford Sif-ton to the Gold Commissioner : ' Throw open for entry at once all the lapsed and abandoned claims withheld from entry by reason of Tread-gold Order in Council.'
The minister's instructions in this matter have been carried out, and upon the receipt of the telegram the following notice was posted by the Gold Commissioner :
Dawson, Y.T., April 17, 1902,
4.30 p.m.
Notice is hereby given that from the above period all the lapsed and abandoned claims withheld from entry by reason, of the Treadgold Order in Council are ouen_ to locations by free miners under the Placer Mining Regulations.
(Sgd)	D. PATULLO,
Assistant Gold Commissioner.
Might I ask my hon. friend, while I am on my feet, to state which of these Orders in Council were cancelled and which were "not ?

I will try to answer that question; but I will say to my bou. friend lirst that tlie telegram which be lias read does not touch tlie point to which I am referring. I will read a memorandum from Mr. Iiyley, of tlie Department of the Interior :
The claims which were reserved from entry on Dominion Bonanza, and tributaries, were open for entry some time before the Order in Council of June, 1901.
This memorandum was sent to me from the gallery. I * suppose that if the officer had been in the department, he would have given the exact date. So that it will he seen that the grant is not so large as my hon. friend thinks.
If that had anything to do with this, why was it not brought down with the return ?

I suppose there are many things which might have to do with the debate here which would not form part of the return. It would depend on the wording of the order. I do not know what tlie order called for.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to summarize the effect of this order. The order in a nutshell is that if the grantees should succeed in raising capital, it will be their privilege to erect works upon the Klondike for the purpose of generating electric power. It will be their privilege to use, subject to certain restrictions, water for hydraulic purposes. It will be the right of the public to take such power as the concessionaires do not use, and to pay therefor such price as may be fixed by tbe Governor in Council. It will be tbe right of the public to compel tlie company to sell to them whatever water is available at such price as may be fixed by the Gold Commissioner, or, in case of appeal, by the Territorial Court of the district. These material rights are secured to the public, arid all they have to pay for these rights is what may be fixed by the Governor in Council or by the Territorial Court. Tlie public are not excluded from an inch of the country. They have an equal right with these grantees to enter on any of the abandoned claims. The only exclusive grants conveyed to the grantees are in respect to the water privileges for generating power, and, sub motu, to use a certain portion of the water themselves. You cannot find in these documents anything giving the grantees any exclusive privilege except as the people's representatives fix. These are some of the reasons, and the chief reasons doubtless, why capitalists have failed to find in this scheme any such attractions as to induce them to embark capital in it.	.
Have these people not six years to raise that capital, and is not that privilege tied up for that time ?

It is not tied up one day if we choose to repeal it. These gentlemen, we hope, will succeed iu raising the money necessary to build these works. If they do not, hon. gentlemen opposite will have the credit of preventing them. They have already paralyzed the enterprise.
Have any petitions been received from the Yukon in favour of this concession being continued ?

We have received the most complete communication from the Yukon in regard to this matter, and the general policy of the government that could be desired. We heard the voice of the people a few months ago. I believe, Mr. Speaker, the candidate of hon. gentlemen opposite lost his deposit. So you see there is some money left in the treasury there yet.
Because the other candidate was pledged to repeal this concession.
Sent here on purpose to repeal the concession.

I do not know that he was. He was pledged to promote the best interests of the Yukon, and he is doing it, and we are doing it.
I wish hon. gentlemen opposite were doing the same thing. I may not have dealt with this matter to the satisfaction of hon. gentlemen opposite; but I think I have dealt with it at least in such a way as to show the House and the country that this measure is one in the interest of the Yukon. Unless it is prevented from coming to fruition by obstacles thrown in its way, the time is not far distant when the people who make these charges will wonder at the attitude they have assumed; and among those who will be repentant for their mistakes will be some hon. gentlemen opposite, who will have ample opportunity to do so in the shades of opposition.

The hon. gentleman did not give the information I asked for. I asked him to state which of these Orders in Council had not been gazetted, I understood him to say that the Orders in Council did not come into force until they were gazetted. It is perfectly obvious that the first Order in Council must have been gazetted because it was acted upon.
How ?
By the closing of the abandoned claims to public entries, as the correspondence amply shows.
I do not think that the closing of the claims proves that the Order in Council was acted upon.
Will the hon. gentleman state whether or not the Order in Council was gazetted ?

I am pleased to give the hon. gentleman any information neoessary, and there is no occasion for him to show any temper or heat, though I suppose we should make some allowance. The second Order in Council was never gazetted. I did not make any inquiry, but if I can see any of the officials before eight o'clock, I shall do so.
Under what law was it passed ?
The hon. gentleman knows all the law.
That is why I want you to state it.
Under tiie Dominion Lands Act, section 51.

Which does not ajgply at all.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Mr. ROBERT A. PRINGLE (Cornwall and Stormont).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with every attention to the remarks of the Postmaster General and Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir William Mulock). I only wish that the task of replying to the hon. gentleman had fallen on worthier shoulders. It is probably for me rather a difficult task to stand up here and advocate the claims of those whom we may term the gum-boot miners, the men whose enterprise, labour and endurance of hardships have made for Canada all that is worth while in the Klondike to-day.
I was surprised to find the hon. Minister of Labour standing up here and, instead of advocating the cause of the miners, advocating the cause of the concessionaires of the monopolists, of the men who have obtained as I shall show an iniquitous concession from this government. And, Sir, what is the answer of the hon. Minister of Labour to the very able arraignment made by the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Cas-grain) ? His one answer to the accusation is :	Why, Sir, in the election of December 2, the Hon. Mr. Ross was returned as a member of the House of Commons; he was returned as a supporter of this government. But let us for a moment pause and see on what platform the hon. gentleman was returned. Was he returned as a supporter of this concession which we are now attacking ? Or was he returned as opposed to that concession ? Let us look for a moment at the platform of the Liberal party, in that election and see what it advocated. Let us examine the address of the hon. gentleman who was returned as a supporter of this government. I think this examination will convince you that he was returned pledged to oppose this concession, pledged to see that this concession was abolished. This is the platform ^dopted by the Liberal convention, and in every clause it is an arraignment of the present government. It begins :
Whereas, in the opinion of this convention the continued prosperity of the Yukon Territory depends chiefly on the efforts of individual miners and prospectors whose work is conducted under most difficult conditions, and the stability of the business of the country will be insured by furnishing regular employment to workmen ; therefore, be it
Resolved, that every effort should be made by the government to secure, and have such changes adopted as would secure, the ends desired ; that this convention most strongly recommends :-
1.	Reduction of fees for miners' licenses and for recording and renewing claims.
2.	The abolition of payment of commutation for assessment work, and compelling the per-

formanoe of assessment work upon the claim Itself or upon the claims as grouped.
Then follow seven or eight clauses, and the platform continues :
Whereas, in the opinion of the convention the matter of such supply

That Is dealing with the supply of water-
-on fair and reasonable terms should best be dealt with by the government itself, and should not be left to private individuals ; therefore, be it
Resolved, that the government be requested immediately to make careful examination and obtain reports upon the subject with a view to cancelling forthwith the Treadgold concession and undertaking such supply as a national enterprise.
Then, Sir, the hon. Minister of Labour said that the government were accused of granting these concessions by misrepresentation and fraud. Wbo accused them of it ? Was it not the Liberal convention who accused them ? At a meeting of Liberals held in tlbe Yukon, the resolutions were passed stating that these concessions were granted by misrepresentation and fraud, and asking the government to cancel these concessions or, at least, to have an investigation in regard to it. Now, the platform goes on to say :
Resolved, that in the opinion of this convention many of the concessions now held were obtained by fraud and impositions ; that it is in the interest of this territory that such concessions should be annulled, and to that end that inquiry should be set on foot to ascertain the circumstances of such fraud and imposition and action taken by the Attorney General of Canada in the premises.
I repeat that these accusations of fraud and imposition come from the Liberals in the Yukon. I will not read all the platform adopted by the Liberal convention. But I will read the last clause :
And that the owners of hydraulic concessions already granted should be compelled to carry out the strict terms of their leases, and that in default of their so doing, their leases should be cancelled.
What was the answer of the Hon. James Ross to the platform of the convention as laid down ? In his address to the electors of the Yukon, he saitf:
I freely subscribe to every measure suggested therein. In respect to most of the planks, they are in perfect accord with the policy I have sought to have adopted in the Yukon. I recognize that the whole business life of the Yukon depends upon the success of the prospector and miner and they above all others should be encouraged.
Then in regard to the charges of fraud and misrepresentation, what does the hon. gentleman say ? He says :
The thorough investigation of the charges of fraud made in respect to the manner in which certain concessions are alleged to have been obtained, and if such fraud is established, the immediate commencement of such proceedings as may be required to vacate the grant and the enforcement of strict compliance with the con- I Mr. PRINGLE.
ditions embodied in all crown grants in the Yukon.
And let me read one other little paragraph :
I believe, that the Yukon is only in its infancy and that so far from its resources being exhausted, they have scarcely been touched, and the prosperity of the future will dwarf into insignificance all the success of the past. I was engaged in an endeavour to revise and codify not merely the mining laws but all the laws specially applicable to the Yukon when my illness interrupted the work. I think this work most essential in order that the laws may be fixed, clear and certain. With respect to the mining laws I propose to have them codified and then submitted to representative miners for criticism, alteration and approval in order that they may as far as possible meet with the approval of the mining community.
So, there is the platform upon which the Hon. James Hamilton Ross was elected as a representative of the people of the Yukon and as a government supporter in this House. Now, the hon. Minister of Labour dwelt a great deal upon the election of Mr. Ross asi si government supporter. Let me say a word further in regard to that election. I find from the returns that, at that election, there were 5,100 votes cast, of which Mr. Ross received 2,971, and Mr. Clarke, 2,079, there were 100 spoiled ballots. But I find, from examination of the papers, that there was a great deal of dissatisfaction with regard to that election. I know that in the election which followed, on the 17th of January, the three leaders of the poll aggregated only 1,018 votes, though circumstances were such as to favour a larger vote than that of the 2nd of December, and the element beaten on the 2nd of December was triumphant on the 15th of January all along the line. At Miller's creek, where the whole population does not exceed forty, there were 101 votes cast for the hon. member for the Yukon. At. Cariboo crossing where the population is less than twenty, 109 votes were cast for the hon. member for the Yukon, go I do not think that the Postmaster General should take such great credit for the election of the Hon. James Boss.
Now, Sir, while 1 am pleased with the statements made by the Postmaster General in regard to the charges of misrepresentation and fraud, let me for a moment refer to a very large meeting that was held by the Liberal party in the Yukon, where resolutions were passed in reference to this matter. This was a meeting of the Liberal Association :
The Liberal Association of Dawson met at the Pioneer Hall on Saturday night, and condemned in no uncertain tones the Order in Council of December 7, making Treadgold & Co. heirs to all the Klondike on this side of the Dome. A resolution was passed unanimously calling on the ministers of the Crown to secure its cancellation, and also to Mr. Commissioner Ross urging him to use all the powers at his disposal to prevent the law ever being enforced. A resolution was also passed unanimously that the

first resolution be telegraphed at once to each of the ministers and to Mr. Ross.
This meeting was held in March, 1902.
The vice-president, F. T. Congdon, called the meeting to order and stated its objects. Mr. Congdon's remarks were to the point at once. He pointed out that public feeling had in a few days been aroused as it had not been aroused in a long while, yet he thought that notwithstanding the seriousness of the occasion and the enormity of the mistake that had been made, it was not an occasion warranting extreme action ; indeed; he thought that the best results would be obtained by calm discussion, and the proper advising of the ministers In whose hands lay the remedy. Above all he thought no political capital was to be made of the ill-advised action of the government. The grant or Order in Council of December 7th had clearly been secured by the grossest misrepresentation and in violation of all the principles of right. Canadian soil was not the property of the government. The government only held It in trust for the people at large.
Who is it that makes this statement ? The man who is the present Governor of the Yukon, tlie man *who is a supporter of the present government. He goes on to say :
The facts so familiar to each and every one of his hearers, he believed it had not been called to the attention of the government, and he thought the government had been grossly imposed on. The Order in Council has already been passed and the law of contracts stood in the way of the cancellation of the contract at' the will of one of the makers ; but there is another provision of the law just as powerful and binding where a contract can be shown to have been made by misrepresentation and fraud, its provisions could be set aside, and he believed there would be no difficulty in this case in showing such misrepresentations to have been made and many important facts withheld.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there were resolutions passed at that large gathering of Liberals in the Yukon, and this is one of the resolutions :
Resolved, that the commissioner's attention be called to the fact, and that he be requested to represent to the government that in the opinion of this meeting, the insertion of any such features in' the Orders in Council could only have been procured by the grossest misrepresentation and fraudulent concealment ; that it never could have been represented to the minister who proposed said Orders or to the Governor in Council that the Orders were an interference with and abrogation of vested rights ; that it was retroactive in operation and most far reaching and uncertain in effect ; that it was certain to produce distrust and lack of confidence among the mining communities of this territory and prove fatal to the progress of the territory ; nor could it have been presented and made apparent that the only consideration promised for the enormous interests granted was a monopoly to supply water at an exorbitant and prohibitive price.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I regret sincerely tlie absence of the bon. the Minister of the Interior. If we are to believe report, he sailed from England on the same ship that
Jlr. Treadgold sailed on, and they are now, no doubt, in the city of London. I regret his absence, because I would like to have heard his explanations in regard to all these different concessions, and especially in regard to this Treadgold concession. I regret also the absence of the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Ross). I find, Sir, that he is paraded in the official organ of the Liberal party as having reached parliament and as having obtained great and important results for the miners of that section of the country. Let me just refer to the reception of Governor Congdon upon his arrival in the Yukon, and to his statements in regard to this Treadgold concession. I will refer to the Yukon ' Sun,' the official organ, as I understand, of the Liberal party. There is also an interview with Governor Congdon in the ' Dawson Daily News.' What does the Governor say in regard to this concession :
As to the Treadgold concession, I may say I favour its cancellation.
This was on Thursday April, 9, 1903, months after the election of the hon. member for the Yukon.
I am in the same position regarding the subject as I always have been. I am satisfied that he should have no more privileges than any one else. I will not say that I favour the total cancellation

He has changed his mind since being appointed Governor. Prior to his appointment as Governor he was in favour of the total and absolute cancellation of the Treadgold concession. He now says :
I will not say that I favour the total cancellation of the Treadgold concession, that is, I shall not*put it in that way, but say I believe he should have no privileges that others do not have. As to what parliament is likely to do with the matter I cannot say. I feel that if the government will install a supply of water for the camp it will be a great enterprise and give an impetus to the mining industry. Mr. Ross is working on the scheme, and will urge parliament to send a corps of experts here to investigate the feasibility and desirability of such a system. It is the intention of Mr. Ross to get the government to send the most competent engineers that can be found in the world. Parliament doubtless will deal with this matter deliberately, and it is not to be expected an appropriation will be made for the installation of such a gigantic plant now in the short time the session will last. Heavy projects progress slowly, and if Mr. Ross succeeds in getting an appropriation this season for the expenses of a corps of experts to investigate the field and desirability of the scheme, he will be doing well. If after all a government supply of water is not to be obtained we should have water from some source. But the government does not know our needs and will first have to satisfy itself as to the prospects for permanency of the placers and the need of water over the camp as a whole. The needs of a few would not justify such a great expenditure as is contemplated.
