speechtext: What Is the date of that paper ?

April 9, 1903, the ' Dawson Daily News.' Now, Sir, let me quote from the ' Yukon Sun.' One cannot read any of the editorials of the 'Yukon Sun' without coming to the conclusion that it is the organ of the Liberal party in that territory. In the first place, I will quote from the 'Yukon Weekly Sun' of Saturday, April 4 :
The Treadgold concession stands a poor show. Must be ratified by the present parliament or it falls to the ground. Mr. Ross will oppose its ratification.
Why is he not here V

If the Treadgold concession comes up in the House for ratification, Yukon's member will oppose it. Section 5 of ' An Act to amend the Yukon Act,' passed last session, provided that all regulations passed applying or relating to Yukon Territory, will remain in force only until approved by resolution of both Houses of parliament. Prom the records received here from Dawson, it appears that people there are under a misapprehension in regard to this provision. All the regulations to be operative must be approved by parliament to keep them in force beyond the date of prorogation of the present session. The Treadgold Order in Council must therefore be approved at the present session or it will fall to the ground. As already said, if it comes up in the House, Mr. Ross will oppose it.
I have been in this House since the opening almost every day, and up to the present time I have not heard any great opposition coming from the hon. member from the Yukon. That hon. gentleman has been doing great things, but, I challenge any hon. gentleman here to tell ns what he has done in the House. Here is an editorial in the official organ of the Liberal party at Dawson, the Yukon ' Sun ' of March 28tli. It says :

Is he a lightning striker ? We should remark that he is. Saturday afternoon he arrived at Ottawa. Sunday he received the members of the House and Senate and made friends for Yukon. Monday he was introduced in the House, upon which occasion he was cheered to the echo. The premier of Canada introduced him. Immediately after the introduction he secured the passage of a Bill granting extended powers to the Yukon council. Tuesday he spent the forenoon in the Department of the Interior looking after matters pertaining to the Yukon. Wednesday he had the price of free miners certificate reduced to $7.50.
I can give him or somebody credit for having these fees reduced. I find that it was managed within a very short time, and the fee is now reduced to 87.50. Then it says :
The record fees from $15 to $10, renewal fees from $15 to $10, and payment of money in lieu of assessment work abolished. What he did yesterday is not known at the time this is written, but the telegraphic advices pointed on the first page of this issue will tell. If Jim Ross keeps up his present gait it will only take Mr. PRINGLE.
him a week to perform all the seeming impossibilities of the platform prepared here for him, bound him to.
Why, the platform provided for him bound him to abolish this Treadgold concession, and according to this editorial of the official organ of the Liberal party in the Yukon, if he kept up his gait, in a week he was going to have this Treadgold concession abolished. He seemed to have slackened his gait, because we have not heard anything of the Treadgold concession since the hon. member arrived in Ottawa. It says further :
The judgment of the voters of the Yukon in electing Mr. Ross is apparent. No man would have the assurance to even insinuate that Mr. Clarke could have done the good work for the Yukon that Mr. Ross has already done. Mr. Ross goes to Ottawa as a friend of the party in power. He was received with distinguished honours and is able to win some consideration for us each day. Mr. Clarke would have gone as an avowed enemy of the party in power, would have talked anarchy to every reporter who would listen to him along the route, and we would have received about as little consideration in parliament as he might with reason expect. The judgment of the people of the Territory of Yukon can be depended upon. And that judgment was never better demonstrated than in their selecting ' Jim ' Ross to represent them in parliament.
But, in the same edition of this paper, Mr. .Tim Ross is going to abolish the Tread-gold concession, and he is going to establish a national work to supply water for the miners of that country. Now, it is not very hard to understand, after the explanations I have given in regard to this election, how the hon. member was elected for the Yukon. I find, at any rate it is alleged in certain documents, that in the Yukon Territory, there is one official for every fifteen miners in the district, and I have no doubt that these officials did not neglect to vote for the hon. gentleman. I desire to approach this matter in a fair, impartial and calm spirit. The hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) accused the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) of making an inflammatory speech. In that he accused him improperly. I think, we in this House, should agree, and that the hon. the Postmaster General, who is also Minister of Labour, should agree with the proposition that the policy should be to give every advantage to the practical miner over the mere speculator, and that is the policy that I desire to advocate.
I know that it is very often difficult to advocate the policy of the miner against the hon. Postmaster General, who is advocating the policy of the monopolists, and who is advocating the policy of these concessionaires. I would have expected that the hon. Postmaster General would have advocated the cause of the miner, the cause of the labourer, the cause of the men who have done so much to bring to the knowledge of the people of the world Dawson and the

Klondike. We have only to look back a few years, to tbe time when these names were unknown throughout the civilized world, but to-day, Dawson and the Klondike are known from one end of the world to the other, and if they are known they are known through the efforts of the hardy men who went into that country as prospectors and who developed the mines of that region. These are the men we should protect, and these are the men who are entitled to the protection of the members of this House. Let me quote briefly from a little work that was published by a man who was in Dawson City and who went into that country to see the conditions existing there. What did he find ? Did he find that the affairs of the country were administered properly ? No Sir, he found that the condition of the miners there under the regulations adopted by the government was worse than the condition of the Uitlanders in South Africa. The work is entitled ' The Klondike Stampede ' and it is edited by Mr. Tappan Abney, special correspondent of ' Harper's Weekly ' in the Klondike. He says :
In the Klondike, those who best knew the country's needs had no voice whatever in its government ; all laws were made at Ottawa, and those sent out to enforce them were responsible only to the home government, or to the officials to whom they owed their appointment. Dawson was an ' alien ' camp, where, if the position of the majority of the residents was different from the ' Uitlander ' at Johannesburg, it was only that the laws were in intent more liberal. Distant, weeks and months from the seat of responsibility, it is not difficult to understand how, even if government intended well, the condition of the miner might be scarcely better than that of his unfortunate confrere in the Boer republic. In fact, conditions which actually prevailed at Dawson were likened by British citizens direct from1 the Transvaal as even worse than what they left.
The natural difficulties that stood in the way of putting into immediate operation an effective government were so great that one should not judge the Klondikers too harshly. On the other hand, if there were not serious disorders it was due less to the duality of government than to the orderly character of the population, and to the fact that men were there enduring the privations of an Arctic climate to make their fortunes and get away, not to help set in order the political households of their Canadian friends.
Now, Sir, he goes on to say
While the law required the ' gum-boot ' miner to stake in person, so-called 'dredging permits,' in five-mile blocks, were granted over fifteen hundred miles of Klondike and Yukon streams to men who, for the most part, had never seen, nor intended to see, the Yukon. Such, in brief, are the regulations now in force which further provide for the sale of timber-berths to private parties, whereby miners are virtually prevented from cutting wood, even for their own use, except on such terms as the monopolists concede. The tendency of the new legislation is against the ' gum-boot ' miner, the man whose enterprise, labours, and hardships have made for Canada all that is worth while in the Klondike to-day. This is always 90
the inevitable trend, but never in any camp has so much been done in so short a time in that direction as in the Canadian camp.
He goes on to deal with the public officials in the Yukon, and he says :
Afterwards, emboldened by the impotency of the commissioner to correct these abuses, favoured ones began to be admitted during office hours, upon passes, and recorded claims ahead of men who had been waiting often for days in line outside. It became recognized by everyone who was obliged to deal with the office that the only way of getting even what belonged to him was to bribe an official. Appeal to the Gold Commissioner was as likely as not met with dismissal in an arbitrary, unjust, or illegal manner. During the greater part of the rush there was no one to verify measurements of claims (only survey by Dominion land surveyors being recognized officially). The commissioner was in ignorance of the location and identity of creeks; he would give two different names to the same creek, not knowing them to be the same; he would grant the same claim to different men, and yet refuse, when the fact was proven, to refund the record fee to one of them; he allowed two discoveries on one creek, and claims became so mixed, in consequence of overlapping between discoveries, that he was obliged to close the creek, to the great loss of miners, who were not allowed to record (pending arrival of official surveyors), and who were holding the claims in person, in compliance with the mining law. Thus, between the incompetency of the commissioner and the corruption of his clerks, legitimate business came almost to a standstill. The general law of Canada, providing that no person should suffer from the Incompetency of an official, was of no effect to the poor miner, who had neither money nor time to obtain the remedy.
Tbe author of this work is an entirely independent naan who went into that country, and he tells here of the way in which he found the public business administered. It is my opinion, Sir, that the evils were not so great at the time that work was written as they are at present. Since the publication of that work we find that large concessions have been granted in that territory to what are called concessionaires, and that tlie miners have been practically driven out of certain sections of the country. We find that as early as 1898 the government began to close the placer ground of this territory against location by the placer miners. In that year a large tract of Dominion creek was from time to time closed. In the same year also, fractional claims were closed against location. In February, 1898, the Minister of the Interior directed that Bonanza and Eldorado, and their tributaries and benches should be closed against location, and I may say that so far as I can ascertain these were amongst the richest creeks in that section of the country. This was followed in October, 1899, by a regulation closing all lapsed claims in the territory against relocation. In the year and a half that followed, silently at Ottawa and without the knowledge of the Yukon people, and on the flimsiest pretexts, the greater part of the richest placer ground was included in what

A
was called hydraulic concessions. On Hunker creek were granted to Williams two and a half square miles; to Milne, two square miles; to Anderson, two and half square miles. On the Klondike, including Bear and Lindow creeks, to Boyle, fifty square miles. While the miner could only take up so many feet as a claim, the government were granting here concessions of from ten to fifty miles. On Bonanza there was given to Philip, five square miles; to Bronson & Bay, fifteen square miles; to Matson & Doyle, three square miles, and on Quartz creek, fcur square miles were granted to the same Boyle. I may say that this man Boyle seems to be a very favoured individual of the government of this country. He seemed to have no trouble in getting concession after concession in the richest and best portion of the Yukon Territory. I find Mr. Boyle sold these concessions later on to other parties at enormous figures. As I say, on Poors creek another concession of about four square miles was granted to the same Boyle, while the other creeks were almost similarly blanketed by concessions which were obtained-in the words of the Liberal convention; in the words of the Liberals present at that meeting-I am only repeating their language when I say that these concessions were obtained largely by fraud.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

Now Sir, the miners of the Yukon take this ground, and it seems to be a proper ground to take-the Liberal party in the Yukon take this ground, and they evidently consider it a proper ground, namely : that these concessions which were granted on misrepresentation and fraud should be annulled. I believe, Sir, that every one of them can be cancelled because of the breach of the conditions stipulated in their leases.
Now, Sir, we come to Mr. Treadgold, and I want to say here that I have not a word-to say personally in regard to Mr. Tread-gold, in regard to Walter Barwick, K.C., in regard to Mr. Ewing or any of the men who have obtained concessions from this government. I have nothing whatever to say with regard to these men. I don't think they are philanthropists; I don't think they were getting this concession for the benefit of the miners, but I do think and I have no doubt that they were getting this concession for the benefit of themselves, and a very valuable concession it was. If the report of the Dawson Board of Trade, and if the report of the engineers of that company be correct, it was a concession which would make these men millionaires in very short order. Mr. Treadgold appeared on the scene in 1898, and I am informed that he was welcomed to the Yukon as being a representative of British capital. He began at once to acquire placer claims of value. In 1899 and 1900 he purchased interests in the Boyle Mr. PRINGLE.
concession, and other of the infamous concessions which I have already referred to. On the 31st of May, 1900, on the pretense of bringing water to work low grade gravels, he, with Walter Barwick, K.C., and O. N. Ewing, asked for a controlling interest in the rest of the Klondike basin. It is interesting to turn to the request of these concessionaires. On the 31st of May these gentlemen put in their requisition to the hon. Minister of the Interior and in that requisition they state :
The applicants are prepared to undertake the establishment of hydraulic works which will supply water to the auriferous deposits now without water, &c.
In that request of theirs they asked for concessions which the people of the Yukon contend should never have been granted; and, Sir, was there any change made when the government passed the Order in Council ? The Order in Council was passed in the identical language in which these gentlemen asked for the Order. There does not appear to have ever been any discussion by the minister as to whether the request of these gentlemen was reasonable or unreasonable. The Minister of the Interior evidently advised his colleagues that they must grant to these applicants everything they asked for, and the Order in Council was passed on the 12th of June, 1901; and What were they to get under that Order ? They were to get one dollar per miners' inch per hour for water supply. It was a most iniquitous concession, on their own showing, because they came down very shortly afterwards and said :	' We will be very glad
to take twenty-five cents per miners' inch.' The Order was amended shortly afterwards, I think on the 29th of June, 1901, as follows :
The charge which the grantees shall be entitled to make for the use of such water on each placer claim shall not exceed 25 cents per miners' inch per hour.
These gentlemen came down very quickly from a dollar to twenty-five cents.
Now, the hon. Minister of Labour has accused the hon. member front Montmorency of speaking from unofficial documents, from newspapers and from anonymous communications, and he has spoken disparagingly of every source from which the hon. member from Montmorency spoke. Why should he condemn the Yukon Board of Trade, a body composed of both Conservatives and Liberals ? I was surprised, Sir, to hear him condemn that body and term them irresponsible parties. Here is what the board of trade says in regard to this matter :
The Treadgold concession and water grant, as granted by an Order in Council which, when ratified by the parliament at its next session, will become law, is, in the opinion of this board, one of the most iniquitous measures that was ever inflicted upon a people.
The Dawson Board of Trade may be irresponsible, but they are the best represen-
2S53

tative body we can find in the Yukon Territory, and they say that In their opinion this concessionwill work a great hardship upon the people of this territory, since it will mean the virtual bankruptcy of all the property holders of Dawson and surrounding territory, and instead of the Klondike becoming the prosperous country we expect, it will virtually become the property of Mr. Treadgold and those who are associated with him in his scheme.
Why is this concession granted ? Is it granted for the benefit of the miners of the Yukon or for the benefit of these individuals ? We know that everybody in that country is opposed to it. The hon. gentleman said that he had petitions from some sources favouring the concession. I would ask the hon. gentleman to lay those petitions on the Table of this House; we want to see them, because we are advised that the people of the Yukon are a unit agaiust this concession, and we are advised that when the bon. member for the Yukon takes his seat in this House, he will give us active and vigor jus assistance in doing away with it,
Let me read a little from the petition of the board of trade :
The petition of the undersigned residents of the Yukon Territory humbly showeth :
1.	That by Order in Council of April the 21st, 1902, certain privileges are granted to Malcolm Orr Ewing, A. N. C. Treadgold and Walter Bar-wick, in connection with the proposed establishment by them of a system of water supply for washing out gold-hearing gravel in the district therein described, including the Klondike river, Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks and their tributaries.
2.	That the benefits conferred upon the grantees are of incalculable value and involve an enormous exploitation of the public resources of this territory for the benefit of a few favoured concessionaires.
3.	That In the opinion of your petitioners the accumulation of extraordinary powers in the hands of a single corporation such as is effected by the above Order in Council, will lead to the paralysis of the independent commercial and industrial life of the community and will prove in the highest degree oppressive and injurious to the public welfare, since the grantees are thereby enabled to crush out competition and to reduce to a position of practical servitude the individual miners in the extensive district affected which includes the richest portion of the Klondike.
4.	That the need of this territory Is not the . creation of monopolies but their prevention, and
the encouragement of the individual miners by securing equal privileges and opportunities to all as far as the law and the administration can provide them.
We linre a computation made by a very competent gentleman as to the revenues that would be derived by these concessionaires from the concession which is being granted to them by this government. If this computation is at all correct, the amount of money which these people would derive in a very short time is simply fabulous. Let me refer for a moment to the statement made :
Now in order to convey to you some idea of Lhe magnitude of the grant which Mr. Treadgold and his associates are looking for and which it appears likely they will receive, if the intention of the Minister of the Interior is allowed to be carried out, it having been recommended by him, we believe that the said Treadgold and his associates receive the sole and prior right to divert and take water from the Klondike river up to 5.000 miners' inches for distribution and use in the district, said district comprising the beds, banks, valleys, slopes and hills of the Klondike river, of Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks, and their tributaries, also the right to divert and use the water of Rock creek, which water we are informed by Mr. Joseph McGillivray, a mining engineer of long experience, amounts to 8,000 inches, natural flow, and which would give Mr. Treadgold and associates the sole right to divert and sell 13,000 inches of water. Now, a miner requires with which to sluice his dirt 50 inches of water, which is the amount considered necessary to make a sluice-head, and should the Treadgold Company at the rate which, we understand, is the contemplated charge (25 per cent miners' inch per hour) it would cost the miner $12.50 per hour or $300 per day of 24 hours, which is the length of the working day here during the summer season. Now this grant of 5,000 inches from the Klondike river and the natural flow of Rock creek, amounting to 8,000 inches, making a total of water at Treadgold's command of 13,000 inches, or 260 sluice-heads of 50 inches per sluice-head, costing the miner in this country $78,000 per day, or $10,140,000 per year of 130 sluicing days, which is the length of the sluicing season here, would mean this : that the holder of the same would practically own the country, all the hill claim owners would have to come to him for water, or allow their claim to remain vn-oparated for lack of same, and Mr. Treadgold and his associates would .be receiving all the profits, that would accrue from the thousands of hill claims, situate on the immense and huge gravel deposits with which this country abounds.
I do not see why these gentlemen should get a concession of such tremendous advantage to them. The hon. the Postmaster Genera] has predicted that the opposition will repent the attack on this scheme. It was equally predicted that he would repeat the attack made on the Yukon Railway deal of some years ago. Let me just refer for a moment to the language of the right hon. the Prime Minister, when the little item of $328,508 which this country had to pay to Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, was before this House. - Here is the item :
To pay amount of judgment of Exchequer Court in favour of Messrs.
Mackenzie & Mann to recoup them for their outlay in connection with proposed contract for a railway from Stickeen river to Teslin lake. $327,678 10 Costs for evidence, &c	 830 20

In the discussion on this item the right hon. gentleman said :
Of course I am hound to say at once that there is no legal recourse against the Canadian government which can be enforced in a court of law, but we admit that Mackenzie & Mann have

a moral claim against the honour of the Canadian people against the honour of the Canadian government and against the honour of the Canadian parliament for the money which they have expended in an enterprise which was national in its character, &c., &c. For these reasons we submit to the Canadian parliament that these men should not be subjected to the heavy loss which would be entailed on them, but as this is a loss which must be borne by somebody, it should be borne by the country and not by the contractors, &c., &c. Of course, if it had not been for the charter which parliament had granted-I will not say improvidently or imprudently, granted, but granted in ignorance of the conditions existing in that country, there would not have been any necessity for such haste.
I have no doubt that my hon. friend the Postmaster General will come down later on in the day and seek to get some compensation for these gentlemen's interests in the Treadgold concessions, because he has told us that they have expended over $50,000 in that concession. Though I am satisfied that this government will never in the face of the opposition from their own friends in the Yukon, in face of the opposition of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ross) who was elected to represent the Yukon district in this House, permit this iniquitous concession to become law, they will no doubt ask for a vote to recoup these people for the expenditure they have made in connection with this concession, just as was done in the MacKenzie & Mann affair. I am not reflecting in any way on Messrs Mackenzie & Mann or anybody else in connection with their scheme, but X say that when the government rushed into it, the conditions of the country were not known or the government would never have committed such a piece of folly. Let me quote again from the work of Tappan Abney on ' The Klondike Stampede.' Referring to the Mackenzie & Mann deal, Mr. Tappan said :
The Canadian Minister of the Interior, the Hon. Clifford Sifton, granted to a firm of contractors, Mesrs Mackenzie & Mann, provisional right to construct a railway from the Stikeen river to the Teslin lake, in return for immense grants of gold-bearing land in the Klondike. Surveys were made and material delivered at the terminus of the proposed road, and tickets were sold in the principal cities of Europe and the United States for through passage to Dawson.
But, he added :
Before the agreement with Mackenzie & Mann was ratified by parliament, however, a committee of miners sent out from Dawson in the fall of 1897 to protest against the royalty tax, discovered and pointed out to parliament the true inwardness of the proposed franchise, the profits on which had been already figured out as $34,000,000, and, as a result of the flood of light they let in upon parliament concerning the Yukon, the Bill was killed.
Then he proceeded :
3,750,000	acres of mineral land in Klondike were to be granted to the contractors, whereas the whole area about Dawson that had been Mr. PRINGLE.
prospected contained only 864,000 acres. They were to be allowed to run their lines along 960 miles of creeks, whereas Bonanza and Eldorado are only thirty-one miles long ; the land was to be held in fee simple, instead of by annual lease ; and royalties on gold were to be only one per cent instead of ten per cent, which were required of all others. In return for which they were to build a narrow-gauge railroad, from a terminus only twenty-six miles nearer Dawson than Skagway-150 miles of tracks, useless for seven months of the year-with right to charge exorbitant tolls, and with a monopoly of railway ingress to the Yukon for five years. It was a grab of nearly everything worth having in the Yukon district.
If that Yukon agreement was a grab of nearly everything worth-having in that district, this Treadgold concession, if we are to believe the Liberals of the Yukon, the board of trade and the miners of that district, is a grab of nearly everything worth having in that territory.
I would like to refer for a moment to something that certainly is not ancient history. I should like to read a telegram sent on March the 6th, 1903, by the board of trade, and to comment on the reply which was sent by the right hon. Prime Minister. I may be very obtuse, but I cannot comprehend exactly the meaning of that answer. This is the message which the board of trade sent:
Dawson opposes any attempt to pass Order in Council or Act of parliament that will in any way confirm the Treadgold concession, are having monster petitions signed, and reliable data prepared to forward to Ottawa asking the government to aid in furnishing water for mining purposes. The people are a unity in making demands and will insist on government cancelling monopoly of Treadgold's octopus.
The reply to that telegram is dated, Ottawa, March the 9th, 1903, sent to H. C. McCullough, president of the board of trade. Evidently the right hon. the First Minister did not share in the opinion of his hon. colleague, the Postmaster General, that this is an irresponsible body.

If the hon. gentleman will allow me ? On several occasions he has charged me with saying that the board of trade of Dawson is an irresponsible body. I said nothing of the kind. I did not allude to them ; I did not say anything to embrace them, I alluded to the quotations from the press and scrap information of that kind.

Well, I should sincerely regret to misquote the hon. Postmaster General. What I understood him to say-and I took a note of it at the time-was that the hon. member for Montmorency quoted from irresponsible parties.
I did not say that all his quotations were from irresponsible parties. I pointed out that there were quotations of the kind I said.

Would the hon. minister tell me which of these quotations were from

irresponsible parties Were they tbe quotations from the convention of the Liberal party ? Were they the quotations from the platform of the Hon. James Ross ? Were they the quotations from the platform of the Liberal party as laid down in their convention ? Were they the quotations from the board of trade ? Or what quotations were from irresponsible parties ? If the hon. gentleman will tell me, I will be in a position to take that up.
Now, Sir, failing to get an answer from the Postmaster General, I will proceed with a discussion of these telegrams. To my mind they are ambiguous, I will not say they are deceptive, though that is the term used by some of the parties in the Yukon. What does it mean ? Does it mean that no confirmation is needed ? Does it mean that the Treadgold concession is dead, and that there is no action contemplated by legislation or government order ? Here is the telegram which is signed by the right hon. the Prime Minister :
You are altogether misinformed with regard to what is called the Treadgold concession. No such action contemplated' either by legislation or by government order.
Now, what is the action referred to by the telegram sent to the Dawson Board of Trade ? The only construction that we could place on it is that there is no action contemplated either by legislation or by government order to confirm and make legal and valid this Order in Council that the Postmaster General has told us is not binding as yet, and cannot be binding until such time as it is published in the official ' Gazette.' I do not wish to weary the House, but I wish to refer to one or two other points in connection with this matter, which seems to me a very important one so far as the miners of this country are concerned. And it is worth noting that, while we have labour representatives in this House, I do not know that they will get up to advocate the cause of the labouring men in the country if it interferes with a concession granted by the government. We have a statement made by the Postmaster General that the deputation waited upon the government last year, but that they never asked for the abolition of this concession, but only for certain changes to be made in it. I have here the report of these gentlemen on their return to the Yukon. Let us see what they said :
Gentlemen, as there seems in some quarters to be a desire for a report as to the results of our mission with regard to the Treadgold concession, I wish to lay before the committee a synopsis of our doings at Ottawa.
According to instructions, we met and conferred with the Hon. Jas. H. Ross on our arrival, and found him disposed to assist us in every way possible.
An interview was arranged with the premier and the hon. Minister of the Interior, at which were present Hen. James H. Ross, Ralph Smith, Arthur Wilson, and myself. The matter was
laid before the premier and Mr. Sifton in its entirety, and the total abolition of the concession was demanded.
It is not for me to say who was right or who was wrong. But when the Minister of Labour gets up in this House and says that this deputation never asked for the abolition of the Treadgold concession, it is only right that I should refer to the report of these gentlemen when they returned to the Yukon. Now, what did they find out '!

We found out that the concession had been already granted and that the only method by which we could secure redress was by working with the government, which showed every disposition to rectify the mistakes which had been made.
But, Sir, what did the government do ? They rescinded the Order in Council, rescinded it in toto, and then issued another order which gave to these people greater concessions than they had in the first order. We find, subsequent to the time when this deputation arrived in the city, and subsequent to the interview with the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior, the order was passed rescinding the Order in Council of the 12th June, and subsequent order. It says :
Extract from a Report of the Committee of the Honourable the Privy Council, Approved by His Excellency April 21, 1902.
On a memorandum, dated April 17, 1902, from the Minister of the Interior, stating that he has been in consultation with the Hon. James H. Ross, Commissioner of the Yukon Territory, with regard to certain objections which have been raised to the Orders in Council of June 12, 1902, June 29, 1901, and December 7, 1901, granting Messrs. Malcolm H. Orr-Ewing, of Malvern, England; A. N. C. Treadgold, of London, England, and Walter Barwick, of Toronto, Ontario, certain rights, powers and privileges, as set out in the above-mentioned Orders in Council, and such objections have also been the subject of consultations with the grantees.
The minister recommends as the result of the said consultations, with the assent of the said grantees, that the Orders in Council cited above, be rescinded.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these Orders in Council were rescinded. If the government had made mistakes in regard to these Orders in Council they had the consent of the grantees to rescind them, and they were rescinded on the 17th April. At that time the government was possessed of the knowledge that the people of the Yukon were utterly and totally opposed to these concessions. Yet, three days afterwards, on the 20th April, they grant to these very same people concessions which gave to them greater rights than they previously had. I shall take that subject up a little later on, and shall show that by the last concessions granted to these people they had greater rights than under the previous concession. Now, let me refer also, while I am on the subject, to the statement made by the Minister of the Interior with regard to this de-

putation. In ' Hansard ' of last year, 1902, volume 2, pages 4951 and 4952, you will find a discussion that tools place last session in regard to this deputation. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) asked the Minister of the Interior the following :
I would like to know whether the concession * in its amended torm has met with any opposition in the Yukon at the present time.
I do not think so. Mr. Ross informed me that the delegates who had been sent from Dawson had seen the amended Order in Council and agreed that it would be perfectly satisfactory.

With regard to the abandoned claims, the information I have would show that in many cases those claims afterwards proved to be very valuable. Another objection that was brought to my attention was that a scheme of this kind was not required in the Yukon at the present time, because it could not be properly carried out until the lower levels had been more thoroughly worked. As I understand it, the operations of a scheme of this kind would prevent the working of the lower levels. Am I correct in that ?
Yes.

There is one other circumstance I would like to mention. There was a memorial of some kind presented to the minister by a number of miners. I saw a copy of that printed in the public press. I would like to know whether the amended Order in Council meets the objections either wholly or partially which were made by the miners in this memorial ?

To all intents and purposes, I think I can say that it does. I went over the memorial with the delegates, Mr. Wilson and Mr. Sugrue. Mr. Wilson was one of the elected members of the Yukon council and Mr. Sugrue was a newspaper man. I went over the memorial with them, and they agreed that the Order in Council in its amended form substantially met their objections. Possibly some of the abandoned claims may turn out to be very valuable.
Now, Sir, floes that agree with the report of the delegates upon their return to the Yukon ? In their report they state an entirely different set of affairs. They say :
We found that the concession had already been granted and that the only method by which we could secure redress was by working with the government.
Now, Sir, it has been stated here by the Minister of Labour that the hon. member for the Yukon was returned to this House as a government supporter. No doubt lie was returned as a government supporter. But I want to remark that he was pledged from the start to the finish of his campaign to oppose this Treadgold concession. I have read you the platform of the Liberal party, I have read you his endorsation and his acceptance of that platform. Let me also read you the statements made by Mr. Cong-don on Mr. Ross's behalf during the campaign. Mr. Oongdon was an active supporter of the Hon. James Ross, now the Governor, and in his speech at South Dawson during the campaign, on October 14, 1902, he said : Mr. PRINGLE.
The government had entered into a contract with Treadgold and only the parliament of Canada could abrogate that agreement. Mr. Ross had asked for the cancellation of the Treadgold concession, but the government found itself tied in such a manner that it could only secure a modification of the grant.
Now, Sir, that shows that Mr. Ross was advocating the cancellation of that concession. Then there was another statement made by Mr. Oongdon, but as that was referred to by my hon. friend from Montmorency, I will not now refer to it. I say that throughout that territory there has been a constant agitation against that concession, an agitation by all parties irrespective of politics. Let me refer you to one or two resolutions that were passed at a mass meeting of citizens held April 2, 1902. There were statements made there which I think would be unfair probably to make in this House. Men standing high in the politics of this country were connected with some of these concessions in statements made at that meeting. I think, Sir, it would be entirely unfair for me to repeat those statements, as I have no proof and nothing to show that these men were in any way connected with these concessions. This is a report of the meeting at which certain statements were made by Mr. Woodworth and other gentlemen. I will simply read the resolutions, and not the statements which were made by these men. The resolutions passed at this meeting held in Dawson are reported in the press of April 22, 1902. The first resolution is this :
We request the government of the Dominion of Canada to immediately inquire into the means by which the Anderson, Milne, Boyle, Bronson and Ray, Doyle Matson, Slavin and Gates and Miller creek concessions were obtained, as to whether said concessions were obtained by fraud and misrepresentation and granted in error and improvidence, and as to whether the regulations have been complied with in the grant or continuance of said leases.
Whereas, the Anderson, Milne, Boyle, Bronson and Ray, Matson, Doyle, Slavin and Gates and Miller creek concessions comprise much of the richest known placer mining ground in the Yukon Territory and ought never to have been leased to the pretended lessees.
Therefore, resolved, that all ground within the limits of said concessions be open to location by the placer miner whether held by concession or not.
Whereas, by express agreement of the holders of the Matson and Doyle concessions are entitled to the mining claims forfeited within the bounds of their concessions, providing they file a plan and apply for the same within one year from date of lapse of said claims, and whereas, under express or implied agreement the Slavin and Gates, Bronson and Ray, Boyle, Milne and Miller creek concessions in a similar manner are claims lapsing within their boundaries, and whereas all said concessions were obtained by fraud and misrepresentation and comprise within their boundaries some of the richest placer mining ground in the Yukon Territory, therefore resolved, that the government of the Dominion of Canada be requested to take steps to prevent said lapsed ground becoming a part of said concessions.
28G1

The leases and agreements by which the Anderson, Milne, Boyle Bronson and Ray, Doyle, Matson, Slavin and Gates and Miller creek concessions be cancelled and revoked upon such terms as may be just.
Now, Sir, I wil-l deal for a few moments with the Order in Council granted on the 21st of April, 1002. The Minister of Labour has gone over these concessions clause by clause, and he has endeavoured to point out to this House that the concessionaires did not obtain so much by the final Orders in Council as they obtained by the previous orders. I cannot agree with him in that contention. Now, Sir, in clause 1 of the Order in Council, 21st April, 1902, the first paragraph of that Order in Council is identically the same as the first paragraph of the Orders in Council previously granted, and which had been rescinded. Under that first paragraph these parties are given-	[DOT]
The sole right to divert and take water from the Klondike river at any point or points between its entry into the Yukon river and Flat creek for the purpose of generating power with which to pump water to work the auriferous deposits in the district (hereinafter termed ' The District ' ) comprising the beds, banks, valleys, slopes and hills of the Klondike river, of Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks, and of their tributaries.
Now, X say that they are given the sole and absolute right and by the section that follows they are given six years to exercise that right. They tie up for a period of six years the development of the water power in that locality. Mr. Speaker, I take the ground that if any man went in and attempted to develop the power in that district these gentlemen could at once apply for an injunction and restrain him from doing any work in that connection. It has been my pleasure to read several of the best works in regard to placer mining in the State of California. I recognize that in a new country such as the Yukon there are difficulties in the way of government, in the way of making orders and regulations incidental to meeting the requirements of the people, but I venture to say, Sir, that you cannot find in the history of any mining country where a concession was given such as tlie Treadgold concession. I find in the history of California- that in the placer mining districts of that state, during the boom in placer mining, there were 6,000 miles of sluices built. There was no monopoly given to any one company, and there was no concession such as this tying up the whole country. Companies were formed and there was competition between these companies and that competition gave to the miners a reasonable rate for the water which they required. There was no such concession as this monopoly which has been granted in favour of the concessionaires. Now, the hon. Minister of Labour also referred to a little change that was made in regard to section 3., He says that :
The right to divert and use the water of Rock creek subject to any grants lawfully subsisting and subject to the rights of free miners' bona fide working claims.
And so on is a change. I would like to just point out to the hon. Minister of Labour in regard to the water of Rock creek that there are no claims worked on Rock creek so that the reservation in this case amounts to nothing. Rock creek was a source of water for distribution to the Klondike river. There are a number of clauses in this Order in Council and it would take me a very long time to point out all the iniquities of them. The hon. minister has pointed to section 10 of this Order in Council. I do not know, why he did. It is a most sweeping clause. Clause 10 reads as follows :
The right, subject to no payment except the royalty prescribed upon output to make entry for and work any abandoned mining claim or claims on Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks.
Up to that point it is absolutely the same as the previous Order in Council, but this language has been added :
Such right to be exercisable only when the grantees by the construction of works in pursuance of this franchise are in a position to deliver water upon such claim or claims for the working therof.
I fail to find in this final Order in Council where the grantees are bound to do anything. They are not bound to expend one dollar, while, in the former Order in Council, they are bound to expend $250,000. By' this Order in Council, I repeat, they are not bound to expend one dollar.
Now, I am not going to take up the legal aspect of the case, because there are those who will follow me who will deal more particularly with that subject. My mind is in a very hazy condition in regard to the legal aspect of the case as construed by the hon. Minister of Labour. He tells us in one breath that this Order in Council is no good, that it does not become any good until such time as it is officially published in the 1 Canada Gazette.' In another breath he tells us that the Order is good. From my reading of the statutes I am satisfied that the Order is not good. We have to speak of the Order in Council just as we find it, and we find that in the preamble of the Order in Council these hon. gentlemen quote as their authority for the passing of that order certain statutes being section 5, Chap. 15, of the Act 55-56 Vic., and section 8 of the Yukon Territory Act as that section was enacted by section 2 of chapter 11 of 62-63 Vic. Let us look at 62-63 Vic. for one moment:
Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Governor in Council may make ordinances for the peace, order and good government of the territory, and of Her Majesty's subjects and others therein ; but no ordinance made by the Governor in Council, or the commissioner in council, shall-

(o.) appropriate any public land or other property of Canada without authority of parliament, or impose any duty of customs or any excise ; nor shall any tax be imposed except as in this Act provided.
in so making the said grants and concessions by Order in Council, the government have exceeded their authority and have committed a gross breach of the duty entrusted to them under the constitution.
I say that this statute is the authority against the contention of the hon. minister, and that they have no authority to give away or to grant the public domain of this country without coming to the parliament of Canada. Now, I must apologize for taking up so much time, but I feel that while these men are far distant from us, some members of this House have to advocate their cause. There is no doubt a great grievance existing in that country. There is no doubt that concessions have been granted since 1S98, which have been to the detriment of the miners of that country. There is no doubt that this concession which we are now discussing is a concession which will destroy that country, which will have the effect of injuring not only the trade of that country but of injuring the trade of Canada, and I say that my only excuse for taking up some much time is that I felt that it was a pleasure to advocate the cause of the miners of the Yukon.

Mr. Speaker, there are two or three phases of this question that I would like to offer a remark or two upon, and which have beeu mentioned by my hon. friend who has just spoken. There is no member of this House, I may say, if the hon. member will permit me, for whom I have a greater respect, or of whose courtesy and ordinary fairness I have a higher opinion than I have for that of the hon. gentleman. I must confess that he presented to me, as I think my hon. friend presented to the House,__ a striking example of how prejudiced and unreasonable a frame of mind an hon. member of this House can get into when he honestly and sincerely thinks that he is as fair and impartial as a man can be. The hon. gentleman has approached this question, as he assured us, in a spirit of the utmost fairness; yet, I think the first adjective that he applied to the transaction was that it was a transaction of a most iniquitous character. IIow calm and hdw impartial my hon. friend must be, when, in discussing a plain, and it seems to me a very reasonably clear business transaction, he has no more moderate or reasonable a criticism to pass upon it than to declare that it is an iniquitous transaction. Now, Sir, my hon. friend (Mr. Cas-grain) asked this House to express its opinion with regard to this transaction. And what are the terms of his amendment ? It says :
That this House is of opinion that the said powers, franchises and concessions constitute in favour of the said Treadgold a gigantic monopoly, which while depriving the treasury of enormous revenues is most detrimental to the mining industries of the Yukon. And that Mr. PRINGLE.
I presume that my hon. friends opposite, will at least admit that they are under some obligation to furnish to this House evidence to justify it in expressing the opinion set out in the motion. I shall take the liberty of examining somewhat closely the terms of the resolution, to ascertain if I can, what evidence has been furnished- dignify it if you will by the name of evidence-to justify the House in putting itself upon record in such a form. Is it because there is a monopoly in the terms of the Order in Council, that my hon. friend has objection to it ? Is it the monopolistic character of this grant that he makes the most complaint of ? Well, I am at a loss to understand how it would be possible, under the conditions which must exist in the Yukon, to have a privilege of this kind exercised except it would be in a monopolistic form. To go back to the original conditions that existed in the Yukon ; we know that for two or three years after the placer mining qualities of the territory were discovered the richest yield in these placer diggings was capable of being taken out with ease, and a trifling outlay then brought large financial results. As the years went on, the conditions changed and year after year it becomes less possible to take out placer gold except by the exercise of greater labour and the introduction of machinery. Unless you can resort'to mechanical appliances ; unless you can get the hydraulic system in operation in that country, you cannot under present conditions turn to profitable account the admittedly large deposits of placer gold which are to be obtained in that territory. You have got to have mechanical means to assist you, and these mechanical appliances have been found necessary in other countries where placer gold digging has been followed with any success. It is therefore conceded that in order to work these placer diggings expensive hydraulic machinery must be employed. Now, Sir, it goes without saying that such appliances can only be obtained by a very large outlay of money, and by persons or companies having considerable capital at their command. In the very nature of things it requires a monopoly to carry on such work. The hon. gentleman told us that in certain placer districts of the United States it had been possible to allow two or three companies to operate on one of these rivers. How are you going to put in these creeks in the Klondike three or four different systems, with three or four different mechanical plants, to compete one with another. In the first place it is necessary to have the head water dammed and there cannot be four different dams across one river at the same point. To accumulate the water so that it may be

obtained to sluice down the river, it cannot be done by more than one concern. Unless I totally misapprehend the conditions which exist there can only be one company in operation and if that be the case then that company must of necessity have a monopoly. I do not believe therefore that this House will be justified in condemning that transaction because it is a monopoly, when in the very nature of things, if you require that this hydraulic process should be employed to maintain that industrial enterprise in this country, it has to be done in form of monopoly, and cannot be done in any other form. Therefore, to condemn the monopoly, in the words of this resolution is to condemn a thing that is imperatively necessary, unless you are to abandon this country altogether and allow these deposits to go unproductive. My hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) goes on to say in his motion :
While depriving the treasury of enormous revenue.
What evidence is there that under the operation of this system-which as I have said is a necessary and proper system- what evidence is there that it is going to deprive the country of an enormous amount of revenue. Every dollar's worth of gold that is taken out by this process is taken out subject to the royalties which are imposed upon the production of gold taken out in any other part of that district. There is no difference between the royalty upon this and the royalty upon any other gold.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: What about representation ?

I can very well understand that there are reasons, very strong and proper reasons, why, in order to induce men of capital to put in $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 and perhaps more to construct this machinery, there would have to be very attractive and valuable inducements held out to them, and concessions would have to be made in the way of the removal of restrictions which would generally be applicable, and might very properly be applicable in the earlier history of the country when placer mining was conducted under very different circumstances. You must bear .in mind, Mr. Speaker, that in adopting this system the government had the idea in mind of insuring the continuance of the development of that country, so that all the placer mining should be made as profitable as possible. In order that that should be done a large expenditure must necessarily be made, and in order that the money for this expenditure could be obtained you had to offer to capitalists an attractive proposition. We happen to know that when the question of the hydraulic development of that section of the country was first mooted a number of people visited Ottawa from the United States and elsewhere. When some people heard that we were going to impose conditions upon this system of mining they turned away their faces and went away from the country, because they said : The conditions that you are talking about imposing are such that it would not be profitable for us to embark in this enterprise and to risk a large amount of money contingent upon the possibility that the country might not prove as rich in its gold-bearing properties as was represented. There were persons who came to Ottawa at that time, and who, as I am credibly informed, were satisfied that they could not embark in the enterprise under any condition which the government would entertain favourably. Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) does not appear to consider that you ought to present an attractive programme to people whom you invite to go into operations of this character. The hon, gentleman thinks that every body should see at a glance that it was certain to be an enormously profitable undertaking.
My hon. friend from Cornwall and Stormont (Mr. Pringle) said that the amount of money the Treadgold syndicate would make was simply fabulous. He figured out that they would make ten million dollars a year profit. Well, if any one who had command of the means would believe that my hon. friend's statement was to be relied on, he and everybody who had the same belief would be tumbling over one another in order to secure this concession on any terms, and would not care how drastic or severe they might be. The negotiations were not conducted by the Minister of the Interior alone. It is only fair and just to him to say that all through this transaction he was acting in conference with his colleagues and with a sub-committee of Council. Realizing that we were dealing with new problems to us, we were doing the best we could to reach a conclusion and to arrange a bargain which would be advantageous to the country and just to all concerned. Reflections are being cast on the Minister of the Interior, anc>
this is spoken of by hon. gentlemen opposite as a fraudulent transaction, as a transaction which is based on fraud. What is the evidence to justify any such statement as that? The present Judge Davies, of the Supreme Court, I am reminded, was one of the committee, and was aiding and assisting us in these negotiations.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What does that prove ?

My hon. friend from Cornwall and Stormont refers to the fact that the formal application made by the Messrs. Treadgold was received one day and was immediately and instantly accepted and replied to by the government the next day ; the idea intended to be conveyed being that these gentlemen swooped down on the government, gobbled them up, and carried away in an instant the contract for these con-

cessions. If my hon. friend liad been here for the months during which these negotiations took place, he would have known very much better. He would have known that the reason the letter came to be dated so short a time before the Order in Council was passed, was because the negotiations which had taken place from day to day, from week to week, and from month to month, were finally concluded, and when they were concluded, the terms that were acceded to by the government were put into the form of that application.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him how much deliberation was expended on the question of allowing them to charge a dollar an inch for the water ?

A very great deal. I confess that the question was absolutely new ; and, as regards a reasonable price, we had to confer with others ; but upon the best opinion we could get, the amount was put in, because it was believed it was a fair price. We found afterwards that we were entirely mistaken ; I frankly acknowledge that ; as people are likely to be mistaken when dealing with entirely new matters, as to a new country, far away from the scene where the decisions are arrived at and where the administrative acts take place.
Now, our lion, friends have no evidence to prove that this arrangement, in addition to being a monopoly, is going to deprive the treasury of enormous revenues. If it is a successful adventure, that is to say, if these people are able to raise the necessary money to carry out the undertaking, it may prove to be a very great money saver to the country ; and the country may secure the development of that section of the Yukon, which might not, under any other conditions, be susceptible of development. It may in that way bring enormous revenues to' the country which we would not otherwise have. But'there is no testimony that it might involve a loss to the treasury of any large sum.
Our lion, friends ask the House to say that this arrangement would be most detrimental to the mining industry of the Yukon. What evidence have they adduced in support of this proposition ? How is the mining industry of the Yukon going to be harmed if we succeed in having this great hydraulic system in operation in that country ? Where does the power reside to say what is the proper compensation to be paid to these people for the privileges which they are able to lease or sell to the owners or licensees of mines in that district ? Does not the Governor in Council hold in his hand all the necessary power to prevent any wrong being done to the miners ? What do the licensees throughout the district want ? They want water. And what may they properly give J for it ? What is a fair price for it ? My Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
lion, friend says they are going to be asked 25 cents per miners' inch, and that it is going to cost $300 a day to every one who lias a sluice. speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

I will show my hon. friend where it is. We have named no price in the order for the use of water. It does not at all follow that it was necessary to name any price. On the contrary, we think it is quite unnecessary to name it. That is why we are hearing complaints to-day. My hon. friend asks me to point out where there is anything in this Order in Council showing control by the government of the rates for the use of the water.

The concluding portion of the resolution says
And that in so making the said grants and concessions by Order in Council, the government have exceeded their authority and committed a gross breach of thq^duty entrusted to them under the constitution.
I think my hon. friend rather failed to make clear the proposition that there lias been any act on the part of the gover-ment in this transaction which is at all in

excess of the powers properly belonging to it. It is quite true that this Yukon country belongs to the Crown. It is quite true that it is not in the power of the Governor in Council or any minister of the Crown to dispose of or sell, any property of the Crown except and until there has been a statutory enactment conferring that authority. Now, if any wider language is necessary than that

Lands containing coal of other minerals, including lands in the Rocky Mountains Park

Regulations have, however, been made and have been promulgated, and under the regulations that have been piromul-gated all that has been done under the Order in Council was in the fullest degree authorized. So, my hon. friend has not taken substantial ground. He is following a delusion; he is deceiving himself, when he supposes that an Act of parliament which says that the Governor in Council has power to sell or lease these lands in any such manner and under such regulations as he clioses, is not sufficient to cover this case. I think there can be no ground for the belief that a constitutional doubt arises as to w'lmt has been done. We are the government and they are the opposition, and it is not necessary to use any argument to convince them that we never do anything right, while they are unimpeachable, their opinion is the standard of correctness and propriety, and so they can vote for this resolution without the slightest hesitation or reluctance. I intended to refer earlier to the statement of the hon. member for Cornwall and Stormont (Mr. Pringle), when he took occasion to drag in the question of the Mackenzie & Mann contract and to say that this is a similar contract and one in which the government has been guilty of improvidently and unreasonably committing itself to a bargain such as never should have been sanctioned or approved. I remember hon. gentlemen opposite, one after another, rising in their places, with eyes glittering at the prospect pointing out the hundreds of millions of dollars, and the hundreds of thousands of acres of land wiiich were being given away, lands which were simply a land of gold-all you had to do was to go out and dig it up. Why, it was so vast in extent, so enormous in its richness that we were simply throwing away wealth that would have made the whole country rich, and probably would
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: have sufficed without the imposition of other taxes to maintain the government institutions of the country for a century. And, notwithstanding all this, and though these lands have lain there open to any man who clioses to make application for them, teem-iug as they told us with this incalculable and inexhaustible wealth, yet not a single individual has been found who has discovered enough to make it worth his while to apply for a square mile or for even a hundred square feet of that whole territory for mining purposes-not a single solitary one. I recall to my hon. friends, therefore, the wild folly of their statements when this subject was under discussion, and I ask them to beware that they are not putting themselves in that same untenable and indefensible position that they put themselves in when they opposed the proposition that we then laid before them.
