Mr. Speaker, I was prepared, when the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) stood up to discuss this question and, when I heard him find fault with the remarks that have been made by hon. gentlemen on this side who preceded him, to hear this question discussed without any exhibition of prejudice or feeling. But if the hon. member who preceded the Minister of Railways and Canals in discussing this question to-night, showed any spirit of prejudice, I venture the assertion that he has been entirely outdone by the Minister of Railways and Canals himself. Looking at this question from a general standpoint, it appears to me that the same rule applies to this Act as should be applied to other legislation or legislative acts. The general principle should be that any legislation or legislative Acts which tend or pretend to confer upon any individual, or any corporation or body of people, rights that are different from the rights that are enjoyed by the public in general, should be such as will bear the very closest scrutiny by the opposition and by the country. But I do not think, in viewing the Orders in Council that have been under discussion here to-day that they come within that category, for they strike me as being in direct violation of that very wholesome principle. That Order in Council bears upon its face its own condemnation. It is perfectly apparent from the terms of that Order in Council and the offer that was
made by Mr. Treadgold and his associates, that the Treadgold company did not forget, when they were presenting their memorial to the government, to ask for almost everything that was in sight. And, Sir, notwithstanding the greed, if I may use the term, displayed by the Treadgold Company in asking for these concessions, it appeared that the government was perfectly willing to go them one better. They have signified their willingness to go them one better in the language that they used in the Orders in Council. After reciting the offer that haA been made by these people, the government say
And that the said parties shall be and are hereby granted all and every the powers, privileges, rights and franchises asked for.
Well, Sir, it is wonderful to my mind that the Treadgold Company did not ask for a fence around it, and if they had, I do not doubt the government would have given them a fence, and also given them a gatekeeper, judging from the way they have treated this company. Now, it has been said, and said correctly, that while the government were so generous in granting to the Treadgold Company these rights and privileges, they were yet careful enough only to grant these rights subject to certain conditions. Well, one is apt to understand the use of that term ' condition ' as implying that some onus or some duty is placed upon the person against whom that condition is established, or that some duty is cast upon that person in regard to the granting of the right. But I call the attention of the House for a moment to one or two of these conditions, and the manner in which the Treadgold Company were tied up by the government's action. I would point out that the government said to these people when they came and asked for these rights, yes, take all you want, all you ask for you may have; but you must take those rights subject to these conditions. The first of these conditions is, yes, take all you want but you must not pay any taxes upon it. That is the first condition, certainly a very onerous one, and the Treadgold people must have struggled and argued strenuously with the government to prevent them from imposing such an onerous condition as that. But perhaps they thought that was the only condition of an onerous nature that would be imposed upon them, and so no doubt they waited for the next clause of this Order in Council. The next clause goes them one better, and says :	Yes, you may have all
these rights that you are asking for in this memorial you have presented to the government, and in addition to your not paying any taxes, we go you one better and we say that you should not pay any rent, nor should you pay any occupation rent. No doubt the Treadgold people felt themselves very greatly aggrieved by that condition, but that is the language of the condition that

is imposed upon them. Let me point out something more. After granting to these people all they asked, and saying they should pay no taxes, no rent, and no occupation rent, that they should only pay the royalty upon the output equal to the very lowest royalty that was imposed upon gold and silver, then they added another clause as if to make the matter doubly binding and doubly pleasing to the Treadgold people, for they say : Yes, and even if you don't work the mine, we will put the further condition upon you that you won't have to pay the $200 to the government. Why, Sir, you may go through the whole list of these conditions and with very few exceptions they are of the nature X have described.
Now one word with regard to some of these matters where I think it is perfectly apparent to any careful reader that the government have wrought an injustice and injury to the free miners of the Yukon territory. You will notice that in the regulations of council which have been referred to here to-night, in the first clause, subsection one, which has been read more than once, it says
Provided that license holders of mining locations situated on the Klondike river should be entitled,
And so on, as against the grantee. Now what does that mean ? Could language make more plain the meaning and intention of the concessionaires and of the government ? It says : License holders who may hereafter procure licenses, but it confines the benefits which are there pretended to be granted, to these miners who are already holding licenses, and it does not extend to any future miner who may go in there in opposition to this corporation. It seems to me to be an extraordinary block to free miners going into that country. Yet the Minister of Xiailways and Canals will ask this House and gentlemen who have discussed this question,, where or in what way is this going to effect prejudicially the miners of the Yukon Territory ? Sir, is it not perfectly plain that such a clause as that in these regulations, absolutely shuts out future competition over a large portion of that country to free miners ? But that clause has a still more sweeping effect, taken in connection with the other clause of this regulation which provides that upon a claim being abandoned these people may enter upon that claim and work it. Now take that clause in connection with the regulation in regard to the supply of water. If there is a shortage of water, if there is not water enough to work all these mines efficiently, then the water is to be divided proportionately between them. Yet, I say, taking these two Orders in Council and taking these regulations I have referred to, the result will be almost inevitable, it seems to me, it is impossible to work it out in any other way, Mr. PORTER.
that these miners who are already in there and who alone are protected by that first subsection, will, a large portion of them, be shut out by the operation of this Order in Council. That is another way in which, I say, it appears clear to me that the Order in Council is going to work prejudicially to the interests of that country. Now, I want to call attention to just one other clause in regard to this matter and that is to clause thirteen. I shall not take occasion to refer to those clauses which have been spoken of particularly, but this feature of section thirteen has not, I think, been mentioned in this discussion. Section thirteen provides that
The right, subject to the regulations hereinafter contained, to construct, lay, maintain, supply with water and operate bed-rock flumes, and any other flumes for supplying water in the district.
What does that really mean ? It means that Mr. Treadgold and his associates are granted this right and this exclusive right for the purpose of prospecting that country. When they build their bed-rock flumes in these rivers and creeks they cannot do It without discovering where the best mining locations are all along that line, and when they discover a mining lc cation this Order in Council provides that they have the right to grab it up the same as they grab all the others. That in itself is sufficient to condemn that Order in Council aud to show conclusively that the concessions that are granted, as far as the interests of that great country are concerned, were disadvantageous to the Yukon Territory and to the miners there. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals took occasion to ask opposition members who are discussing this question to furnish some evidence that the concessions granted to these people, were operating, or were going to operate disadvantageously to the people of that country. 1 am surprised that the hon. minister should ask such a question in the face of such an array of testimony as has been offered from this side of the House during the discussion. When he asks that question he actually discredits his own party, and he actually discredits the best people in the Yukon Territory. In addition to what has been already quoted in regard to the action of the Liberal party, of the Liberal chib, of the board of trade and other bodies who, we have a right to assume, are familiar, from their contact with that subject and from their living in the country, with the conditions and needs of the territory, I am going to present to the House an expression of opinion from the citizens of Dawson. I hold in my hand a paper printed in Dawson, which, in its issue of February 20, last, contains the report of a meeting of citizens of Dawsou held for the purpose of discussing the railway policy of the government and amongst other things the Treadgold concession. A number of resolu-

tions were passed by that meeting. These resolutions were to be forwarded to the government and the government were urged to take action upon them. The sixth resolution demanded:	*
The cancellation of all hydraulic concession leases fraudulently obtained, also hydraulic concession leases, the terms of which have not been complied with that are now liable to cancellation.
Seventh. The strict enforcement of the terms of all hydraulic concession leases, so that the holders of same will be obliged to operate and mine the ground held by them.
There is another way in which this Order in Council operates to the disadvantage of the people of that country, as has already been pointed out. It ties it up for six years. Those living upon the spot and being familiar with the subject say : compel these people to operate and mine the ground held by them.
Eighth

And this is a sweeping one

The cancellation in every instance of hydraulic concession leases where the same are in any way liable to cancellation, so that the ground now tied up and lying idle within the boundaries of the same be thrown open to miners and worked.
There was an opportunity offered to this government, *as has already been pointed out, before the passage of the last Order in Council to rescind the first Order in Council and to meet the requirements of the people of the Yukon Territory, thus serving the best interests of these people and the best interests of the mining industry of that country. They did pass an Order in Council rescinding the former Order in Council, but they were not content with satisfying the people of the Yukon but they showed that it was not their interest to serve the people of the Yukon, but that their interest lay in some other direction, and accordingly the last Order in Council was passed. Speaking to the resolution which I have just read Mr. George Black, a citizen of Dawson, made use of this language.
Every man in the territory wishes that the laws should have the approval of the people and meet with the requirements of local conditions. If the mining law in this territory had been made with the approval of the people the country to-day would be in a different condition. But we have the experience of the past four or five years and it is not too late for the people to act	
If our.laws had been made by the elected representatives of the people, we would have no need for this meeting to-night. Concessions would not have been plastered over the country.
I must warn the people against any decrease in vigilance in relation to the Treadgold concession. As it stands to-day the owners of that concession have the sole right to sell water. When the monopoly clause was taken from the Treadgold concession the right of other people to secure water rights was also cancelled. So
in reality Treadgold has still the sole monopoly on- the water rights.
That is the view which people living in tlie Yukon and who are familiar with this subject take of the matter and I think we are pretty safe in acting upon their judgment. I am surprised in the face of evidence of that nature that the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals should stand up in his place in this House and ask for further evidence than that which has been given him to show that this is a monopoly. Now, he takes occasion to remark further that works of this character must be carried on by companies in the nature of a monopoly. I cannot, for my part, agree with the statement. The statement may be right to a certain extent, it may be necessary to induce, in some way, companies, or corporations, or capitalists, to invest their money in enterprises of this kind for the development of the country, but it is only necessary to go as far as the interests of that country demand and it is not necessary, as the government has done, to practically give away the Yukon Territory to a monopoly in order to secure a supply of water. As I understand the attitude taken by the opposition during the discussion of this question they do hot object-I do not, at any rate, for one, object-to one company investing their money in this enterprise for the purpose of benefiting the territory and the mining industry there. I do not care whether there is one company or a dozen companies if the rights of the people are so guarded as against the one company, that the company will not be allowed to gobble up everything there is in the country. It has been truly said and I know from the researches I have made myself in different books, that in California and in Australia you cannot find an instance where a concession such as this, has been granted to any corporation.
While there are companies working there and providing water for carrying on mining operations; while there are such companies innumerable in California and Australia, I have failed to discover any company that has been given such sweeping rights, such exclusive rights, such privileges in defiance of the rights of the people as have been given to this Treadgold Company in the Yukon Territory. The Minister of Railways seems to take a very great deal of satisfaction from the fact, that, as he says, the right t# fix the charge for supplying water to the miners in the Yukon may be regulated by the Gold Commissioner, and therefore that the people may safely conclude that the government would not-to use his own expression-be so foolish as to sanction the making of any charge that would be exorbitant or unreasonable. Why, Sir, the action of the government that he was reviewing at the very time, answered him completely. He said that the government would not be so foolish as to sanction

a charge of say twenty-five cents per miners' inch for this water, but did lie forget that a year or two before this very same government had sanctioned a charge of $1 a miners' inch or four times as great as the twenty-five cents which he thought the government would not be so foolish as to allow being charged. In view of this, what warrant has the Minister of Railways to say to the House or to the country, that the government would not be foolish enough to allow a charge of twenty-five cents. The minister gave us a construction of clauses (B) and (C) in the regulations, and he said that these two clauses must stand separate and apart as they meant separate and distinct things. Well, it is perfectly apparent to any one that such a construction as that can only be placed upon these clauses by torturing the English language. One clause says :
The grantees shall compensate the owners of any mining claim.
The next clause says :	'
Any question of compensation arising under this grant shall be determined, &c.
Why, it is absolutely plain that they cannot be read apart, and if it lacked any further evidence than the mere reading, look at clause (F) of the very same regulation in regard to the charge that is to be made, and see what it says. Does that clause use the word ' compensation 7 ' Not at all. It says that the ' charge ' which the grantee shall make and so on. And if you want any further evidence look at the order made on the 7th of December, following, and see what that says. Clause (S) of the regulations therein contained uses the same language as in clause (F) which I have referred to, and instead of the word ' compensation ' the word ' charge ' is used there again. It seems to be only playing with the matter for the Minister of Railways to submit such a construction to an intelligent House of Commons.
Then the Minister of Railways took occasion to refer to the very great exertions that were put forth by the government, and the long time it had occupied in the discussion of these Orders in Council before action was taken by the governnient. Well, it strikes me as a very singular thing, that if the government did take all the care and trouble that the Minister of Railways would have us believe it did take, to use liis own words, in negotiating and perfecting the matter in this Order in Council; it is a very strange thing I say that when they got it perfected and fully negotiated and satisfactory, that they had not the courage to make it law. Why have they refused; why have they delayed in making it law ? If it is right it should have been made law at the time, and if it is not right it should never become law, and the government have a perfect right now in the interest of the

country to cancel it. I submit for these reasons, and for the reasons that have been urged by other members on this side of the House, that the government ought to avail of the first opportunity of rescinding this Order in Council. They cannot show their disposition to serve the people of the Yukon better than by voting for the resolution that has been moved by my hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain).

Mr. Speaker. For my part I have no fault to find with the argument which has been made by my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Porter}. May I be permitted to tender him my congratulations upon the fact that his speech has been singularly free from the fraud and fury which has characterized some of the previous utterances of members on that side of the House. But in all that has been said, no one so far as addressed himself to the question as to why the government was induced to pass this Order in Council and to give this concession to Mr. Treadgold and his associates. There must have been reason; there must have been some cause for the government to take the action which they have taken, and which is now challenged by the opposition. For my part I am quite ready to take that responsibility for our action which we owe to tlje House and to the country, and I do not despair that when the whole question has been examined by my hon. friends opposite, that even they will come to a different conclusion than that which has been expressed by them. The reason, and the wherefore, and the cause of this Order in Council, which in its disposition, I admit is somewhat unusual from the course ordinarily followed; the reason and the wherefore of this Order in Council is to be found in the history of the Klondike and in the conditions which now prevail there. The Yukon Territory is a territory embedded in gold, but in which there is a scarcity of water for mining operations. It is an established fact that at the present time there are claims which are worked with great profit, and there are other claims which could be worked with great profit also but for the fact that there is no water to work them. Early in the history of the Yukon the government was appealed to more than once to establish works whereby water could be collected for the purpose of affording facilities to the miners to work their claims. If you look at the several petitions which have been referred to this afternoon; if you look for instance at the petition of the board of trade, you will find that two things are demanded from the government. First of all it is asked that the Treadgold concession should be abolished. And, why ? Simply in order that something else may be substituted for It. That is to say, that as soon as the Treadgold concessions was abolished, the government

should substitute works of its own for the purpose of collecting water and distributing it to the miners of that locality. Here is the petition of the board of trade. The argument contained in it has been cited three or four times and it is not necessary for me to read it again, but the conclusion, so far as my memory serves me, has never been read yet, and here it is :
Your petitioners therefore pray :
(11 That the Order in Council of April 21, 1902, may be cancelled completely, and that no special privileges shall hereafter be granted within this territory with respect to wood, mining, water, or any other class of rights affecting the general public, but that all persons shall be restricted in such matters to the rights conferred upon every member of the community by the mining regulations.
(2) That the supply and distribution of water for general mining purposes within this territory shall not be controlled by any private person or corporation, but either that it shall be undertaken by the Dominion government as a public work, or the power shall be given to the commissioner of the Yukon Territory in council to construct such a system and to raise the necessary funds by bonds guaranteed by the Dominion.
This was the alternative presented to us. There was a consensus of opinion among all the miners of the Yukon that the systems in existence were not adequate to the people's needs, and that something had to be done for collecting water, creating power and distributing water to tlie miners. How was that to be done ? We were asked to do it as a government work, providing the money by the issue of bonds or otherwise. The matter was looked into, and we found that works of that character demanded by the Yukon hoard of trade would cost millions of dollars-more than one million, and, if my information is correct, more than two million.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Daurier).

speechtext: More than $5,000,000.

More than $5,000,000 I am told. The government were not prepared to expend such an amount of money for the purpose of creating the necessary power to distribute water ; and I want to know if hon. gentlemen opposite, who have criticised the action of the government in this matter, and who have constituted themselves champions of the miners of the Yukon, would be prepared to support the government in expending $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 in order to provide these works.
Might I ask the hon. Prime Minister on whose or what report he liases the estimates for $5,000,000 ?

I understand that it is upon the report of all the engineers who have tested the question. I am not prepared to say myself, though I am so informed, that these works would cost $5,000.000 ; hut I am prepared to stake all the reputation I have that all the estimates 91*
will agree that they would cost at least $2,000,000 ; and I ask the hon. gentleman if he is prepared to advise the government to spend $2,000,000 in order to provide the works demanded by the miners of the Yukon. Nobody would ask the government to do that; and if it was not to he done by the government, it would have to lie done by private enterprise. Application was made to us. Capitalists came to us declaring that they would be prepared to undertake the risk and make the expenditure. We made a contract with them, if I remember rightly, in the summer of 1901. The contract was published in the Yukon, and exception was taken to it. It was represented among other things that the price we had fixed for the sale of water was too high. We had put it at one dollar. On investigation, I am bound to say, we found that it would he on the average too high. There is no question so difficult to determine as what should he the price of water in that district if such a work were to be undertaken. One dollar an inch in some places would not have been too much ; and in other places it would have been exorbitant We reduced the price to twenty-five cents. We had a delegation of miners from the Yukon. That delegation was alluded to this afternoon by the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) and also by the hon. member for Cornwall and Stormont (Mr. Pringle). We discussed the matter with the miners, and they convinced us that even twenty-five cents per miners' inch would be exorbitant in some instances, and we had to provide another method. We cancelled all the Orders in Council, and passed another. We were criticised for doing so. What were we to do ? Were we to remain idle, while the miners in the Yukon were asking us to give them facilities to work their claims ? Only the richest claims were being worked. There were others that might be worked, but owing to the lack of facilities for water, they were not being worked effectively. Therefore we had to provide other methods. If we had failed to respond to the demands of the Yukon miners, hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House would have been the first to blame us. Whether we act or do not act we are sure to be blamed by hon. gentlemen opposite. We thought that the worst we could do was to remain idle ; and we determined to do our best to meet the views and wishes of the mining population of the Yukon, who wanted facilities to enable them to carry on their operations. Therefore we passed the Order in Council which hon. gentlemen opposite ask the House to censure us for passing. Now, I am prepared to discuss this Order in Council. I am prepared to meet my hon. friends on the other side of the House in regard to the salient points of the attack they have made upon us. What is the first disposition of this order ? It is a very natural



one. It provides that these Treadgold concessionaires shall have the power to erect dams and do all the work necessary in the bed of the Klondike river, between the mouth of the river and Fiat creek, in order to create a generating power for electric purposes. But if we did that we ran the risk perhaps of interfering with the operations of the miners who have concessions in the Klondike river and who might be deprived of their water. If we made no provision against that, we might be subject to censure ; but the first thing we did was to provide that, prior even to the right of the company, the miners on the Klondike river would have a primary right to a flow of water sufficient to carry on their operations. Here is what the order says :
The sole right to divert and take water from the Klondike river at any point or points between its entry into the Yukon river and Flat creek for the purpose of generating power with which to pump water to work the auriferous deposits in the district (hereinafter termed ' the district ') comprising the beds, banks, valleys, slopes and hills of the Klondike river, of Bonanza, Bear and H-unker creeks, and of their tributaries.
Provided, that licensed holders of mining locations situated on the Klondike river shall be entitled as against the grantees to the use free from toll of a flow of water sufficient for working their claims, but not exceeding in all three thousand five hundred (3,500) miners' inches, euual to five thousand two hundred and fifty (5,250) cubic feet per minute.
This Is what Is reserved-the right of every miner to have his claim given priority to that of the company. The miners shall take the water first. No matter what improvements are made by the company, there shall be no interference with the rights of private miners in the Klondike. If it be possible in any way to safeguard the interests of the miner more effectively, I would like to know it. The company having erected its works is given the privilege of selling the power itself to anybody who wants it, and for any purpose whatever. But is the company allowed to sell the power at its own price, or to create such a monopoly as would destroy the operations of other industries ? No, Sir. A check is put upon the company-that same check which we impose in the case of similar concessions-and that is the power given the Governor General in Council to regulate the price. The Order in Council reads as follows :-
Provided that if any power is developed and rendered available by the grantees under this section which they do not make use of, then the same shall be offered for sale to the public and the rates to be charged therefor shall be subject to the control of the Governor General in Council.
This is the method always followed in this country in similar cases. It is the method by which we regulate the tolls on railways and by which we are asked to regulate the tolls of the telephone companies, and it is
