the best method yet devised in this country for the working of such franchises. Another power is given the company. The first object for which the company was granted its privileges was to collect and to distribute the water so that all these claims-bench claims, for instance-which are not now being worked may be operated. What is the provision on this point ? That provision has been criticised. My hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) has taken the ground that we have not provided any check to prevent the company charging what it likes. I am prepared to discuss that point with my hon. friend. Bet me call his attention to this point. It is a point which has been already made by my hon. colleague the Minister of Railways and Canals. But I want to call the attention of my hon. friend from Montmorency to it again. For I do not despair of my hon. friend. If he will only forget that he is a lawyer and bear in -mind that he may, some time, be a judge and have to exercise a judicial mind and a judicial authority. I do not despair of convincing him that we have made all the provisions! necessary to protect the miners against the greed of the company. Here is what I find in the Order in Council, and what my hon. friend very deliberately and adroitly avoided this afternoon. The right is given-
Subject to the regulations hereinafter contained, to use, distribute and dispose of the water delivered by the grantees within the district.
This is very clear. The right is given the company to use, distribute and dispose of, by sale or otherwise, the water delivered by the grantees within the district. Let me now call the attention of my hon. friend to the regulations imposed in this connection. The regulations are not there simply for an ornament. They must be held to have a meaning. What are these regulations ? They are as follows
The grantee shall allow all free miners within the district to tail his sluices, hydraulics, ground sluices and drains, free of charge, in the flumes and drains of the grantees, yet not in such a way as to damage or obstruct the free working of the flumes and drains of the grantees by rocks, stones, boulders or otherwise.
Therefore the moment the company constructs a flume facing a claim, the owner of the claim has the right at once to bring his sluices to the flume and take the water. He has no permission to ask. The company cannot refuse. The right is guaranteed to him, whether the company is willing or not, to take his sluices to the flume and draw the water. My hon. friend will agree that the miner has no permission to ask, and that the moment he has tailed his sluice to the flume the water of the company flows into his sluice, and he is at liberty to use it. What follows ? There must be compensation. If

the miner and the company agree upon a price, there is nothing more to be said, but if they do not, then section O comes in :
Any question of compensation arising under this grant shall be determined judicially by the Gold Commissioner, subject to the appeal of the Territorial Court of the district, and the said court may, on special circumstances being shown, make an order for the taking of further evidence.
I would ask my hon. friend from Montmorency to take the case as it stands. Let him suppose that he is the Gold Commissioner for the Yukon. The company has erected its works. I am a miner and have taken my sluice to the flume, and am using water from the flume to wash out my gold dirt. The company cannot prevent me from using the water. It cannot prevent me from taking my sluice to its flume, but the company says : You will pay me so much. I reply that its price is an exorbitant one. Then we go before Mr. Oasgrain, the Gold Commissioner, and he determines what compensation shall be paid. If that is not clear, there is nothing clear. If that is not law, there is no law.
If I should give judgment in that sense, my judgment would be unanimously reversed on appeal.

Let me tell my hon. friend that he minimizes his own ability to give a judgment which would be according to law, justice and equity, and to the terms of this agreement.
My hon. friend may point to the abandoned claims. In the first Order in Council-the Order in Council which was passed in June, 1901-we had given to the company the abandoned claims. That seemed to me perfectly fair. If a miner had abandoned his claims, it was perfectly fair to give the company the right to enter into that claim and work it, but when a delegation came from the Yukon a year ago last winter, they represented that, though perfectly fair, it might work great injustice. To-day a claim may be abandoned because there is not sufficient water to work it. But, as soon as this work has been done, as soon as it is possible for the miners to use the water, which it is contemplated they will receive if this agreement comes into force, the claims which are valueless now will become valuable. This was such a good reason that we determined to give this privilege. The privilege is given to the company of taking and working abandoned claims, subject to the payment of no fees except the royalty on the output, and for this purpose to enter upon Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks, such right to be exercised only when the grantees by the construction of works in pursuance of this franchise are in the position to deliver water upon such claim or claims for the working thereof. That is all. So long as the work is not completed, they 'cannot take 91J
possession of any claim. But when the works are completed, when they can supply water to all the miners, if any of the miners then abandon their claims, surely there is nothing wrong in the company taking the abandoned claim and trying to work it for their own benefit. So far, it seems to me that no misconception can exist in relation to this matter.
That is the Order in Council we have passed-I have gone over the salient points, and I think we have satisfactorily answered all the objections raised. I am aware that the miners in the Yukon still are not satisfied ; I am aware that they have passed resolutions against it; I have received resolutions, as for instance from the Liberal Association, on this subject. I do not know if that resolution has been quoted by my hon. friends on the other side. They have quoted so many this afternoon, that, while I have endeavoured to follow them all closely, this one may have escaped me. Still, if it has been quoted before it will bear repetition. This is a petition sent to me personally :
The petition ol the Liberal Association of Dawson of the Yukon Territory humbly showeth :-
1.	That this supply of water and power to the miners on the creeks is one of the most serious questions affecting the Yukon Territory.
2.	That in the opinion of your petitioners the provision of a water system whereby the miners may be furnished with water on fair and reasonable terms can best be dealt with by the government itself and should not be allowed to fall under the control of private individuals.
That the development of the resources of the Yukon has been seriously impeded by the appropriation of extensive areas of rich placer ground by hydraulic concessions believed in some instances to have been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation :
Your petitioners therefor pray :
That the Order in Council of April 21, 1902, granting certain rights and privileges to Malcolm Orr-Ewing, A. N. C. Treadgold, and Walter Barwick may be rescinded absolutely, that the government institute forthwith a careful investigation by competent engineers and obtain reports on the subject with a view to undertaking the construction of a public water supply as a national enterprise.
Well, Sir, notwithstanding the respect which a man has always for his own friends, and notwithstanding the high opinion I entertain of the petitioners who are my own political friends, I cannot but feel that they have put the cart before the horse. They say in effect:	First cancel the concession
and then hold an investigation. I think it would have been more logical to ask us first to have an investigation and then, if need be, cancel the Treadgold concession. And that is just what we intended to do. After the investigation we shall know whether the Treadgold concession should be cancelled or not. But, Sir. let us note the consequence. My friends of the Liberal Association ask us, if we cancel the Treadgold concession, to establish a national work to give them

the water they want. I have only to say this in answer to the observations made by my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Porter). He asks, speaking of the Order in Council : Why have you refused to make this law; why have you not proclaimed it; why have you not gazetted it ? For the simple and obvious reason that we have received objections and remonstrances against it. We have amended it again and again so as to make it acceptable to the miners of the Yukon. Still, though we have amended it, in my opinion, in a way that should make it acceptable, still we have remonstrances from the board of trade and political associations asking us not to carry it further, but to cancel it. Before we proclaim it, before we place it beyond the possibility of being abolished, it is only fair and reasonable that we should investigate all the matters connected with it to see what should be done in the future. I am giving the reasons, why I think, we were justified in making this Order in Council, at all events, why the motion that is presented by my hon. friend should not be accepted by this House.
Ii. BORDEN (Halifax). Did I correctly understand the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to give the opinion that these Orders in Council came into force only when they were gazetted ?
So far as that is concerned, the others were cancelled.

That is a remarkable answer. I ask my right hon. friend the question whether he expressed the opinion that these orders came into force only after they are gazetted. And he says they are cancelled. What was the use of cancelling them if they never came into force ? Will the right hon. gentleman tell me that ? It seems to me remarkable that the right hon. gentleman, who has studied this question for two or three years, can give no other answer to what seems to me a fair and courteous question than that which he lias just given. I venture to say that the Order in Council of June, 1901, was acted upon over and over again, though it was not gazetted. I asked my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) whether it was gazetted, and I have a memorandum from him stating that it was not. Yet any one who has perused the file of correspondence knows that that Order in Council was regarded as valid and was acted upon. Yet he stands here and ventures to tell this House, and through this House the country, that an Order In Council is not valid until it is gazetted. I do not think he had better chide us on this side for not knowing what we are talking about when be places himself in a position of that kind.
My right hon. friend has told us something about this petition of his Liberal friends in the Yukon, and has taken iUjout as logical a position with regard to Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
that as with regard to the gazetting of these Orders in Council. He says that bis Liberal friends 'in the Y'ukon have asked too much when they demand that this shall be made a national work. It is a pity that he was not always as careful about the requests made to him by his Liberal friends in different parts of Canada. He seemed very sensitive about this request. But is it necessary because his friends in the Yukon ask him to do something unreasonable that he should turn a deaf ear to a portion of this petition-
The development of the resources of the Yukon has been seriously impeded by the appropriation of extensive areas of rich placer ground by hydraulic concessions believed in some instances to have been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation.
Because they ask him to make this a national work, is it necessary that he should turn a deaf ear to the statement of his own political friends-a statement which is qor-robated by the city council and the board of trade of the Yukon-that these concessions have been obtained by fraud aud misrepresentation. My hon. friend the Postmaster General tells ns that the government have been deliberating a long time about holding an investigation into this matter. Since when have the government been intending to bold an investigation ? And bow does it happen, if they have been intending to bold an investigation into these matters, that, up to the present time, no investigation whatever was spoken of in the House until this matter was brought up on this side ? Has my right hon. friend any explanation of that, because if he has, I will sit down and give him a chance to make it to the House. Apparently my right hon. friend has none. Then further than that, I would invite his attention to this clause of that same petition by bis Liberal friends :
That an inquiry may be set on foot to ascertain the circumstances under which the leading hydraulic concessions were obtained, in order that action may he taken by the Attorney General of Canada in the premises.
What are the premises ? The premises are that these mining concessions were obtained by fraud and misrepresentation, and my right bon. friend who is responsible more than any other Minister of the Crown for the government of Canada, has not up to tlie present time seen fit to instruct his Attorney General to take the proceedings demanded by his Liberal friends in the Yukon. What further is there ?
That the Attorney General of Canada do issue a flat, authorizing proceedings to be taken in his name in every case where action is begun against an hydraulic concession in which fraud or misrepresentation is charged, including all such actions as are now pending.
So I think, even if my right hon. friend comes to the conclusion that it is not expedient in the public interest to begin these works as public works, he finds ample food

for thought, for consideration, and what is more, for action, in the suggestions which have been made to him by his own political friends in the Yukon, who are familiar with these matters as no member of this House can be familiar with them. Has my right lion, friend the slightest idea as to what these gentlemen mean when they refer to fraud and misrepresentation by which these concessions have been obtained ? Has he heard anything during the past year ? Has anything been communicated to him ? Have any documents been shown to him ? Has he understood anything on this subject which he has not communicated to the House tonight ? Can he enlighten us as to what his Liberal friends in the Yukon mean when they say deliberately that these concessions have been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation ? Perhaps some information on those points would not have been out of place when my right lion, friend proceeded to enlighten this House to-night with regard to this Treadgold concession.
Great deliberation was exercised in making this concession, says my right lion, friend, and says the Postmaster General, a deliberation of such extreme value that the sum of $1 per miners' inch was placed as the price to be paid by the miners of tills country to those gentlemen who were being urged to accept this concession, a price which, within six mouths afterwards, was reduced by the government to twenty-live cents, and that reduction, I believe, was made with the consent of the concessionaires themselves. Yet my right hon. friend, and the Minister of Railways and Canals who enlarged upon the work performed by a sub-committee of the Privy Council, and the presence of a certain gentleman on it who now occupies a seat on the judicial bench, these gentlemen tell us what a marvellous amount of deliberation was bestowed by the government on these matters. Was there any difficulty in finding out what would be a fair price for the miners' inch ? How long does it take to communicate with the Yukon? Is there not a telegraph line which this government has erected, and which communicates with other telegraph lines in this country ? Could not my right hon. friend have got an answer back the next day ? How long does it take a letter to go ? What was the need of the extreme haste with regard to this matter which led the government to fix a price to be paid by the miners of that country for water to be supplied by these concessionaires, which their own action, six months afterwards, proved to be absolutely ridiculous and absurd? Yet my right hon. friend gets up and informs the House and the country, indeed two ministers of the Crown get up and inform the House and the country of the wonderful amount of time that was spent in deliberating upon the terms of this concession, and of the remarkable value of the services which they rendered to the country in giving their time
and attention to this subject, and in framing a regulation which gave to the miners of the Yukon the privilege of paying one dollar per miner's inch for the use of water.
Now there are one or two observations made, both by the Minister of Railways and Canals and by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, which I am bound to say I did not expect to hear from either one of these gentlemen; because they both have reputations as lawyers in this country, and I hardly expected that either one of them would have adopted the argument in this House with regard to the meaning of this word ' compensation ' which has been put forward by both of them. My right hon. friend has carefully assured the House that there is a provision in this Order in Council by which the price which the miners are to pay for water to be furnished to them is to be controlled by some tribunal, that is to say, by the Gold Commissioner, subject to appeal to the Territorial Court of the district, i >id my right hon. friend, did the Minister of Railways and Canals, read the first Order in Council ? Did either one of them take the trouble to read that, and did they see at the end of it the subsection (f) in the regulations, which provides that the charge which the grantee should be entitled to make for the use of such water on such claim should not exceed one dollar per miners' inch per hour ? Those regulations are precisely the regulations which are also contained in the second Order in Council, and which are relied upon by my right hon. friend and by the Minister of Railways and Canals as determining the price to be paid. Will my right hon. friend say that these words fulfil any office in the second Order in Council ? which they do not fulfil in the first Order in Council ? Will the Minister of Railways and Canals say that ? Well, I think not. Here is the language of the first Order in Council :
(b.) The grantees shall compensate the owner of any mining claim or lands for any damage which any such owner may sustain by reason of any of the grantees' works breaking or being imperfect.
(c.) Any question of compensation arising under this grant shall be determined judicially by the Gold Commissioner, subject to appeal to the Territorial Court of the district, and the said court may upon special circumstances being shown, make an order for the taking of further evidence.
(f.) The charge which the grantees shall be entitled to make for the use of such water on each claim shall not exceed one dollar per miners' inch per hour.
Now, my right hon. friend bases his argument on the contention that provisions in (b) and (c) which I have read to the House, are contained in the second Order in Council and provide ample security to the miner that he should not be overcharged. Why, if these hon. gentlemen had not stood up in this House and made such an argument to-night, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, I would

not have believed that they would have attempted to make such an argument. Are not the same provisions contained in the first Order in Council which definitely fixes the charge ? Further than that, if anything were necessary to be added, let my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways look at the top of page two of the second Order in Council and see what is there contained :
Provided that if any power is developed and rendered available by the grantees under this section which they do not make use of, then the same shall be offered for sale to the public, and the rates to be charged therefor shall be subject to the control of the Governor General in Council.
What was the need of such a regulation as that if the provisions contained in the regulation quoted by my right hon. friend were quite sufficient for the purpose ? Why,
. Mr. Speaker, any one wlio looks at this Order in Council, who looks down the first, second and third pages, will see everywhere that these concessionaires for the purposes of their undertaking have the right of entering upon and using private lands, and every one knows that rights of that kind are not usually granted without provision for compensation. Therefore, it would be an absurd thing to expect that in an Order in Council of that kind you should not find, either in the Order in Council itself or in some regulation attached to it, a provision that acts, done in derogation of those private rights should be compensated for by the individuals who have committed those acts. It is the most reasonable and the most natural thing in the world; and yet my right hon. friend and the Minister of Railways and Canals seek to torture those words, and to make the people of the Yukon believe that there is some guarantee and some safeguard to the miners in the words which are contained in the first Order in Council as well as in the second.
Now, this matter has been gone over very fully by lion, gentlemen who have addressed the House and I was pleased with the frankness with which the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) admitted beyond all question that this concession is a monopoly. He says it is a monopoly, and he says you must have a monopoly there because you cannot develop a country without creating a monopoly, and he says further that the miners of the Yukon do not know what is good for them. They do not understand their own true interests, that a monopoly of this kind is necessary in the interests of the miners of the Yukon Territory and with considerable force and with all the vigour and all the energy that are so characteristic of the hon. Minister of Railway and Canals he insists that the miners of the Yukon reallv need this monopoly although they are protesting loudly to this parliament and to the whole country that their interests are being absolutelv destroyed by these regulations.
They have said that they needed it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: They have said that they needed it ?
Yes, but they want the government to furnish it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That they' needed this concession ?

They said that they needed this water.
Mr. BORDEN Halifax). That they needed water ? They have water in the Klondike river and there is one mine owner in that district who raises 1,500 gallons of water per minute for Ihis own use to a height of 300 feet at a cost of less than 25 cents per inch. I will give the exact figures in regard to it. There is one man who has done for his own property and at much less expense a considerable portion of what is proposed to be done by these concessionaires under this second Order in Council. I brought this matter to the attention of the House last year, I have a memorandum under my hand and if I thought it necessary to stop for the purpose I could give it to the House again.
I would like to ask my right hon. friend the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) where are the details of these different schemes that were proposed to the government. In the Order in Council that was passed in June, 1901, we had a very pretty recital in these words :
Whereas, the details of different schemes submitted have been considered and discussed.
I do not see the details of any of the different schemes brought down for the information of the House, and if, as the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals stated, different persons came and proposed different schemes to the government it seems a singular thing that the House should be deprived at this late date of the inestimable privilege of reading them and of considering what these different schemes really were.
Now, my hon. friend the member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) made some reference in the course of his remarks to the hon. member who represents the Yukon (Mr. Ross), a very able, and I believe, a very estimable gentleman, although I do not know him sufficiently well to understand whether or not he is worthy of all the encomiums which have been bestowed upon him in the government organ in the Yukon, or whether he can be called a 'lightning striker ' on all occasions. Whether he can be called a lightning striker on most occasions, I do not know, but certainly in so far as this Treadgold concession is concerned, he cannot be considered a lightning striker because this parliament has
MAY 12, 1903 i
been in session for eiglit weeks, and although that hon. gentleman was elected on a platform which pledged him to secure the repeal of this concession, he has not been able to attempt anything in regard to it.
I was greatly amused indeed to hear the hon. Postmaster General boasting of the return of the hon. gentleman who at present is the representative of the Yukon Territory. I was particularly amused at that because the very platform on which that hon. gentleman was elected to this House was a platform which denounced the action of this government in regard to its administration of the Yukon Territory. Although the election of the hon. gentleman was heralded through the press of this country as a victory for the government, and as a certificate of good character for this government in regard to the Yukon Territory, it was a certificate of exactly the opposite nature because the hon. gentleman who now fills the position of representative of the Yukon would have been snowed under by 1,500 of a majority had he not pledged himself upon the public platform and through his duly authorized agents in that territory to do all he could upon coming to this parliament to remedy the evils caused by this government and particularly in regard to the concessions that have been spoken of. There is no doubt of that because the present Gold Commissioner of the Yukon, when certain eastern newspapers had reached Dawson and when lie had read that these newspapers proclaimed that this was a Liberal victory, took occasion to write to a newspaper in the Yukon Territory to say that it was nothing of the kind and that the truth was that Liberals and Conservatives had joined together in support of that hon. gentleman who now represents the Yukon because he had pledged himself to undo the wrongs which had been done by this government and because they thought him more capable of obtaining a remedy for these wrongs than the gentleman who was his opponent on that occasion. Let the Postmaster General not descend to any pettiness of that kind because his own Gold Commissioner, appointed by him only a few weeks ago, has taken occasion to rebuke utterances of that kind and the language which he used then in rebuking these eastern newspapers is just as much a rebuke to the hon. Postmaster General for the language which he had used to-day. Now, the hon. Postmaster General talked in the style that has been heard sometimes in this House about irresponsible individuals who are making charges. When he was asked by my hon. friend from Cornwall to whom he referred by irresponsible individuals, the hon. Postmaster General was somewhat at a loss to answer, and eventually, on being asked if he made the assertion that the board of trade of Dawson was irresponsible he took back
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I never made that assertion.

Well, who was it that the hon. gentleman referred to as being irresponsible ? Has the hon. gentleman, after cogitating over that matter for an hour, discovered who is irresponsible ? I want the House to understand that he did not refer to one .irresponsible individual but to irresponsible individuals. It is not the board of trade, it is not the city council, it is not his Liberal friends, it is not the members of the Liberal Association, it is not the editor of the government organ. We are reduced to the editor of the independent journal in the Yukon, who apparently is the only person to whom the hon. gentleman refers when he mentions irresponsible individuals. I will give the hon. minister some responsible individuals and I will give him some of their utterances, because my hon. friends who have been addressing the House to-night, have forgotten a very excellent presentment of this case which is to be found in a report of a committee appointed at a mass meeting of Yukon citizens, and I will tell him when I get through who it was who signed this report and I will ask the hon. gentleman whether he regards this individual as being irresponsible :
The undersigned -who were appointed by the general committee nominated at the mass meeting held at Dawson on the evening ot Monday, the seventeenth of February instant, as a sub-committee to collect information and make a report in regard to the objectionable features of the Treadgold concession, beg to report as follows

The hon. Postmaster General and the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals will observe that this committee took credit to themselves for doing what the government did. They collected information about this concession. They took apparently as much trouble in regard to it as the government might have taken considering the figure which the government directed the miners to pay for the water furnished them by the concessionaires. Then this is the result of their deliberations:
It is easy to understand how intelligent gentlemen at the capital should be misled both as to the value of the water supply contemplated by the Treadgold concession, as to the size of the capital proposed to be invested by him and as to the value of the concessions made to him, but in the opinion of your committee no one in possession of the information which your committee has been able to obtain, by search^ at the gold commissioner's office, by numerous interviews with miners, engineers, and other men practically acquainted with the conditions of this territory, and from every source available, can doubt that the supply of water contemplated by the scheme of the applicants for the concession is a mere stalking horse under cover of which he may obtain absolute possession of enormous mining tracts practically embracing the richest known mining district in the territory.

Perhaps, in order to secure the attention of the Postmaster General to this, I may tell him that this report is signed by a very important friend of his. It continues :
It seems to your committee that while from a logical or scientific point of view the instruments containing the Treadgold concession are of a most imperfect and inartistic kind.
Notwithstanding, you will observe the great work of preparation which the government put upon it.
They are, from the point of view of Mr. Treadgold and his associates, framed with clever adroitness.
Does not my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Blair) think that, after all, Mr. Treadgold put more work upon it than did the government ?
Hear, hear.

It continues :
They are complex, involved and obscure, and as a consequence difficult to readily understand, and appear to have been purposely framed in that way to deceive into the belief that the Treadgold people were conferring an enormous benefit on the country and were receiving small return, whereas they are in effect giving little or nothing and receiving vast benefits.
What a different view they seem to take of the situation from that which my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals presented with so much ardour to the House to-night. He wanted something attractive for capitalists. He told us you could not get capitalists to come forward unless you had something attractive, so the government were bound to make this attractive-and I don't know whether the capitalists made it attractive also or not.
Hear, hear.

The report continues :
Your committee has special reports made by individual members of the committee on the various features of the concession, which reports have been submitted to the committee and approved by it and are herewith attached and returned to the general committee for its information.
To summarize the many opinions and views adverse to the concession is most difficult, but your committee desires to lay special stress on the following particulars :-
(1.) That the concession instruments ignore to a very large extent and override the rights and vested interests already created by private enterprises and private capital.
(2.) That Treadgold makes no adequate covenants to insure fair and reasonable supply of water to miners who may require it.
(3.) That the maximum of price is too high and that his powers of impounding water and obtaining abandoned claims and his exclusive, sole and prior right with regard to water, afford him a most potent lever to compel payment of his exorbitant rates of abandonment of property.
(4.) That the closing to the prospector and the miner of large tracts of country, the ignoring of private rights, the exclusive rights and the other special privileges granted to the con-

cession, will create a state of uncertainty in the most important section of the community that will be most injurious to the interests of the territory and will tend both to deprive the government of revenue and the business community of the territory of a large branch of trade.
(5.) That the expropriation clauses are not framed with due regard to the rights of individual owners and have no adequate provisions for indemnification.
I may say, of course, I should perhaps have explained before reading this : that it is directed to the Order in Council as at first framed, and whatever benefit my hon. friends on the other side can get from any differences between the first Order in Council and this Order in Council, they, of course, go to mitigate any criticism in the document I am reading. But I entirely agree with the hon. gentlemen who have addressed the House to-night, and who have said that so far as the interests of this country are concerned, and so far as the protection of the Yukon miners is concerned, there is very little difference indeed between the concessions granted under the first Order in Council and that granted by the Order in Council of last year.

Hear, hear.
Mr.' BORDEN (Halifax). This report continues :
In conclusion your committee very greatly fear that if the concession is allowed to stand in its present form and without most radical amendments and alterations that a monopoly will be created that will practically comminate the richest part of the Yukon Territory. In the opinion of your committee the best scheme for supplying water for mining purposes would be one initiated, operated and controlled by the government, but above all it is undesirable that a monopolist of the water supply should at the same time be a competitor in mining operations with miners dependent upon him for their water supply.
Hear, hear.

And it is one of the most powerful criticisms that has ever been made against this concession granted to Treadgold and his associates : that not only do you put these gentlemen in practical control of the water supply of the Yukon, but you also put them in actual and every day competition with the very men to whom they are to supply that water.
Hear, hear.
Who signs that report ?
Hear, hear.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit to my right hon. friend that one of two propositions is true : Either there is something in these matters that have been so alleged, which the government should have investigated long ago, or else Mr. Fred. T. Congdon is not fit to be Commissioner of the Yukon.
Governor of the Yukon.

Governor of the Yukon, or commissioner, or whatever his official title is ; he has put his name as chairman of that committee to a document which contains as grave an indictment of this concession as anything which has been said on this side of the House to-night-as grave an indictment of this concession, I repent, as anything which has been said by any gentleman on this side of the House tonight.
Hear, hear.

And yet, without such investigation as is demanded here ; without the government making any such amendment in that Order in Council as removes the objectionable features complained of. that gentleman takes the position of commissioner to the Yukon, and I believe he has lately said to the people of that country :	that this question of the Treadgold
concession is one to be dealt with by the government and the parliament here at Ottawa. And, Sir, we are now trying to get this government in this parliament to deal with it, and we are proposing a resolution here to-night which does not go one whit further in condemnation of this Treadgold concession than the voice of not only the business men of the Yukon, not only the civic government of the Yukon, but even of those gentlemen in the Yukon who are the best friends and supporters of the government that stands at the head of affa'irs in Canada to-day. And yet my right hon. friend thinks apparently that there is nothing in this complaint which demands any attention at the hands of this House, or which requires this House to hasten the action of the government by some such resolution as that which has been proposed by my hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain). I shall not go into the argument of the legal question. I have heard no answer to the argument which has been put forward by my hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) and by my hon. friend from Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) and the other hon. gentlemen who have addressed the House to-night.
Until there is some answer given to it other than'that which I have heard, X do not think it is worth while for me to take up the time of the House in attempting to discuss that question. In conclusion, it seems to me, not only from the legal standpoint, but, what is even of more importance from the standpoint of public policy in regard to these concessions, that the resolution which has been proposed to the House by my hon. friend from Montmorency is one that ought to command the support of this House and that ought to be assented to by this government; and this Treadgold concession, which has created so much scandal in that western country, should once and for all be done away with. If the government decides to deal with this matter, let it deal with it by open competition among people throughout the country who are willing to undertake a work of this kind. Let it deal with it in such a way that there shall be competition after the waterworks shall be once established. Let it deal with it in such a way at least that the government shall have complete and ample supervision over their operations after it lias once established them in that country.

Mr. Speaker, with all tha skill and all the ingenuity which is born of long experience in the disputes of the courts, my hon. friend who proposed this motion, and those who spoke previous to the leader of the opposition laboured strenuously to establish two things : First, that this concession was issued illegally and improvidently, and second, that the miners do not approve of it. I said that my hon. friends laboured strenuously to establish these two propositions, and I am forced to admit, in view of the heat displayed by the hon. leader of the opposition, that he must be thoroughly' convinced that they did not labour successfully.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Okas. Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: Oh, oh.

He found it necessary to add another count to the indictment which is brought against this concession, and he added, not by direct statement, but by inference, by suggestion, the charge of fraud. Now, my answer to that is that if the hon. leader of the opposition was in earnest, if he really meant what he [DOT] said when he stated that this concession was tainted with fraud, it was his clear duty to say so in the motion he submitted for the consideration of this House.
Is my hon. friend referring to me ?
I aui referring to the leader of the opposition.

I was not quite sure. In the remarks I made I read merely a quotation from the Liberal club in the Yukon, and I said that statements made by gentlemen of the standing which I attributed to those gentlemen deserved consideration at the hands of this government.

My hon. friend rested his case largely on that; but I said a moment ago that he proceeded further, and made the charge, not openly, but by means of an insinuation. I repeat the statement now, and I immediately proceed to prove it. My hon. friend said, in discussing this matter, that the lion. Minister of Railways suggested that this concession had to 'be made attractive to capitalists, and he added that the capitalists had made it attractive to other people. Tell me what that means if it is mot an insinuation of fraud. Now, I say that if the hon. leader of the opposition intended to charge fraud, his clear duty was not to proceed by insinuation, but to make a direct charge.
The charge had already been made by the hon. gentleman's friends.

No friend of mine, or no man would continue to be a friend of mine, who would make a charge of that description, not being prepared to prove it. Now, my hon. friend did not go over the ground covered by my hon. friends who preceded him, and I think that I have substantially answered the greater part of his speech. I would like mow merely to refer to what he said with respect to the Commissioner of the Yukon, Mr. Congdon, and I would like to draw the attention of the House to this fact, that the memorandum prepared by the present Commissioner of the Yrukon Territory had reference to the first Order in Council, that that memorandum asked for amendments to that Order in Council, and that these amendments having been made, and that that gentleman having accepted the responsibility of taking the position of Commissioner of the Yukon, declared thereby that he was content with those amendments; and, so far as those amendments go, the answer to the memorandum to which my hon. friend alluded is complete. I shall endeavour now to deal with some things that fell from my hon. friends who preceded the hon. leader "of the opposition. They tried to make good the last charge to which I have referred, that is to say, that the miners of the Yukon do not approve of this concession, by referring to newspaper articles and to resolutions passed at miners' meetings. With those who are not familiar with the strong, vigorous and picturesque language which characterizes those Who frequent mining camps, those resolutions and articles must have

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
some effect; but I for my part take the responsibility of saying that while those resolutions and articles may express the first opinions formed of these concessions by the miners of the Yukon, their sober, second thought is represented by the evidence they gave on the 2nd of December last, when they returned the government candidate with a majority of 891. This not only shows how, on sober, second thought, they considered this matter, but it also shows that they are satisfied that this government will lend not merely a patient and willing, but an anxious ear to any representations they have to make, and that as the first Order in Council was amended to suit their requirements, if in the second objections are to be found, these objections wall be met in the same spirit in which the first objections were met at the time the second Order in Council was passed. I am satisfied that the miners of the Yukon have confidence that this government will deal with them fairly and equitably, and that when it can be established that there is any real grievance existing in any part of this Dominion, no matter how remote it may be, that grievance shall be remedied by this government when it is made known.
I am going to deal with the second Order in Council. I do not intend to discuss the first, because, having been repealed, it is absolutely out of the way. But so far as I have been able to follow the argument of my hon. friends on the other side of the House, their argument is that that second Order in Council was unconstitutional, was illegal, that it was not within the power of the government to pass it. In giving my answer to that, I want to say that I give my firm deliberate opinion, because I have had occasion to discuss this question very recently in the Supreme Court in connection with tiie question of royalty in the Yukon, when this whole question of Orders in Council with respect to mining in the Yukon was before the court. For the benefit of my hon. friends. I will tell them that they can find the wihole report of the case in the current number of the Supreme Court reports, Volume 32, number 4. The cases begin at page 586.
Are these the cases in which leave to appeal has been applied for ?

Yes.
Mi\ CASGRAIN. And granted ?

Yes.
Leave to appeal was applied for and granted on both sides. The Crown appealed on one question, and the miners on the other. We may as well state the facts clearly while we are at it. What is my reason for coming to the conclusion that it was within the powers of the government to make this Order in Council ? Section forty-seven of the Dominion Land Act, as amended, pro-

vitles that the Governor In Council may make regulations to provide for the sale or lease or other disposal of mining property in the North-west Territories.
The North-west Territories of course include the Yukon. Then it is provided that the Governor in Council shall have the power by regulation to determine the conditions under which this property shall be disposed of. Acting on the power conferred by this section, mining regulations were made, as far back as 18S9, authorizing a subordinate official in the Yukon to dispose of the mines there. But if the Governor in Council has the power to determine by regulation the conditions under which this property shall pass out of the hands of the Dominion government, surely he has the right to do that himself. Surely what the Governor General in Council can do by deputy, he can do by himself. That is my opinion, and I think, without boasting, that it may have some value. If the Governor General in Council can by regulation authorize a subordinate official to sell, surely he can as effectively sell, by virtue of a deed passed by the Council itself. That is at all events my opinion and I give it for what it is worth, and perhaps my hon. friends may in time come to the conclusion that it is worth something. The development district depends very largely upon the creation of hydraulic power. So long as you have rich mining deposits it is easy to take the gold from the bosom of the earth by the ordinary means which the individual miner controls. But when you have exhausted the richer deposits and have to deal with what is called a poor pay streak, then in order to work that successfully, you must have hydraulic power. Therefore, the only question is, whether or not, in the first instance, it was right for the government to authorize the development of that power by a private company, or whether it would have been proper for the government itself to develop it. Whether right or wrong, the conclusion come to by the government was that it was better to give the development of that power to a private corporation-that it was more in the interests of the country that the work should be done by a private company than by the government. The question for the House to consider is whether the granting of that power to a private corporation was surrounded by such conditions as would moke the grant as advantageous to the public as possible and as little onerous to the miners. What are the terms of the grant ? I am now dealing with the only Order in Council which is in existence. That Order in Council gives to Mr. Treadgold and his associates two things. First, the right to divert the Klondike river for the purpose of generating power. They have first the right to divert and take water from the Klondike river in order to develop
power, which power is to be used for mining purposes, but what my hon. friends were careful to overlook is that the right thus given is made subject to the right, which is vested in every miner, of himself taking first from the river sufficient water for the working of his claim, but not to exceed 3,500 miners' inches. The miner has the first right to take that amount of water from the Klondike, and it is only after he has exercised that right that Mr. Treadgold and associates are entitled to take any water whatever for the purpose of generating power. What is the meaning of that right to take 3,500 miners' inches ? Let us take the definition of a miners' inch given by my hon. friend from Montmorency. He says it is equal to a volume of water twelve feet square, so that if you multiply 3,500 by twelve feet square, you will see that volume of water which each miner is entitled to take per minute. In addition to the right to take from the river the water necessary to develop power, the company have the right to distribute water in the district Let me quote the words of the concession so that you may understand the extent to which this right to divert the water goes. Subsection two provides that the company shall have :
The prior right-subject to the provisions contained in clause one-to divert and take water from the Klondike river for distribution and use in the district up to 5,000 miners' inches.
That is the right they have got, and I should be curious for somebody to make me understand exactly what that means- the right to divert and to take up 5.000 miners' inches. After they have taken that, is their right exhausted ?
Out of that 5,000 how much is already disposed of to the miners ?

The miner gets his 3,500 miners' inches first before everybod else. Under section ten, the company have an additional right, subject to no payment except the royalty prescribed upon output, to make an entry for and work any abandoned mining claim or claims on Bonanza, Bear and Hunker creeks, such right to be exercisable only when the grantees, by the construction of works in pursuance of this purchase, are in a position to deliver water upon such claim or claims for the working thereof. What does that section mean ? It means that after the hydraulic works have been built and are in operation and the grantees are prepared to divert the water necessary to enable any man to take up an abandoned claim and work it. then, if no one else will take it up. they can do so. After the company have developed the power and taken the water and are ready to distribute it, then only, and not until then, have they the right to take up any abandoned claim. Any one else can take it in the interval.

My hon. friends have objected that tliey have the right to take up the abandoned claims without being subjected to the preliminary formality or obligation imposed upon the other miners, that is, of paying the entry fee and representation fee. What does the representation fee mean ? The word indicates its meaning. Any man may go on property and work it, but, in order that he may maintain his title to it, it is necessary for him to expend at least $200 to develop that property every year, because a mining location is granted for a year. But, if a man goes away from the country-say, for instance, water is scarce and the facilities are not such as to enable him to work his property successfully-he is represented by the $200 in lieu of the work to be done on the property. That is what is meant by ' representation.' What is the reason for this fee ? It is to provide that the properties may not lie fallow, not remain undeveloped. But, if you have such conditions as that in connection with this enterprise, to carry out which, I am told, it will be necessary to spend perhaps four or five millions of dollars to develop power-I know nothing about the facts, but I am told this is the case-and if they develop the power, and take an abandoned claim and seek to develop it, what is the use of a representation fee from them 1 Are they not represented by the works they have done and by the utilizing of the power that they have created ? It seems to me that the reason of the exception in tlieir favour in that respect is absolutely elementary. Now, my hon. friend was very severe and very sarcastic when he spoke of the legal members of the government who had occasion to give a legal construction to this concession. He was good enough to say that no first year's student-if I understood him-would venture to take the responsibility for the opinion expressed by, for instance, a gentleman with such a reputation at the bar as that of the hon. Minister of Railways-leaving out the other two. I am afraid he is going to have another legal student, because I hold, and I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the House, that the construction put upon the concession by the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is arguable, and not only that it is arguable, but that it is the only construction that can be put upon the document if you are going to give effect to all its parts. Take, first, section 2 :
The prior right to divert and take water from the Klondike river for distribution and use in the district up to five thousand miners' inches.
Then, section 9 :
The right, subject to the regulations hereinafter contained, to use, distribute and dispose of by sale or otherwise the water delivered by the grantees within the district.
Section 2 is to be read in connection with section 9. The right to distribute the water and dispose of it by sale is vested in the Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
concessionaires, subject to the regulations hereinafter contained. What are those regulations ? They are to be found on page 4. And one of them is that any question of compensation arising under the grant shall be determined judicially by the Gold Commissioner. I do not mean to say that that is drawn as artistically as it might be by a first-class lawyer. There may be better draughtsmen than the gentleman who drew this. But I say that it is susceptible of the construction put upon it, and if effect is to be given to it, this is the only construction. Then take section 10 :
The right, subject to no payment except the royalties prescribed upon output to make entry for and work any abandoned mining claim or claims on Bonanza. Bear and Hunker creeks, such rights to be exercised only when the grantees by the construction of works in pursuance of this franchise are in a position to deliver water upon such claim or claims for the working thereof.
There is a provision again that they shall deliver the water on the claims for the working of the claims. How is the compensation to be settled ? By private bargain, or in the manner fixed by subsection c, of the regulations. There is no other way under the Order in Council to determine the question and make an authoritative decision. That is the only construction you ban put upon it.
Would my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) put the same construction on the first Order in Council V
I am not looking at the first Order in Council at all. That has passed out of the realm of discussion. I am not going to argue on a thing that is not in force.
I do not think my hon. friend would argue that.

My hon. friend draws my attention to the fact that one of the grievances alleged by the miners of the Yukon country is that the hydraulic company would enter into competition with the miners. What is the hydraulic power for ? They develop the power and they take the abandoned claims-the claims that nobody else wants-and develop them. So far as the miner is concerned, he is entitled to his own property and he is working his own property. The company do not compete with them. It is not because the hydraulic miner is in the neighbourhood dealing with another property that he competes with the ordinary miner. I do not see how there could be competition. That is the way in which this Order in Council appeals to me. The people of the Yukon country require the water for the development of their property. And not only that, but it seems to me it would be a matter of oversight on the part of the government if, with the knowledge we have of the properties in that country, we were not prepared to encour-

age any one wlio was willing to go in and develop hydraulic power. Any man who will go in there and invest four or five million dollars to develop hydraulic power deserves to be encouraged. He is going into a patriotic work to enable us to develop the country, which, without that would develop very slowly and would never come to its full state of development. So long as the powers given to the company are surrounded by such safeguards as will enable them to operate for their own profit and advantage, but not to the detriment of the people of that country, there is no blame attachable to the government. What, in fact, is the concession ? It is a grant to the hydraulic company the right to take from the Klondike river a certain quantity of water to generate power. And that right can only be exercised after the miners have been satisfied to the extent of having 3,500 miners' inches. After they have received that quantity of water the balance may be taken for the purpose of generating power. It seems to me the point towards which my hon. friends opposite should have directed their attention, was to show that when we granted to the free miner that quantity of water, 3,500 inches, we granted them a quantity insufficient for their works. Not a single word has been said on that point. From the representations that come from the Yukon, and, so far as my knowledge goes, having listened attentively to all that has been read, it seems to me that there is a complete misapprehension on the part of those who have made representations with regard to the nature of this concession.
It seems to me that the miners of the 'Yukon should have shown that when we gave them that quantity of water we did 'not give them what was necessary to satisfy their demand. If we gave them water necessary to satisfy their demand, and if in addition we supplied them with this power, it seems to me they ought to be thankful to the government for what we have done. We give them what they wanted, and we give them the additional advantage they have now. It seems to me that is something to the credit of the government. The grantees 'have the right, it is true, to take water from the Klondike river and distribute it in the district. You understand there is a difference between taking water from the Klondike river for the purpose of generating power, and taking water for the purpose of distributing it. They have got that latter power also, but no representation has been made, no statement has been made that either of these rights vested in tlie Tread-gold Company operate detrimentally to the miners. No statement has been made that the miner is not entirely satisfied with the right which he has to take his quantity of water in preference to all the others. In addition to that, they have the right to enter upon an abandoned claim and to work it. Now what does that mean ? It means
that after they have developed this concession a year-and they have already had it for a year without spending any money upon it-after they are in a position to deliver water on these claims, if any one else wants the claims they are entitled to have them. That is all they have a right to with respect to these abandoned claims, and there is nothing more in it. Looking at it in that aspect, there is nothing in this that we cannot justify, nothing which we cannot all stand up for, nothing in it which does not show foresight, and careful consideration. But if there is anything wrong in it, as the Prime Minister said when he addressed the House, as the Postmaster General said when he addressed the House, we are prepared to listen, as we were originally, to any grievance that may be made known to us and we are prepared to remedy it.
Mx-. SAMUEL BARKER (Hamilton). I think most gentlemen in this House must have been surprised to hear the Minister of Justice argue gravely that the sober second thought of the people of the Yukon was in favour of this Order in Council because they elected tlie Hon. Mr. Ross to represent them in this House. Surely the hon. gentleman, in saying that, must presume a good deal upon the forgetfulness of the members of this House. After it has been proved that the Hon. Mr. Ross was elected on the distinct platform that he would see to getting this Order in Council cancelled, to assert that the sober second thought of the people of the Yukon was in favour of the Order in Council is most extraordinary on the part of the Minister of Justice. 1 understood tlie Minister of Justice to say further -that the present governor of the Yukon had changed his mind as to the expression of opinion read by the leader of the opposition a few minutes ago. I have here a paper printed in Dawson one month ago, containing an interview with the governor of the Yukon, who gave his opinion at that late date upon this very question. It is very emphatic, and I will read it :
As to the Treadgold concession, I may say I favour its cancellation. I am in the same position with regard to the subject as I always have been.
And his opinion had been expressed in that strong language that was read a short time ago by the leader of the opposition.
I am satisfied that he should have no more privileges than any one else. I will not say that I favour the total cancellation of the Treadgold concession, that is, I shall not put it in that way, hut say I believe he should have no privileges that others do not have. As to what parliament is likely to do with the matter I cannot say.
If anybody could say more emphatically that he remains of the same opinion that he formerly expressed, I do not see in what words he might say it. Now I wish to refer

to a statute the Minister of Justice read, and to another statute that lie did not read. Clause 47 that was read by the minister has this provision :
Lands containing coal or other minerals, including lands in the Rocky Mountains Park, should not he subject to the provisions of this Act respecting sale or homestead entry, but the Governor General in Council may, from time to time, make regulations for the working and development of mines on such lands, and for the sale, leasing, licensing or other disposal thereof.
That is sale or other disposal of the mines. But there is a section in the Yukon Territory Act passed in 1899, which reads :
Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Governor General in Council may make ordinances for the peace, order and good government of the territory.
What statute are you reading from ?

This is the Yukon Territory Act of 1899, 62 and OH Vic., Chap. 11, section 2.
Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Governor in Council may make ordinances for the peace, order and good government of the territory, and of Her Majesty's subjects and others therein; but no ordinance made by the Governor in Council, or the Commissioner in Council shall

(c.) appropriate any public land or other property of Canada without authority of parliament.
That seems to me pretty clear and emphatic. But notwithstanding that Adt, in this Order in Council the government did grant to Mr. Treadgold and his companions the right to purchase any Crown lands required by the grantees for the purpose of their works, ait a price not exceeding $10 per acre. I think the Minister of Justice will have to admit, I do not see how he can get out of it, that this is in direct contravention of the Yukon Act which expressly provides .that the Governor in Council shall not appropriate any public lands without the authority of parliament. The hon. gentleman then went on to argue upon other clauses of the Order in Council, and lie laid some stress upon the provision that the properties of the grantee shall be exempt from representation, arguing that the reason they were exempted from the charges called * representation ' was because of the expenditures they were making, I presume, unusual expenditures. A few minutes afterwards the Minister of Justice tells us that they have been there for a year and have not spent a dollar, but under the very terms of the Order in Council they are not obliged to spend a dollar for six years; and yet during the whole of these six years they are free from the charges called representation. Surely by reason of this concession the public are excluded from these lands, while these people have practically a six years' option to use them.
What other powers can the concessionaires exercise if after six years they have forfeited the use of the water in the Klondike ?
They have first the sole right to divert and take water from the Klondike river for the purpose of generating power with which to pump water.
Suppose they lose that right ?

Does the hon. Postmaster General mean to say that the other privileges they have obtained under this Order in Council are of no value ? What about the privilege of providing water for the purposes of the public. There are two distinct powers given in this Order in Council. One enables them to provide power from the Yukon waters, and the other enables them to provide the people with water as a water company in a city might do. Is that not valuable ?	*
Is it not quite an ordinary thing to grant powers that are not terminable and yet do not exclude the granting of similar powers to others ?

It is a very unusual thing j to grant privileges to a water company without obliging them to supply water, i never
heard of such a ease.
I have no doubt there are plenty of cases.

There is not a word in the Order in Council compelling the concessionaires to supply water to anybody. They have the right to do it, but you took out the peremptory words that they must supply, and you gave the company the mere privilege of supplying water if they chose to do so.
The only water they have the right to sell is surplus water.

They have the right to sell all the water they please, that comes within what may be called their territory. What I am speaking about is a distinct thing altogether from the right to create and sell power. What does the Order in Council say about power ? The hon Postmaster General made a point of that. That provision is also in somewhat equivocal terms. It says that 1 provided ' any power is developed which the grantees do not make use of themselves it shall be offered for sale to the public. Is it likely that these people are going to generate j)ower that they have no need of, unless it is to their interest to do so ? What is there to protect the interest of the public ? The Minister of Railways and Canals told us frankly that this is a monopoly, and if so why was it necessary to say that if they created any power beyond what they needed for their own use, they should sell it. Why was it not said that they must furnish water for those who needed it, and that the government could settle what the terms would be ? The fact is, that from beginning to end this Order in Council has been drawn by a set of gentlemen who are seeking to get from the public all they possibly can without undertaking any obligation whatever in return. That is the spirit of it from first to last, and any person who reads that document will come to that conclusion. In clause 5 they are given the right to purchase Crown land, a right, I say, which the government had no power to give. All through there are rights given and no obligations stipulated for in return. They have the right, subject to no payment, except the royalty prescribed upon the output, to make entry over and work any abandoned mining claims on Bonanza.

Read the next clause.
Mr. BARKER, It says :
Such right to be exercisable only when the grantees by the construction of works in pursuance of this franchise are in a position to deliver water upon such claim or claims for the working thereof.
The hon. gentleman was proceeding to argue that although the concessionaires may lose
the rights in section 1, they would have a lot of other rights. This right in section 10 would also fall to the ground If the concessionaires lost their rights under section 1.
At the expiration of six years and not till then.
The hon. gentleman was arguing differently a moment ago.
No. I say that all these provisions are without limitation, if they are not limited by the six years.
Section 10 is dependent on section 1, which cannot be perpetual.

Does the Postmaster General think that it was right to give these concessions to the Treadgolds to subject the public of the Yukon to a concession deterring capital, and causing consternation, as this Order in Council did cause consternation ; and all because the government did not take a little trouble to care for the country's interests. Another clause gives Treadgolds the right to assign any of the rights conferred upon them to any person whatever. The whole order from first to last was given to these people, or rather prepared for them, so that they could farm it out as they pleased. They could act upon what part they pleased and sell out what they pleased, and the public of the Yukon were to be subject to them and under their domination. I do not want to take the time of the House further, but I repeat tbat I think there cannot be any question that under the Yukon Act I have referred to, there is no power at all in the government to contract that these concessionaires should have the land of the Crown at any price, or free. The Act expressly provides that there shall be no appropriation of the public lands without the authority of parliament, and yet all this dealing has been going on upon the assumption on the part of the ministers that they have the right to appropriate the public lands of the Yukon. We on this side say that they have no such right, and the Minister of Justice did not cite the Act to which I refer and which is express on that point.

What struck me in connection with this interesting and important debate is that the government are perhaps most to blame for having gone into a transaction of this sort without their evidently having any knowledge of the requirements of the country. I asked the right hon. the Prime Minister whether he had any report as to the probable cost of tlie work which is supposed to be covered by tlie Treadgold concession, and I gathered from his reply that the government had no report, and had not caused any reports to be made as to what the cost of this necessary work would be. Surely, in the case

of a private individual owning such a territory and owning valuable property rights which were to be developed to bring in revenue; surely before such a concession as this was granted a private individual would have had his own engineers and his own scientific officers to report as to the probable cost of the work proposed to be done by people asking for such a valuable franchise. I gather that the government took no steps to ascertain what the proposed work would cost. The first Order in- Council was given in June, 1901, and very shortly after that strong opposition was made to the terms of the grant. Later on another order was passed altering in some points the case in which there has been practically a case in which there has been practically a continuous opposition and not one demand from the people of that country for the confirmation of this concession; from that day to this the government apparently have taken no steps whatever to ascertain what the cost of these works would be. Now, as a rule, 1 am against the government undertaking works of this kind, but I hold that it was the first duty of the government before granting the concession, to ascertain what the cost of such work would be to the con-eesionaires. In the face of the government having no such knowledge, they gave to this company an option-because it is simply and solely an option-for six years of what may be enormously valuable privileges, and the concessionaires are not required to spend a dollar of money for six years. Naturally a body of men with a concession like that, having six years in which to make the most of it, will not be in a hurry to carry the work out or to put such a concession on the market. The market for a year past has not been a favourable one for floating a concern of this kind. The conditions may change at any time within six years, and these men may take advantage of any change in the money market. Naturally they would do so. It would be quite proper for them to do so. Having obtained the concession from this government, it would be quite proper for them, as a pure business proposition, to hold it until they could bring it out at the most favourable time to float it. Naturally they will hold it until they can unload it with the largest amount of profit to themselves. And for six years you are depriving these miners, who you say are so anxious to have water, of the possibility of getting water unless these concessionaires can see the chance in the meantime of selling what you give them at a very large profit. I think it was the first duty of the government, when they found that such a work was required, to ascertain what such a work would cost, and how far it was required to be gone on with at once, and, having done that, to have invited tenders, or let the public know that they were open and willing to receive offers for building these water flumes and de-92
veloping the water power in that country. On these two points I think the government are very seriously to blame, and have possibly committed that part of the country to a serious loss.
